# Part IV — Theorem Proving in Lean 4 {#part-4}



## Introduction {#tpil-introduction}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Introduction/

### 1.1. Computers and Theorem Proving {#tpil-computers-and-theorem-proving}

*Formal verification* involves the use of logical and computational methods to establish claims that are expressed in
precise mathematical terms. These can include ordinary mathematical theorems, as well as claims that pieces of hardware
or software, network protocols, and mechanical and hybrid systems meet their specifications. In practice, there is not a
sharp distinction between verifying a piece of mathematics and verifying the correctness of a system: formal
verification requires describing hardware and software systems in mathematical terms, at which point establishing claims
as to their correctness becomes a form of theorem proving. Conversely, the proof of a mathematical theorem may require a
lengthy computation, in which case verifying the truth of the theorem requires verifying that the computation does what
it is supposed to do.

The gold standard for supporting a mathematical claim is to provide a proof, and twentieth-century developments in logic
show most if not all conventional proof methods can be reduced to a small set of axioms and rules in any of a number of
foundational systems. With this reduction, there are two ways that a computer can help establish a claim: it can help
find a proof in the first place, and it can help verify that a purported proof is correct.

*Automated theorem proving* focuses on the “finding” aspect. Resolution theorem provers, tableau theorem provers, fast
satisfiability solvers, and so on provide means of establishing the validity of formulas in propositional and
first-order logic. Other systems provide search procedures and decision procedures for specific languages and domains,
such as linear or nonlinear expressions over the integers or the real numbers. Architectures like SMT ("satisfiability
modulo theories”) combine domain-general search methods with domain-specific procedures. Computer algebra systems and
specialized mathematical software packages provide means of carrying out mathematical computations, establishing
mathematical bounds, or finding mathematical objects. A calculation can be viewed as a proof as well, and these systems,
too, help establish mathematical claims.

Automated reasoning systems strive for power and efficiency, often at the expense of guaranteed soundness. Such systems
can have bugs, and it can be difficult to ensure that the results they deliver are correct. In contrast, *interactive
theorem proving* focuses on the “verification” aspect of theorem proving, requiring that every claim is supported by a
proof in a suitable axiomatic foundation. This sets a very high standard: every rule of inference and every step of a
calculation has to be justified by appealing to prior definitions and theorems, all the way down to basic axioms and
rules. In fact, most such systems provide fully elaborated “proof objects” that can be communicated to other systems and
checked independently. Constructing such proofs typically requires much more input and interaction from users, but it
allows you to obtain deeper and more complex proofs.

The *Lean Theorem Prover* aims to bridge the gap between interactive and automated theorem proving, by situating
automated tools and methods in a framework that supports user interaction and the construction of fully specified
axiomatic proofs. The goal is to support both mathematical reasoning and reasoning about complex systems, and to verify
claims in both domains.

Lean's underlying logic has a computational interpretation, and Lean can be viewed equally well as a programming
language. More to the point, it can be viewed as a system for writing programs with a precise semantics, as well as
reasoning about the functions that the programs compute. Lean also has mechanisms to serve as its own *metaprogramming
language*, which means that you can implement automation and extend the functionality of Lean using Lean itself. These
aspects of Lean are described in the free online book, [Functional Programming in Lean](https://lean-lang.org/functional_programming_in_lean/), though computational
aspects of the system will make an appearance here.

### 1.2. About Lean {#tpil-about-lean}

The *Lean* project was launched by Leonardo de Moura at Microsoft Research Redmond in 2013. It is an ongoing, long-term
effort, and much of the potential for automation will be realized only gradually over time. Lean is released under the
[Apache 2.0 license](https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/master/LICENSE), a permissive open source license that permits others to use and extend the code and
mathematical libraries freely.

To install Lean in your computer consider using the [Quickstart](https://lean-lang.org/install/) instructions. The Lean source code, and instructions for building Lean, are available at
[https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/](https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/).

This tutorial describes the current version of Lean, known as Lean 4.

### 1.3. About this Book {#tpil-about-this-book}

This book is designed to teach you to develop and verify proofs in Lean. Much of the background information you will
need in order to do this is not specific to Lean at all. To start with, you will learn the logical system that Lean is
based on, a version of *dependent type theory* that is powerful enough to prove almost any conventional mathematical
theorem, and expressive enough to do it in a natural way. More specifically, Lean is based on a version of a system
known as the Calculus of Constructions with inductive types. Lean can not only define mathematical objects and express
mathematical assertions in dependent type theory, but it also can be used as a language for writing proofs.

Because fully detailed axiomatic proofs are so complicated, the challenge of theorem proving is to have the computer
fill in as many of the details as possible. You will learn various methods to support this in [dependent type
theory](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Dependent-Type-Theory/#dependent-type-theory). For example, term rewriting, and Lean's automated methods for simplifying terms and
expressions automatically. Similarly, methods of *elaboration* and *type inference*, which can be used to support
flexible forms of algebraic reasoning.

Finally, you will learn about features that are specific to Lean, including the language you use to communicate
with the system, and the mechanisms Lean offers for managing complex theories and data.

Throughout the text you will find examples of Lean code like the one below:

```lean
theorem and_commutative (p q : Prop) : p ∧ q → q ∧ p :=
fun hpq : p ∧ q =>
have hp : p := [And.left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) hpq
have hq : q := [And.right](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) hpq
show q ∧ p from [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) hq hp
```

```lean

```

Pressing the button copies the example with enough surrounding context to make the code compile correctly.
You can paste the example code into [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) and modify the examples, and Lean will check the results and provide feedback continuously as you type.
We recommend running the examples and experimenting with the code on your own as you work through the chapters that follow.
You can open this book in VS Code by using the command “Lean 4: Docs: Show Documentation Resources” and selecting “Theorem Proving in Lean 4” in the tab that opens.

## Dependent Type Theory {#tpil-dependent-type-theory}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Dependent-Type-Theory/

Dependent type theory is a powerful and expressive language, allowing
you to express complex mathematical assertions, write complex hardware
and software specifications, and reason about both of these in a
natural and uniform way. Lean is based on a version of dependent type
theory known as the *Calculus of Constructions*, with a countable
hierarchy of non-cumulative universes and inductive types. By the end
of this chapter, you will understand much of what this means.

### 2.1. Simple Type Theory {#tpil-simple-type-theory}

“Type theory” gets its name from the fact that every expression has an
associated *type*. For example, in a given context, `x + 0` may
denote a natural number and `f` may denote a function on the natural
numbers. For those who like precise definitions, a Lean natural number
is an arbitrary-precision unsigned integer.

Here are some examples of how you can declare objects in Lean and
check their types.

```lean
/- Define some constants. -/
def m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 1 -- m is a natural number
```

```lean
def n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 0
```

```lean
def b1 : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) -- b1 is a Boolean
```

```lean
def b2 : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
/- Check their types. -/
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [m]](#tpil-m)
```

```lean
[m]](#tpil-m) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [n]](#tpil-m)
```

```lean

```

```lean

```

Any text between `/-` and `-/` constitutes a comment block that is
ignored by Lean. Similarly, two dashes `--` indicate that the rest of
the line contains a comment that is also ignored. Comment blocks can
be nested, making it possible to “comment out” chunks of code, just as
in many programming languages.

The `def` keyword declares new constant symbols into the
working environment. In the example above, `def m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 1`
defines a new constant `m` of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` whose value is `1`.
The `#check` command asks Lean to report their
types; in Lean, auxiliary commands that query the system for
information typically begin with the hash (#) symbol.
The `#eval` command asks Lean to evaluate the given expression.
You should try
declaring some constants and type checking some expressions on your
own. Declaring new objects in this manner is a good way to experiment
with the system.

What makes simple type theory powerful is that you can build new types
out of others. For example, if `a` and `b` are types, `a -> b`
denotes the type of functions from `a` to `b`, and `a × b`
denotes the type of pairs consisting of an element of `a` paired
with an element of `b`, also known as the *Cartesian product*. Note
that `×` is a Unicode symbol. The judicious use of Unicode improves
legibility, and all modern editors have great support for it. In the
Lean standard library, you often see Greek letters to denote types,
and the Unicode symbol `→` as a more compact version of `->`.

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) -- type the arrow as “\to” or "\r"
```

Once again, you should try some examples on your own.

Let's take a look at some basic syntax. You can enter the Unicode
arrow `→` by typing `\to` or `\r` or `\->`. You can also use the
ASCII alternative `->`, so the expressions `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) -> [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`
mean the same thing. Both expressions denote the type of
functions that take a natural number as input and return a natural
number as output. The Unicode symbol `×` for the Cartesian product
is entered as `\times`. You will generally use lower-case Greek
letters like `α`, `β`, and `γ` to range over types. You can
enter these particular ones with `\a`, `\b`, and `\g`.

There are a few more things to notice here. First, the application of
a function `f` to a value `x` is denoted `f x` (e.g., `[Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) 2`).
Second, when writing type expressions, arrows associate to the *right*; for
example, the type of `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)` is `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` which is equivalent
to `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))`. Thus you can
view `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)` as a function that takes a natural number and returns
another function that takes a natural number and returns a natural
number. In type theory, this is generally more convenient than
writing `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)` as a function that takes a pair of natural numbers as
input and returns a natural number as output. For example, it allows
you to “partially apply” the function `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)`. The example above shows
that `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) 3` has type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, that is, `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) 3` returns a
function that “waits” for a second argument, `n`, which is then
equivalent to writing `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) 3 n`.

You have seen that if you have `m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, then
`(m, n)` denotes the ordered pair of `m` and `n` which is of
type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`. This gives you a way of creating pairs of natural
numbers. Conversely, if you have `p : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, then you can write
`p.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `p.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`. This gives you a way of extracting
its two components.

### 2.2. Types as objects {#tpil-types-as-objects}

One way in which Lean's dependent type theory extends simple type
theory is that types themselves—entities like `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`—are first-class citizens, which is to say that they themselves are
objects. For that to be the case, each of them also has to have a
type.

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Given that every expression in Lean has a type, it is natural to ask:
what type does `Type` itself have?

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Type
```

```lean
Type : Type 1
```

```lean

```

You have actually come up against one of the most subtle aspects of
Lean's typing system. Lean's underlying foundation has an infinite
hierarchy of types:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Type
```

```lean
Type : Type 1
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Type 1
```

```lean
Type 1 : Type 2
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Type 2
```

```lean
Type 2 : Type 3
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Type 3
```

```lean
Type 3 : Type 4
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Type 4
```

```lean
Type 4 : Type 5
```

```lean

```

Think of `Type 0` as a universe of “small” or “ordinary” types.
`Type 1` is then a larger universe of types, which contains `Type 0`
as an element, and `Type 2` is an even larger universe of types,
which contains `Type 1` as an element. The list is infinite:
there is a `Type n` for every natural number `n`. `Type` is
an abbreviation for `Type 0`:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Type
```

```lean
Type : Type 1
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Type 0
```

```lean
Type : Type 1
```

```lean

```

The following table may help concretize the relationships being discussed.
Movement along the x-axis represents a change in the universe, while movement
along the y-axis represents a change in what is sometimes referred to as
“degree”.

| sort | `Prop` (`Sort 0`) | `Type` (`Sort 1`) | `Type 1` (`Sort 2`) | `Type 2` (`Sort 3`) | ... |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| type | `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` | `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` | `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) -> Type` | `Type -> Type 1` | ... |
| term | `[True.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)` | `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` | `fun n => [Fin](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Finite-Natural-Numbers/#Fin___mk) n` | `fun (_ : Type) => Type` | ... |

Some operations, however, need to be *polymorphic* over type
universes. For example, `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α` should make sense for any type
`α`, no matter which type universe `α` lives in. This explains the
type signature of the function `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) List
```

```lean
[List.{u}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) (α : Type u) : Type u
```

```lean

```

Here `u` is a variable ranging over type levels. The output of the
`#check` command means that whenever `α` has type `Type u`,
`[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α` also has type `Type u`. The function `[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)` is
similarly polymorphic:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Prod
```

```lean
[Prod.{u, v}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) (α : Type u) (β : Type v) : Type (max u v)
```

```lean

```

To define polymorphic constants, Lean allows you to
declare universe variables explicitly using the `universe` command:

```lean
[universe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Universes/#Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u
```

```lean
def F (α : Type u) : Type u := [Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) α α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) F
```

```lean
F.{u} (α : Type u) : Type u
```

```lean

```

You can avoid the `universe` command by providing the universe parameters when defining `F`:

```lean
def F.{u} (α : Type u) : Type u := [Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) α α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) F
```

```lean
F.{u} (α : Type u) : Type u
```

```lean

```

### 2.3. Function Abstraction and Evaluation {#tpil-function-abstraction-and-evaluation}

Lean provides a `fun` (or `λ`) keyword to create a function
from an expression as follows:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) => x + 5
```

```lean
fun x => x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
-- λ and fun mean the same thing
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) λ (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) => x + 5
```

```lean
fun x => x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

The type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` can be inferred in this example:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun x => x + 5
```

```lean
fun x => x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) λ x => x + 5
```

```lean
fun x => x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 5 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

You can evaluate a lambda function by passing the required parameters:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (λ x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => x + 5) 10
```

```lean
15
```

```lean

```

Creating a function from another expression is a process known as
*lambda abstraction*. Suppose you have the variable `x : α` and you can
construct an expression `t : β`, then the expression `fun (x : α) => t`,
or, equivalently, `λ (x : α) => t`, is an object of type `α → β`. Think of
this as the function from `α` to `β` which maps
any value `x` to the value `t`.

Here are some more examples

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => fun y : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x + 1 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x + 2
```

```lean
fun x y => if [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)y[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) then x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 else x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (y : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) => [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x + 1 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x + 2
```

```lean
fun x y => if [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)y[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) then x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 else x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun x y => [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x + 1 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x + 2
```

```lean
fun x y => if [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)y[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) then x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 else x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

Lean interprets the final three examples as the same expression; in
the last expression, Lean infers the type of `x` and `y` from the
expression `[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x + 1 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x + 2`.

Some mathematically common examples of operations of functions can be
described in terms of lambda abstraction:

```lean
def f (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := toString n
```

```lean
def g (s : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := s.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___length) > 0
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => x
```

```lean
fun x => x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
fun x => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => g (f x)
```

```lean
fun x => g (f x) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun x => g (f x)
```

```lean
fun x => g (f x) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean

```

Think about what these expressions mean. The expression
`fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => x` denotes the identity function on `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, the
expression `fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` denotes the constant function that
always returns `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, and `fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => g (f x)` denotes the
composition of `f` and `g`. You can, in general, leave off the
type annotation and let Lean infer it for you. So, for example, you
can write `fun x => g (f x)` instead of `fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => g (f x)`.

You can pass functions as parameters and by giving them names `f`
and `g` you can then use those functions in the implementation:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun (g : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) => g (f x)
```

```lean
fun g f x => g (f x) : ([String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) → ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean

```

You can also pass types as parameters:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun (α β γ : Type) (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (x : α) => g (f x)
```

```lean
fun α β γ g f x => g (f x) : (α β γ : Type) → (β → γ) → (α → β) → α → γ
```

```lean

```

The last expression, for example, denotes the function that takes
three types, `α`, `β`, and `γ`, and two functions, `g : β → γ`
and `f : α → β`, and returns the composition of `g` and `f`.
(Making sense of the type of this function requires an understanding
of *dependent products*, which will be explained below.)

The general form of a lambda expression is `fun (x : α) => t`, where
the variable `x` is a “bound variable”: it is really a placeholder,
whose “scope” does not extend beyond the expression `t`. For
example, the variable `b` in the expression `fun (b : β) (x : α) => b`
has nothing to do with the constant `b` declared earlier. In fact,
the expression denotes the same function as `fun (u : β) (z : α) => u`.

Formally, expressions that are the same up to a renaming of bound
variables are called *alpha equivalent*, and are considered “the
same.” Lean recognizes this equivalence.

Notice that applying a term `t : α → β` to a term `s : α` yields
an expression `t s : β`. Returning to the previous example and
renaming bound variables for clarity, notice the types of the
following expressions:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) (fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => x) 1
```

```lean
(fun x => x) 1 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) (fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) 1
```

```lean
(fun x => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) 1 : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean

```

```lean
def f (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) := toString n
```

```lean
def g (s : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) := s.[length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___length) > 0
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check)
(fun (α β γ : Type) (u : β → γ) (v : α → β) (x : α) => u (v x)) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) g f 0
```

```lean
(fun α β γ u v x => u (v x)) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) g f 0 : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean

```

As expected, the expression `(fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => x) 1` has type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
In fact, more should be true: applying the expression `(fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => x)` to
`1` should “return” the value `1`. And, indeed, it does:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => x) 1
```

```lean
1
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) 1
```

```lean
true
```

```lean

```

You will see later how these terms are evaluated. For now, notice that
this is an important feature of dependent type theory: every term has
a computational behavior, and supports a notion of *normalization*. In
principle, two terms that reduce to the same value are called
*definitionally equal*. They are considered “the same” by Lean's type
checker, and Lean does its best to recognize and support these
identifications.

Lean is a complete programming language. It has a compiler that
generates a binary executable and an interactive interpreter. You can
use the command `#eval` to execute expressions, and it is the
preferred way of testing your functions.

### 2.4. Definitions {#tpil-definitions}

Recall that the `def` keyword provides one important way of declaring new named
objects.

```lean
def double (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
x + x
```

```lean

```

This might look more familiar to you if you know how functions work in
other programming languages. The name `double` is defined as a
function that takes an input parameter `x` of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, where the
result of the call is `x + x`, so it is returning type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`. You
can then invoke this function using:

```lean
def double (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
x + x
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) double 3
```

```lean
6
```

```lean

```

In this case you can think of `def` as a kind of named `fun`.
The following yields the same result:

```lean
def double : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
fun x => x + x
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) double 3
```

```lean
6
```

```lean

```

You can omit the type declarations when Lean has enough information to
infer it. Type inference is an important part of Lean:

```lean
def double :=
fun (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) => x + x
```

```lean

```

The general form of a definition is `def foo : α := bar` where
`α` is the type returned from the expression `bar`. Lean can
usually infer the type `α`, but it is often a good idea to write it
explicitly. This clarifies your intention, and Lean will flag an
error if the right-hand side of the definition does not have a matching
type.

The right hand side `bar` can be any expression, not just a lambda.
So `def` can also be used to simply name a value like this:

```lean
def pi := 3.141592654
```

```lean

```

`def` can take multiple input parameters. Let's create one
that adds two natural numbers:

```lean
def add (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
x + y
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) add 3 2
```

```lean
5
```

```lean

```

The parameter list can be separated like this:

```lean
def double (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
x + x
```

```lean
def add (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
x + y
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) add (double 3) (7 + 9)
```

```lean
22
```

```lean

```

Notice here we called the `double` function to create the first
parameter to `add`.

You can use other more interesting expressions inside a `def`:

```lean
def greater (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x > y [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) y
```

```lean

```

You can probably guess what this one will do.

You can also define a function that takes another function as input.
The following calls a given function twice passing the output of the
first invocation to the second:

```lean
def double (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
x + x
```

```lean
def doTwice (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
f (f x)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) doTwice double 2
```

```lean
8
```

```lean

```

Now to get a bit more abstract, you can also specify arguments that
are like type parameters:

```lean
def compose (α β γ : Type) (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (x : α) : γ :=
g (f x)
```

```lean

```

This means `compose` is a function that takes any two functions as input
arguments, so long as those functions each take only one input.
The type algebra `β → γ` and `α → β` means it is a requirement
that the type of the output of the second function must match the
type of the input to the first function—which makes sense, otherwise
the two functions would not be composable.

`compose` also takes a 3rd argument of type `α` which
it uses to invoke the second function (locally named `f`) and it
passes the result of that function (which is type `β`) as input to the
first function (locally named `g`). The first function returns a type
`γ` so that is also the return type of the `compose` function.

`compose` is also very general in that it works over any type
`α β γ`. This means `compose` can compose just about any 2 functions
so long as they each take one parameter, and so long as the type of
output of the second matches the input of the first. For example:

```lean
def compose (α β γ : Type) (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (x : α) : γ :=
g (f x)
def double (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
x + x
```

```lean
def square (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
x * x
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) compose [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) double square 3
```

```lean
18
```

```lean

```

While Lean fundamentally considers a defined name to be the same as its unfolding, not all names are unfolded in all contexts.
Take this example that defines `[Natural]](#tpil-Natural)` as an alternative name for `Nat`:

```lean
def Natural := Nat
```

```lean

```

```lean
def Natural := Nat
```

```lean
def five : [Natural]](#tpil-Natural) := 5
```

```lean
failed to synthesize instance of type class
  [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Natural]](#tpil-Natural) 5
numerals are polymorphic in Lean, but the numeral `5` cannot be used in a context where the expected type is
  [Natural]](#tpil-Natural)
due to the absence of the instance above

Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
```

```lean

```

When a name is defined using `def`, it is called *semireducible*: Lean will unfold it when absolutely necessary to establish that two terms are definitionally equal, but most automated features will leave references to the defined name untouched.

### 2.5. Local Definitions {#tpil-local-definitions}

Lean also allows you to introduce “local” definitions using the
`let` keyword. The expression `let a := t1; t2` is
definitionally equal to the result of replacing every occurrence of
`a` in `t2` by `t1`.

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) let y := 2 + 2; y * y
```

```lean
let y := 2 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2;
y [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) let y := 2 + 2; y * y
```

```lean
16
```

```lean

```

```lean
def twice_double (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
let y := x + x; y * y
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [twice_double]](#tpil-twice_double) 2
```

```lean
16
```

```lean

```

Here, `[twice_double]](#tpil-twice_double) x` is definitionally equal to the term `(x + x) * (x + x)`.

You can combine multiple assignments by chaining `let` statements:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) let y := 2 + 2; let z := y + y; z * z
```

```lean
let y := 2 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2;
let z := y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y;
z [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) z : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) let y := 2 + 2; let z := y + y; z * z
```

```lean
64
```

```lean

```

The `;` can be omitted when a line break is used.

```lean
def t (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
let y := x + x
y * y
```

```lean

```

Notice that the meaning of the expression `let a := t1; t2` is very
similar to the meaning of `(fun a => t2) t1`, but the two are not
the same. In the first expression, you should think of every instance
of `a` in `t2` as a syntactic abbreviation for `t1`. In the
second expression, `a` is a variable, and the expression
`fun a => t2` has to make sense independently of the value of `a`.
The `let` construct is a stronger means of abbreviation, and there
are expressions of the form `let a := t1; t2` that cannot be
expressed as `(fun a => t2) t1`. As an exercise, try to understand
why the definition of `foo` below type checks, but the definition of
`bar` does not.

```lean
def foo := let a := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero); fun x : a => x + 2
```

```lean
/-
def bar := (fun a => fun x : a => x + 2) Nat
-/
```

### 2.6. Variables and Sections {#tpil-variables-and-sections}

Consider the following three function definitions:

```lean
def compose (α β γ : Type) (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (x : α) : γ :=
g (f x)
```

```lean
def doTwice (α : Type) (h : α → α) (x : α) : α :=
h (h x)
```

```lean
def doThrice (α : Type) (h : α → α) (x : α) : α :=
h (h (h x))
```

```lean

```

Lean provides you with the `variable` command to make such
declarations look more compact:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α β γ : Type)
```

```lean
def compose (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (x : α) : γ :=
g (f x)
```

```lean
def doTwice (h : α → α) (x : α) : α :=
h (h x)
```

```lean
def doThrice (h : α → α) (x : α) : α :=
h (h (h x))
```

```lean

```

You can declare variables of any type, not just `Type` itself:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α β γ : Type)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (h : α → α)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (x : α)
```

```lean
def compose := g (f x)
```

```lean
def doTwice := h (h x)
```

```lean
def doThrice := h (h (h x))
```

```lean
#print compose
```

```lean
def compose : (α β γ : Type) → (β → γ) → (α → β) → α → γ :=
fun α β γ g f x => g (f x)
```

```lean
#print doTwice
```

```lean
def doTwice : (α : Type) → (α → α) → α → α :=
fun α h x => h (h x)
```

```lean
#print doThrice
```

```lean
def doThrice : (α : Type) → (α → α) → α → α :=
fun α h x => h (h (h x))
```

```lean

```

Printing them out shows that all three groups of definitions have
exactly the same effect.

The `variable` command instructs Lean to insert the declared
variables as bound variables in definitions that refer to them by
name. Lean is smart enough to figure out which variables are used
explicitly or implicitly in a definition. You can therefore proceed as
though `α`, `β`, `γ`, `g`, `f`, `h`, and `x` are fixed
objects when you write your definitions, and let Lean abstract the
definitions for you automatically.

When declared in this way, a variable stays in scope until the end of
the file you are working on. Sometimes, however, it is useful to limit
the scope of a variable. For that purpose, Lean provides the notion of
a `section`:

```lean
[section](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___section) useful
```

```lean
 [variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α β γ : Type)
```

```lean
 [variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (h : α → α)
```

```lean
 [variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (x : α)
```

```lean
 def compose := g (f x)
```

```lean
 def doTwice := h (h x)
```

```lean
 def doThrice := h (h (h x))
```

```lean
end useful
```

```lean

```

When the section is closed, the variables go out of scope, and cannot
be referenced any more.

You do not have to indent the lines within a section. Nor do you have
to name a section, which is to say, you can use an anonymous
`section` / `end` pair. If you do name a section, however, you
have to close it using the same name. Sections can also be nested,
which allows you to declare new variables incrementally.

### 2.7. Namespaces {#tpil-namespaces}

Lean provides you with the ability to group definitions into nested,
hierarchical *namespaces*:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Foo
```

```lean
 def a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 5
```

```lean
 def f (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := x + 7
```

```lean
 def fa : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := f a
```

```lean
 def ffa : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := f (f a)
```

```lean
 [#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) a
```

```lean
Foo.a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
 [#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) f
```

```lean
Foo.f (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
 [#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fa
```

```lean
Foo.fa : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
 [#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) ffa
```

```lean
Foo.ffa : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
 [#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Foo.fa
```

```lean
Foo.fa : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
end Foo
```

```lean
-- #check a -- error
-- #check f -- error
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Foo.a
```

```lean
Foo.a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Foo.f
```

```lean
Foo.f (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Foo.fa
```

```lean
Foo.fa : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Foo.ffa
```

```lean
Foo.ffa : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Foo
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) a
```

```lean
Foo.a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) f
```

```lean
Foo.f (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fa
```

```lean
Foo.fa : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Foo.fa
```

```lean
Foo.fa : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

When you declare that you are working in the namespace `Foo`, every
identifier you declare has a full name with prefix “`Foo.`”. Within
the namespace, you can refer to identifiers by their shorter names,
but once you end the namespace, you have to use the longer names.
Unlike `section`, namespaces require a name. There is only one
anonymous namespace at the root level.

The `[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open)` command brings the shorter names into the current
context. Often, when you import a module, you will want to open one or
more of the namespaces it contains, to have access to the short
identifiers. But sometimes you will want to leave this information
protected by a fully qualified name, for example, when they conflict
with identifiers in another namespace you want to use. Thus namespaces
give you a way to manage names in your working environment.

For example, Lean groups definitions and theorems involving lists into
a namespace `List`.

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[List.nil.{u}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) {α : Type u} : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[List.cons.{u}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) {α : Type u} (head : α) (tail : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) List.map
```

```lean
[List.map.{u_1, u_2}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) {α : Type u_1} {β : Type u_2} (f : α → β) (l : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β
```

```lean

```

The command `[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) List` allows you to use the shorter names:

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) List
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[List.nil.{u}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) {α : Type u} : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```


Like sections, nested namespaces have to be closed in the order they
are opened. Namespaces and sections serve different purposes:
namespaces organize data and sections declare variables for insertion
in definitions. Sections are also useful for delimiting the scope of
commands such as `set_option` and `open`.

In many respects, however, a `namespace`` ... ``end` block behaves the
same as a `section`` ... ``end` block. In particular, if you use the
`variable` command within a namespace, its scope is limited to the
namespace. Similarly, if you use an `open` command within a
namespace, its effects disappear when the namespace is closed.

### 2.8. What makes dependent type theory dependent? {#tpil-what-makes-dependent-type-theory-dependent}

The short explanation is that types can depend on parameters. You
have already seen a nice example of this: the type `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α` depends
on the argument `α`, and this dependence is what distinguishes
`[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`. For another example, consider the
type `Vector α n`, the type of vectors of elements of `α` of
length `n`. This type depends on *two* parameters: the type of the
elements in the vector (`α : Type`) and the length of the vector
`n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.

Suppose you wish to write a function `cons` which inserts a new
element at the head of a list. What type should `cons` have? Such a
function is *polymorphic*: you expect the `cons` function for
`[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, or an arbitrary type `α` to behave the same way.
So it makes sense to take the type to be the first argument to
`cons`, so that for any type, `α`, `[cons]](#tpil-cons) α` is the insertion
function for lists of type `α`. In other words, for every `α`,
`[cons]](#tpil-cons) α` is the function that takes an element `a : α` and a list
`as : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`, and returns a new list, so you have `[cons]](#tpil-cons) α a as : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`.

It is clear that `[cons]](#tpil-cons) α` should have type `α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`.
But what type should `[cons]](#tpil-cons)` have? A first guess might be
`Type → α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`, but, on reflection, this does not make
sense: the `α` in this expression does not refer to anything,
whereas it should refer to the argument of type `Type`. In other
words, *assuming* `α : Type` is the first argument to the function,
the type of the next two elements are `α` and `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`. These
types vary depending on the first argument, `α`.

```lean
def cons (α : Type) (a : α) (as : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α :=
[List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) a as
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [cons]](#tpil-cons) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[cons]](#tpil-cons) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [cons]](#tpil-cons) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
[cons]](#tpil-cons) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) cons
```

```lean
[cons]](#tpil-cons) (α : Type) (a : α) (as : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
```

```lean

```

This is an instance of a *dependent function type*, or **dependent
arrow type**. Given `α : Type` and `β : α → Type`, think of `β`
as a family of types over `α`, that is, a type `β a` for each
`a : α`. In that case, the type `(a : α) → β a` denotes the type
of functions `f` with the property that, for each `a : α`, `f a`
is an element of `β a`. In other words, the type of the value
returned by `f` depends on its input.

Notice that `(a : α) → β` makes sense for any expression `β : Type`.
When the value of `β` depends on `a` (as does, for
example, the expression `β a` in the previous paragraph),
`(a : α) → β` denotes a dependent function type. When `β` doesn't
depend on `a`, `(a : α) → β` is no different from the type
`α → β`. Indeed, in dependent type theory (and in Lean), `α → β`
is just notation for `(a : α) → β` when `β` does not depend on `a`.

Returning to the example of lists, you can use the command `#check` to
inspect the type of the following `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` functions. The `@` symbol
and the difference between the round and curly braces will be
explained momentarily.

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) : {α : Type u_1} → α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) : {α : Type u_1} → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[List.length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length)[List.length](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___length) : {α : Type u_1} → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @List.append
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___append)[List.append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___append) : {α : Type u_1} → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
```

```lean

```

Just as dependent function types `(a : α) → β a` generalize the
notion of a function type `α → β` by allowing `β` to depend on
`a`, dependent Cartesian product types `(a : α) × β a` generalize
the Cartesian product `α × β` in the same way. Dependent products
are also called *sigma* types, and you can also write them as
`Σ a : α, β a`. You can use `⟨a, b⟩` or `[Sigma.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Sigma___mk) a b` to create a
dependent pair. The `⟨` and `⟩` characters may be typed with
`\langle` and `\rangle` or `\<` and `\>`, respectively.

```lean
[universe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Universes/#Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u v
```

```lean
def f (α : Type u) (β : α → Type v) (a : α) (b : β a) : (a : α) × β a :=
⟨a, b⟩
```

```lean
def g (α : Type u) (β : α → Type v) (a : α) (b : β a) : Σ a : α, β a :=
[Sigma.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Sigma___mk) a b
```

```lean
def h1 (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
(f Type (fun α => α) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) x).[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Sigma___mk)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [h1]](#tpil-f-next-next) 5
```

```lean
5
```

```lean

```

```lean
def h2 (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
(g Type (fun α => α) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) x).[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Sigma___mk)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [h2]](#tpil-f-next-next) 5
```

```lean
5
```

```lean

```

The functions `f` and `g` above denote the same function.

### 2.9. Implicit Arguments {#tpil-implicit-arguments}

Suppose we have an implementation of lists as:

```lean
[universe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Universes/#Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u
def Lst (α : Type u) : Type u := [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
def Lst.cons (α : Type u) (a : α) (as : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α) : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α := [List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) a as
def Lst.nil (α : Type u) : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α := [List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
def Lst.append (α : Type u) (as bs : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α) : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α := [List.append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___append) as bs
```

```lean

def Lst.cons (α : Type u) (a : α) (as : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α) : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α := [List.cons](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) a as
def Lst.nil (α : Type u) : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α := [List.nil](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
def Lst.append (α : Type u) (as bs : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α) : [Lst]](#tpil-Lst) α := [List.append](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___append) as bs
```
