## Quantifiers and Equality {#tpil-quantifiers-and-equality}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Quantifiers-and-Equality/

The last chapter introduced you to methods that construct proofs of
statements involving the propositional connectives. In this chapter,
we extend the repertoire of logical constructions to include the
universal and existential quantifiers, and the equality relation.

### 4.1. The Universal Quantifier {#tpil-the-universal-quantifier}

Notice that if `α` is any type, we can represent a unary predicate
`p` on `α` as an object of type `α → Prop`. In that case, given
`x : α`, `p x` denotes the assertion that `p` holds of
`x`. Similarly, an object `r : α → α → Prop` denotes a binary
relation on `α`: given `x y : α`, `r x y` denotes the assertion
that `x` is related to `y`.

The universal quantifier, `∀ x : α, p x` is supposed to denote the
assertion that “for every `x : α`, `p x`” holds. As with the
propositional connectives, in systems of natural deduction, “forall”
is governed by an introduction and elimination rule. Informally, the
introduction rule states:

> Given a proof of `p x`, in a context where `x : α` is arbitrary, we obtain a proof `∀ x : α, p x`.

The elimination rule states:

> Given a proof `∀ x : α, p x` and any term `t : α`, we obtain a proof of `p t`.

As was the case for implication, the propositions-as-types
interpretation now comes into play. Remember the introduction and
elimination rules for dependent arrow types:

> Given a term `t` of type `β x`, in a context where `x : α` is arbitrary, we have `(fun x : α => t) : (x : α) → β x`.

The elimination rule states:

> Given a term `s : (x : α) → β x` and any term `t : α`, we have `s t : β t`.

In the case where `p x` has type `Prop`, if we replace
`(x : α) → β x` with `∀ x : α, p x`, we can read these as the correct rules
for building proofs involving the universal quantifier.

The Calculus of Constructions therefore identifies dependent arrow
types with forall-expressions in this way. If `p` is any expression,
`∀ x : α, p` is nothing more than alternative notation for
`(x : α) → p`, with the idea that the former is more natural than the latter
in cases where `p` is a proposition. Typically, the expression `p`
will depend on `x : α`. Recall that, in the case of ordinary
function spaces, we could interpret `α → β` as the special case of
`(x : α) → β` in which `β` does not depend on `x`. Similarly, we
can think of an implication `p → q` between propositions as the
special case of `∀ x : p, q` in which the expression `q` does not
depend on `x`.

Here is an example of how the [propositions-as-types]](#tpil---tech-term-propositions-as-types) correspondence gets put into practice.

```lean
example (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop) :
(∀ x : α, p x ∧ q x) → ∀ y : α, p y :=
fun h : ∀ x : α, p x ∧ q x =>
fun y : α =>
show p y from (h y).left
```

```lean

```

As a notational convention, we give the universal quantifier the
widest scope possible, so parentheses are needed to limit the
quantifier over `x` to the hypothesis in the example above. The
canonical way to prove `∀ y : α, p y` is to take an arbitrary `y`,
and prove `p y`. This is the introduction rule. Now, given that
`h` has type `∀ x : α, p x ∧ q x`, the expression `h y` has type
`p`` ``y`` ∧ ``q`` ``y`. This is the elimination rule. Taking the left conjunct
gives the desired conclusion, `p y`.

Remember that expressions which differ up to renaming of bound
variables are considered to be equivalent. So, for example, we could
have used the same variable, `x`, in both the hypothesis and
conclusion, and instantiated it by a different variable, `z`, in the
proof:

```lean
example (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop) :
(∀ x : α, p x ∧ q x) → ∀ x : α, p x :=
fun h : ∀ x : α, p x ∧ q x =>
fun z : α =>
show p z from [And.left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) (h z)
```

```lean

```

As another example, here is how we can express the fact that a relation, `r`, is transitive:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (r : α → α → Prop)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (trans_r : ∀ x y z, r x y → r y z → r x z)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b c : α)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (hab : r a b) (hbc : r b c)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) trans_r
```

```lean
trans_r : ∀ (x y z : α), r x y → r y z → r x z
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) trans_r a b c
```

```lean
trans_r a b c : r a b → r b c → r a c
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) trans_r a b c hab
```

```lean
trans_r a b c hab : r b c → r a c
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) trans_r a b c hab hbc
```

```lean
trans_r a b c hab hbc : r a c
```

```lean

```

Think about what is going on here. When we instantiate `trans_r` at
the values `a b c`, we end up with a proof of `r`` ``a b`` → ``r`` ``b c`` → ``r`` ``a`` ``c`.
Applying this to the “hypothesis” `hab : r a b`, we get a proof
of the implication `r`` ``b c`` → ``r`` ``a`` ``c`. Finally, applying it to the
hypothesis `hbc` yields a proof of the conclusion `r`` ``a`` ``c`.

In situations like this, it can be tedious to supply the arguments
`a b c`, when they can be inferred from `hab hbc`. For that reason, it
is common to make these arguments implicit:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (r : α → α → Prop)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (trans_r : ∀ {x y z}, r x y → r y z → r x z)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b c : α)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (hab : r a b) (hbc : r b c)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) trans_r
```

```lean
trans_r : r ?m.4 ?m.5 → r ?m.5 ?m.6 → r ?m.4 ?m.6
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) trans_r hab
```

```lean
trans_r hab : r b ?m.6 → r a ?m.6
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) trans_r hab hbc
```

```lean
trans_r hab hbc : r a c
```

```lean

```

The advantage is that we can simply write `trans_r hab hbc` as a
proof of `r`` ``a`` ``c`. A disadvantage is that Lean does not have enough
information to infer the types of the arguments in the expressions
`trans_r` and `trans_r hab`. The output of the first `#check`
command is `r ?m.1 ?m.2 → r ?m.2 ?m.3 → r ?m.1 ?m.3`, indicating
that the implicit arguments are unspecified in this case.

Here is an example of how we can carry out elementary reasoning with an equivalence relation:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (r : α → α → Prop)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (refl_r : ∀ x, r x x)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (symm_r : ∀ {x y}, r x y → r y x)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (trans_r : ∀ {x y z}, r x y → r y z → r x z)
```

```lean
example (a b c d : α) (hab : r a b) (hcb : r c b) (hcd : r c d) : r a d :=
trans_r (trans_r hab (symm_r hcb)) hcd
```

```lean

```

To get used to using universal quantifiers, you should try some of the
exercises at the end of this section.

It is the typing rule for dependent arrow types, and the universal
quantifier in particular, that distinguishes `Prop` from other
types. Suppose we have `α : Sort i` and `β : Sort j`, where the
expression `β` may depend on a variable `x : α`. Then
`(x : α) → β` is an element of `Sort (imax i j)`, where `imax i j` is the
maximum of `i` and `j` if `j` is not `0`, and `0` otherwise.

The idea is as follows. If `j` is not `0`, then `(x : α) → β` is
an element of `Sort (max i j)`. In other words, the type of
dependent functions from `α` to `β` “lives” in the universe whose
index is the maximum of `i` and `j`. Suppose, however, that `β`
is of `Sort 0`, that is, an element of `Prop`. In that case,
`(x : α) → β` is an element of `Sort 0` as well, no matter which
type universe `α` lives in. In other words, if `β` is a
proposition depending on `α`, then `∀ x : α, β` is again a
proposition. This reflects the interpretation of `Prop` as the type
of propositions rather than data, and it is what makes `Prop`
*impredicative*.

The term “predicative” stems from foundational developments around the
turn of the twentieth century, when logicians such as Poincaré and
Russell blamed set-theoretic paradoxes on the “vicious circles” that
arise when we define a property by quantifying over a collection that
includes the very property being defined. Notice that if `α` is any
type, we can form the type `α → Prop` of all predicates on `α`
(the “power type of `α`”). The impredicativity of `Prop` means that we
can form propositions that quantify over `α → Prop`. In particular,
we can define predicates on `α` by quantifying over all predicates
on `α`, which is exactly the type of circularity that was once
considered problematic.

### 4.2. Equality {#tpil-equality}

Let us now turn to one of the most fundamental relations defined in
Lean's library, namely, the equality relation. In the chapter on [inductive types](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Inductive-Types/#inductive-types),
we will explain *how* equality is defined from the primitives of Lean's logical framework.
In the meanwhile, here we explain how to use it.

Of course, a fundamental property of equality is that it is an equivalence relation:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)
```

```lean
[Eq.refl.{u_1}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) {α : Sort u_1} (a : α) : a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm)
```

```lean
[Eq.symm.{u}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm) {α : Sort u} {a b : α} (h : a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b) : b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Eq.trans
```

```lean
[Eq.trans.{u}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) {α : Sort u} {a b c : α} (h₁ : a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b) (h₂ : b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c) : a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c
```

```lean

```

We can make the output easier to read by telling Lean not to insert
the implicit arguments (which are displayed here as metavariables).

```lean
[universe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Universes/#Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl).{u}
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)[Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) : ∀ {α : Sort u} (a : α), a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm).{u}
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm)[Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm) : ∀ {α : Sort u} {a b : α}, a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b → b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Eq.trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans).{u}
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans)[Eq.trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) : ∀ {α : Sort u} {a b c : α}, a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b → b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c → a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c
```

```lean

```

The inscription `.{u}` tells Lean to instantiate the constants at the universe `u`.

Thus, for example, we can specialize the example from the previous section to the equality relation:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)
```

```lean
example : a = d :=
[Eq.trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) ([Eq.trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) hab ([Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm) hcb)) hcd
```

```lean

```

We can also use the projection notation:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (a b c d : α)
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (hab : a = b) (hcb : c = b) (hcd : c = d)
```

```lean
example : a = d := (hab.[trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) hcb.[symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm)).[trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) hcd
```

```lean

```

Reflexivity is more powerful than it looks. Recall that terms in the
Calculus of Constructions have a computational interpretation, and
that the logical framework treats terms with a common reduct as the
same. As a result, some nontrivial identities can be proved by
reflexivity:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α β : Type)
```

```lean
example (f : α → β) (a : α) : (fun x => f x) a = f a := [Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) _
```

```lean
example (a : α) (b : β) : (a, b).[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = a := [Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) _
```

```lean
example : 2 + 3 = 5 := [Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) _
```

```lean

```

This feature of the framework is so important that the library defines a notation `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)` for `[Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) _`:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α β : Type)
```

```lean
example (f : α → β) (a : α) : (fun x => f x) a = f a := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
example (a : α) (b : β) : (a, b).[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = a := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
example : 2 + 3 = 5 := rfl
```

```lean

```

Equality is much more than an equivalence relation, however. It has
the important property that every assertion respects the equivalence,
in the sense that we can substitute equal expressions without changing
the truth value. That is, given `h1 : a = b` and `h2 : p a`, we
can construct a proof for `p b` using substitution:
`[Eq.subst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___subst) h1 h2`.

```lean
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
(h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
[Eq.subst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___subst) h1 h2
```

```lean
example (α : Type) (a b : α) (p : α → Prop)
(h1 : a = b) (h2 : p a) : p b :=
h1 ▸ h2
```

```lean

```

The triangle in the second presentation is a macro built on top of
`[Eq.subst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___subst)` and `[Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm)`, and you can enter it by typing `\t`.

The rule `[Eq.subst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___subst)` is used to define the following auxiliary rules,
which carry out more explicit substitutions. They are designed to deal
with applicative terms, that is, terms of form `s t`. Specifically,
`[congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg)` can be used to replace the argument, `[congrFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrFun)` can be
used to replace the term that is being applied, and `[congr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congr-next)` can be
used to replace both at once.

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b : α)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (f g : α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (h₁ : a = b)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (h₂ : f = g)
```

```lean
example : f a = f b := [congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg) f h₁
```

```lean
example : f a = g a := [congrFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrFun) h₂ a
```

```lean
example : f a = g b := [congr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congr-next) h₂ h₁
```

```lean

```

Lean's library contains a large number of common identities, such as these:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b c : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
example : a + 0 = a := Nat.add_zero a
```

```lean
example : 0 + a = a := Nat.zero_add a
```

```lean
example : a * 1 = a := Nat.mul_one a
```

```lean
example : 1 * a = a := Nat.one_mul a
```

```lean
example : a + b = b + a := Nat.add_comm a b
```

```lean
example : a + b + c = a + (b + c) := Nat.add_assoc a b c
```

```lean
example : a * b = b * a := Nat.mul_comm a b
```

```lean
example : a * b * c = a * (b * c) := Nat.mul_assoc a b c
```

```lean
example : a * (b + c) = a * b + a * c := Nat.mul_add a b c
```

```lean
example : a * (b + c) = a * b + a * c := Nat.left_distrib a b c
```

```lean
example : (a + b) * c = a * c + b * c := Nat.add_mul a b c
```

```lean
example : (a + b) * c = a * c + b * c := Nat.right_distrib a b c
```

```lean

```

Note that `Nat.mul_add` and `Nat.add_mul` are alternative names
for `Nat.left_distrib` and `Nat.right_distrib`, respectively. The
properties above are stated for the natural numbers (type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`).

Here is an example of a calculation in the natural numbers that uses
substitution combined with associativity and distributivity.

```lean
example (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :
(x + y) * (x + y) =
x * x + y * x + x * y + y * y :=
have h1 : (x + y) * (x + y) = (x + y) * x + (x + y) * y :=
Nat.mul_add (x + y) x y
have h2 : (x + y) * (x + y) = x * x + y * x + (x * y + y * y) :=
(Nat.add_mul x y x) ▸ (Nat.add_mul x y y) ▸ h1
h2.[trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) (Nat.add_assoc (x * x + y * x) (x * y) (y * y)).[symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm)
```

```lean

```

Notice that the second implicit parameter to `[Eq.subst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___subst)`, which
provides the context in which the substitution is to occur, has type
`α → Prop`. Inferring this predicate therefore requires an instance
of *higher-order unification*. In full generality, the problem of
determining whether a higher-order unifier exists is undecidable, and
Lean can at best provide imperfect and approximate solutions to the
problem. As a result, `[Eq.subst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___subst)` doesn't always do what you want it
to. The macro `h ▸ e` uses more effective heuristics for computing
this implicit parameter, and often succeeds in situations where
applying `[Eq.subst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___subst)` fails.

Because equational reasoning is so common and important, Lean provides
a number of mechanisms to carry it out more effectively. The next
section offers syntax that allow you to write calculational proofs in
a more natural and perspicuous way. But, more importantly, equational
reasoning is supported by a term rewriter, a simplifier, and other
kinds of automation. The term rewriter and simplifier are described
briefly in the next section, and then in greater detail in the next
chapter.

### 4.3. Calculational Proofs {#tpil-calculational-proofs}

A calculational proof is just a chain of intermediate results that are
meant to be composed by basic principles such as the transitivity of
equality. In Lean, a calculational proof starts with the keyword
`calc`, and has the following syntax:

```
calc
  <expr>_0  'op_1'  <expr>_1  ':='  <proof>_1
  '_'       'op_2'  <expr>_2  ':='  <proof>_2
  ...
  '_'       'op_n'  <expr>_n  ':='  <proof>_n
```

Note that the `calc` relations all have the same indentation. Each
`<proof>_i` is a proof for `<expr>_{i-1} op_i <expr>_i`.

We can also use `_` in the first relation (right after `<expr>_0`)
which is useful to align the sequence of relation/proof pairs:

```
calc <expr>_0
    '_' 'op_1' <expr>_1 ':=' <proof>_1
    '_' 'op_2' <expr>_2 ':=' <proof>_2
    ...
    '_' 'op_n' <expr>_n ':=' <proof>_n
```

Here is an example:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b c d e : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
theorem T
(h1 : a = b)
(h2 : b = c + 1)
(h3 : c = d)
(h4 : e = 1 + d) :
a = e :=
calc
a = b := h1
_ = c + 1 := h2
_ = d + 1 := [congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg) [Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) h3
_ = 1 + d := Nat.add_comm d 1
_ = e := [Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm) h4
```

```lean

```

This style of writing proofs is most effective when it is used in
conjunction with the `simp` and `rw` tactics, which are
discussed in greater detail in the next chapter. For example, using
`rw` for rewrite, the proof above could be written
as follows:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b c d e : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean

(h1 : a = b)
(h2 : b = c + 1)
(h3 : c = d)
(h4 : e = 1 + d) :
a = e :=
calc
a = b := Essentially, the `rw` tactic uses a given equality (which can be a
hypothesis, a theorem name, or a complex term) to “rewrite” the
goal. If doing so reduces the goal to an identity `t = t`, the
tactic applies reflexivity to prove it.

Rewrites can be applied sequentially, so that the proof above can be
shortened to this:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b c d e : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

The `simp` tactic, instead, rewrites the goal by applying the given
identities repeatedly, in any order, anywhere they are applicable in a
term. It also uses other rules that have been previously declared to
the system, and applies commutativity wisely to avoid looping. As a
result, we can also prove the theorem as follows:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b c d e : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
theorem T
(h1 : a = b)
(h2 : b = c + 1)
(h3 : c = d)
(h4 : e = 1 + d) :
a = e :=
bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)d:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)e:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h1:a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) bh2:b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1h3:c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) dh4:e [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) d⊢ a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) e [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [h1, h2, h3, Nat.add_comm, h4]All goals completed! 🐙

We will discuss variations of `rw` and `simp` in the next chapter.

The `calc` command can be configured for any relation that supports
some form of transitivity. It can even combine different relations.

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b c d : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
example (h1 : a = b) (h2 : b ≤ c) (h3 : c + 1 < d) : a < d :=
calc
a = b := h1
_ < b + 1 := Nat.lt_succ_self b
_ ≤ c + 1 := Nat.succ_le_succ h2
_ < d := h3
```

```lean

```

You can “teach” `calc` new transitivity theorems by adding new instances
of the `[Trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#Trans___mk)` type class. Type classes are introduced later, but the following
small example demonstrates how to extend the `calc` notation using new `[Trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#Trans___mk)` instances.

```lean
def divides (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Prop :=
∃ k, k*x = y
```

```lean
def divides_mul (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [divides]](#tpil-divides) x (k*x) :=
⟨k, [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)⟩
```

```lean
instance : [Trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#Trans___mk) [divides]](#tpil-divides) [divides]](#tpil-divides) [divides]](#tpil-divides) where
[trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#Trans___mk) := [divides_trans]](#tpil-divides)
```

```lean
example (h₁ : [divides]](#tpil-divides) x y) (h₂ : y = z) : [divides]](#tpil-divides) x (2*z) :=
calc
[divides]](#tpil-divides) x y := h₁
_ = z := h₂
[divides]](#tpil-divides) _ (2*z) := [divides_mul]](#tpil-divides) ..
```

```lean
infix:50 " | " => [divides]](#tpil-divides)
```

```lean
example (h₁ : [divides]](#tpil-divides) x y) (h₂ : y = z) : [divides]](#tpil-divides) x (2*z) :=
calc
x | y := h₁
_ = z := h₂
_ | 2*z := [divides_mul]](#tpil-divides) ..
```

```lean

```

The example above also makes it clear that you can use `calc` even if you do not have an infix
notation for your relation. Lean already includes the standard Unicode notation for divisibility
(using `∣`, which can be entered as `\dvd` or `\mid`), so the example above uses the ordinary
vertical bar to avoid a conflict. In practice, this is not a good idea, as it risks confusion with
the ASCII `|` used in the `match`` ... ``with` expression.

With `calc`, we can write the proof in the last section in a more
natural and perspicuous way.

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
example : (x + y) * (x + y) = x * x + y * x + x * y + y * y :=
calc
(x + y) * (x + y) = (x + y) * x + (x + y) * y :=
byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ The alternative `calc` notation is worth considering here. When the
first expression is taking this much space, using `_` in the first
relation naturally aligns all relations:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

Here the left arrow before `Nat.add_assoc` tells rewrite to use the
identity in the opposite direction. (You can enter it with `\l` or
use the ASCII equivalent, `<-`.) If brevity is what we are after,
both `rw` and `simp` can do the job on their own:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

### 4.4. The Existential Quantifier {#tpil-the-existential-quantifier}

Finally, consider the existential quantifier, which can be written as
either `exists x : α, p x` or `∃ x : α, p x`. Both versions are
actually notationally convenient abbreviations for a more long-winded
expression, `[Exists](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) (fun x : α => p x)`, defined in Lean's library.

As you should by now expect, the library includes both an introduction
rule and an elimination rule. The introduction rule is
straightforward: to prove `∃ x : α, p x`, it suffices to provide a
suitable term `t` and a proof of `p t`. Here are some examples:

```lean
example : ∃ x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), x > 0 :=
have h : 1 > 0 := Nat.zero_lt_succ 0
[Exists.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) 1 h
```

```lean
example (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (h : x > 0) : ∃ y, y < x :=
[Exists.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) 0 h
```

```lean
example (x y z : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (hxy : x < y) (hyz : y < z) : ∃ w, x < w ∧ w < z :=
[Exists.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) y ([And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) hxy hyz)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Exists.intro
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro)[Exists.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) : ∀ {α : Sort u_1} {p : α → Prop} (w : α), p w → [Exists](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) p
```

```lean

```

We can use the anonymous constructor notation `⟨t, h⟩` for
`[Exists.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) t h`, when the type is clear from the context.

```lean
example : ∃ x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), x > 0 :=
have h : 1 > 0 := Nat.zero_lt_succ 0
⟨1, h⟩
```

```lean
example (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (h : x > 0) : ∃ y, y < x :=
⟨0, h⟩
```

```lean
example (x y z : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (hxy : x < y) (hyz : y < z) : ∃ w, x < w ∧ w < z :=
⟨y, hxy, hyz⟩
```

```lean

```

Note that `[Exists.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro)` has implicit arguments: Lean has to infer
the predicate `p : α → Prop` in the conclusion `∃ x, p x`. This
is not a trivial affair. For example, if we have
`hg : g 0 0 = 0` and write `[Exists.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) 0 hg`, there are many possible values
for the predicate `p`, corresponding to the theorems `∃ x, g x x = x`,
`∃ x, g x x = 0`, `∃ x, g x 0 = x`, etc. Lean uses the
context to infer which one is appropriate. This is illustrated in the
following example, in which we set the option `pp.explicit` to true
to ask Lean's pretty-printer to show the implicit arguments.

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (g : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
theorem gex1 (hg : g 0 0 = 0) : ∃ x, g x x = x := ⟨0, hg⟩
```

```lean
theorem gex2 (hg : g 0 0 = 0) : ∃ x, g x 0 = x := ⟨0, hg⟩
```

```lean
theorem gex3 (hg : g 0 0 = 0) : ∃ x, g 0 0 = x := ⟨0, hg⟩
```

```lean
theorem gex4 (hg : g 0 0 = 0) : ∃ x, g x x = 0 := ⟨0, hg⟩
```

```lean
set_option pp.explicit true -- display implicit arguments
```

```

We can view `[Exists.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro)` as an information-hiding operation, since
it hides the witness to the body of the assertion. The existential
elimination rule, `Exists.elim`, performs the opposite operation. It
allows us to prove a proposition `q` from `∃ x : α, p x`, by
showing that `q` follows from `p w` for an arbitrary value
`w`. Roughly speaking, since we know there is an `x` satisfying
`p x`, we can give it a name, say, `w`. If `q` does not mention
`w`, then showing that `q` follows from `p w` is tantamount to
showing that `q` follows from the existence of any such `x`. Here
is an example:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop)
```

```lean
example (h : ∃ x, p x ∧ q x) : ∃ x, q x ∧ p x :=
Exists.elim h
(fun w =>
fun hw : p w ∧ q w =>
show ∃ x, q x ∧ p x from ⟨w, hw.[right](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro), hw.[left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)⟩)
```

```lean

```

It may be helpful to compare the exists-elimination rule to the
or-elimination rule: the assertion `∃ x : α, p x` can be thought of
as a big disjunction of the propositions `p a`, as `a` ranges over
all the elements of `α`. Note that the anonymous constructor
notation `⟨w, hw.[right](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro), hw.[left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)⟩` abbreviates a nested constructor
application; we could equally well have written `⟨``w``, ⟨``hw.[right](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)``, ``hw.[left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)``⟩⟩`.

Notice that an existential proposition is very similar to a sigma
type, as described in dependent types section. The difference is that
existential propositions are *propositions*, while sigma types are *types*.
Otherwise, they are very similar. Given a predicate `p : α → Prop` and a family of types `β : α → Type`,
for a term `a : α` with `h : p a` and `h' : β a`, the term `[Exists.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) a h` has
type `(∃ x : α, p x) : Prop`, while `[Sigma.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Sigma___mk) a h'` has type
`(Σ x : α, β x)`. The similarity between `∃` and `Σ` is another
instance of the [Curry-Howard isomorphism]](#tpil---tech-term-Curry-Howard-isomorphism).

Lean provides a more convenient way to eliminate from an existential
quantifier with the `match` expression:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop)
```

```lean
example (h : ∃ x, p x ∧ q x) : ∃ x, q x ∧ p x :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) h [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| ⟨w, hw⟩ => ⟨w, hw.[right](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro), hw.[left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)⟩
```

```lean

```

The `match` expression is part of Lean's function definition system,
which provides convenient and expressive ways of defining complex
functions. Once again, it is the [Curry-Howard isomorphism]](#tpil---tech-term-Curry-Howard-isomorphism) that allows
us to co-opt this mechanism for writing proofs as well. The `match`
statement “destructs” the existential assertion into the components
`w` and `hw`, which can then be used in the body of the statement
to prove the proposition. We can annotate the types used in the match
for greater clarity:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop)
```

```lean
example (h : ∃ x, p x ∧ q x) : ∃ x, q x ∧ p x :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) h [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| ⟨(w : α), (hw : p w ∧ q w)⟩ => ⟨w, hw.[right](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro), hw.[left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)⟩
```

```lean

```

We can even use the match statement to decompose the conjunction at the same time:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop)
```

```lean
example (h : ∃ x, p x ∧ q x) : ∃ x, q x ∧ p x :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) h [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| ⟨w, hpw, hqw⟩ => ⟨w, hqw, hpw⟩
```

```lean

```

Lean also provides a pattern-matching `let` expression:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop)
```

```lean
example (h : ∃ x, p x ∧ q x) : ∃ x, q x ∧ p x :=
let ⟨w, hpw, hqw⟩ := h
⟨w, hqw, hpw⟩
```

```lean

```

This is essentially just alternative notation for the `match`
construct above. Lean will even allow us to use an implicit `match`
in the `fun` expression:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop)
```

```lean
example : (∃ x, p x ∧ q x) → ∃ x, q x ∧ p x :=
fun ⟨w, hpw, hqw⟩ => ⟨w, hqw, hpw⟩
```

```lean

```

We will see in [Induction and Recursion](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Induction-and-Recursion/#induction-and-recursion) that all these variations are
instances of a more general pattern-matching construct.

In the following example, we define `[IsEven]](#tpil-IsEven) a` as `∃ b, a = 2 * b`,
and then we show that the sum of two even numbers is an even number.

```lean
def IsEven (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := ∃ b, a = 2 * b
```

Using the various gadgets described in this chapter—the match
statement, anonymous constructors, and the `rewrite` tactic, we can
write this proof concisely as follows:

```lean
def IsEven (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := ∃ b, a = 2 * b
```

Just as the constructive “or” is stronger than the classical “or,” so,
too, is the constructive “exists” stronger than the classical
“exists”. For example, the following implication requires classical
reasoning because, from a constructive standpoint, knowing that it is
not the case that every `x` satisfies `¬ p` is not the same as
having a particular `x` that satisfies `p`.

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Classical
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (p : α → Prop)
```

```lean
example (h : ¬ ∀ x, ¬ p x) : ∃ x, p x :=
byContradiction
(fun h1 : ¬ ∃ x, p x =>
have h2 : ∀ x, ¬ p x :=
fun x =>
fun h3 : p x =>
have h4 : ∃ x, p x := ⟨x, h3⟩
show [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) from h1 h4
show [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) from h h2)
```

```lean

```

What follows are some common identities involving the existential
quantifier. In the exercises below, we encourage you to prove as many
as you can. We also leave it to you to determine which are
nonconstructive, and hence require some form of classical reasoning.

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Classical
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (r : Prop)
```

```lean
example : (∃ x : α, r) → r := sorry
```

```lean
example (a : α) : r → (∃ x : α, r) := sorry
```

```lean
example : (∃ x, p x ∧ r) ↔ (∃ x, p x) ∧ r := sorry
```

```lean
example : (∃ x, p x ∨ q x) ↔ (∃ x, p x) ∨ (∃ x, q x) := sorry
```

```lean
example : (∀ x, p x) ↔ ¬ (∃ x, ¬ p x) := sorry
```

```lean
example : (∃ x, p x) ↔ ¬ (∀ x, ¬ p x) := sorry
```

```lean
example : (¬ ∃ x, p x) ↔ (∀ x, ¬ p x) := sorry
```

```lean
example : (¬ ∀ x, p x) ↔ (∃ x, ¬ p x) := sorry
```

```lean
example : (∀ x, p x → r) ↔ (∃ x, p x) → r := sorry
```

```lean
example (a : α) : (∃ x, p x → r) ↔ (∀ x, p x) → r := sorry
```

```lean
example (a : α) : (∃ x, r → p x) ↔ (r → ∃ x, p x) := sorry
```

```lean

```

Notice that the second example and the last two examples require the
assumption that there is at least one element `a` of type `α`.

Here are solutions to two of the more difficult ones:

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Classical
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (α : Type) (p q : α → Prop)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a : α)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (r : Prop)
```

```lean
example : (∃ x, p x ∨ q x) ↔ (∃ x, p x) ∨ (∃ x, q x) :=
[Iff.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)
(fun ⟨a, (h1 : p a ∨ q a)⟩ =>
Or.elim h1
(fun hpa : p a => [Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) ⟨a, hpa⟩)
(fun hqa : q a => [Or.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) ⟨a, hqa⟩))
(fun h : (∃ x, p x) ∨ (∃ x, q x) =>
Or.elim h
(fun ⟨a, hpa⟩ => ⟨a, ([Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) hpa)⟩)
(fun ⟨a, hqa⟩ => ⟨a, ([Or.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) hqa)⟩))
```

```lean
example : (∃ x, p x → r) ↔ (∀ x, p x) → r :=
[Iff.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)
(fun ⟨b, (hb : p b → r)⟩ =>
fun h2 : ∀ x, p x =>
show r from hb (h2 b))
(fun h1 : (∀ x, p x) → r =>
show ∃ x, p x → r from
byCases
(fun hap : ∀ x, p x => ⟨a, λ h' => h1 hap⟩)
(fun hnap : ¬ ∀ x, p x =>
byContradiction
(fun hnex : ¬ ∃ x, p x → r =>
have hap : ∀ x, p x :=
fun x =>
byContradiction
(fun hnp : ¬ p x =>
have hex : ∃ x, p x → r := ⟨x, (fun hp => [absurd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#absurd) hp hnp)⟩
show [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) from hnex hex)
show [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) from hnap hap)))
```

```lean

```

### 4.5. More on the Proof Language {#tpil-more-on-the-proof-language}

We have seen that keywords like `fun`, `have`, and `show` make
it possible to write formal proof terms that mirror the structure of
informal mathematical proofs. In this section, we discuss some
additional features of the proof language that are often convenient.

To start with, we can use anonymous `have` expressions to introduce an
auxiliary goal without having to label it. We can refer to the last
expression introduced in this way using the keyword `this`:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (h : ∀ x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), f x ≤ f (x + 1))
```

```lean
example : f 0 ≤ f 3 :=
have : f 0 ≤ f 1 := h 0
have : f 0 ≤ f 2 := Nat.le_trans this (h 1)
show f 0 ≤ f 3 from Nat.le_trans this (h 2)
```

```lean

```

Often proofs move from one fact to the next, so this can be effective
in eliminating the clutter of lots of labels.

When the goal can be inferred, we can also ask Lean instead to fill in
the proof by writing `by assumption`:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (h : ∀ x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), f x ≤ f (x + 1))
```

```lean
example : f 0 ≤ f 3 :=
have : f 0 ≤ f 1 := h 0
have : f 0 ≤ f 2 := Nat.le_trans (byf:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:∀ (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), f x [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) f [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)this:f 0 [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) f 1⊢ f 0 [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) f 1 [assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)All goals completed! 🐙) (h 1)
show f 0 ≤ f 3 from Nat.le_trans (byf:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:∀ (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), f x [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) f [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)this✝:f 0 [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) f 1this:f 0 [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) f 2⊢ f 0 [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) f 2 [assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)All goals completed! 🐙) (h 2)
```

```lean

```

This tells Lean to use the `[assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)` tactic, which, in turn,
proves the goal by finding a suitable hypothesis in the local
context. We will learn more about the `[assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)` tactic in the
next chapter.

We can also ask Lean to fill in the proof by writing `‹p›`, where
`p` is the proposition whose proof we want Lean to find in the
context. You can type these corner quotes using `\f<` and `\f>`,
respectively. The letter “f” is for “French,” since the Unicode
symbols can also be used as French quotation marks. In fact, the
notation is defined in Lean as follows:

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation) "‹" p "›" => show p by [assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)
```

```lean

```

This approach is more robust than using `by [assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)`, because the
type of the assumption that needs to be inferred is given
explicitly. It also makes proofs more readable. Here is a more
elaborate example:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (h : ∀ x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), f x ≤ f (x + 1))
```

```lean
example : f 0 ≥ f 1 → f 1 ≥ f 2 → f 0 = f 2 :=
fun _ : f 0 ≥ f 1 =>
fun _ : f 1 ≥ f 2 =>
have : f 0 ≥ f 2 := Nat.le_trans ‹f 1 ≥ f 2› ‹f 0 ≥ f 1›
have : f 0 ≤ f 2 := Nat.le_trans (h 0) (h 1)
show f 0 = f 2 from Nat.le_antisymm this ‹f 0 ≥ f 2›
```

```lean

```

Keep in mind that you can use the French quotation marks in this way
to refer to *anything* in the context, not just things that were
introduced anonymously. Its use is also not limited to propositions,
though using it for data is somewhat odd:

```lean
example (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := ‹Nat›
```

```lean

```

Later, we show how you can extend the proof language using the Lean macro system.

## Tactics {#tpil-tactics}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Tactics/

In this chapter, we describe an alternative approach to constructing
proofs, using *tactics*. A proof term is a representation of a
mathematical proof; tactics are commands, or instructions, that
describe how to build such a proof. Informally, you might begin a
mathematical proof by saying “to prove the forward direction, unfold
the definition, apply the previous lemma, and simplify.” Just as these
are instructions that tell the reader how to find the relevant proof,
tactics are instructions that tell Lean how to construct a proof
term. They naturally support an incremental style of writing proofs,
in which you decompose a proof and work on goals one step at a time.

We will describe proofs that consist of sequences of tactics as
“tactic-style” proofs, to contrast with the ways of writing proof
terms we have seen so far, which we will call “term-style”
proofs. Each style has its own advantages and disadvantages. For
example, tactic-style proofs can be harder to read, because they
require the reader to predict or guess the results of each
instruction. But they can also be shorter and easier to
write. Moreover, tactics offer a gateway to using Lean's automation,
since automated procedures are themselves tactics.

### 5.1. Entering Tactic Mode {#tpil-entering-tactic-mode}

Conceptually, stating a theorem or introducing a `have` statement
creates a goal, namely, the goal of constructing a term with the
expected type. For example, the following creates the goal of
constructing a term of type `p ∧ q ∧ p`, in a context with constants
`p q : Prop`, `hp : p` and `hq : q`:

```lean
theorem test (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q ∧ p := byp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

You can write this goal as follows:

p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p

Indeed, if you replace the “sorry” by an underscore in the example
above, Lean will report that it is exactly this goal that has been
left unsolved.

Ordinarily, you meet such a goal by writing an explicit term. But
wherever a term is expected, Lean allows us to insert instead a
`by <tactics>` block, where `<tactics>` is a sequence of commands,
separated by semicolons or line breaks. You can prove the theorem above
in that way:

```lean
theorem test (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q ∧ p :=
byp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p [apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ prightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hprightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)right.leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ qright.rightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hqright.rightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hpAll goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

We often put the `by` keyword on the preceding line, and write the
example above as:

```lean
theorem test (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q ∧ p := byp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ prightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hprightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)right.leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ qright.rightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hqright.rightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hpAll goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

The `[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply)` tactic applies an expression, viewed as denoting a
function with zero or more arguments. It unifies the conclusion with
the expression in the current goal, and creates new goals for the
remaining arguments, provided that no later arguments depend on
them. In the example above, the command `[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)` yields two
subgoals:

leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ prightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p

The first goal is met with the command `[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hp`. The `[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact)`
command is just a variant of `[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply)` which signals that the
expression given should fill the goal exactly. It is good form to use
it in a tactic proof, since its failure signals that something has
gone wrong. It is also more robust than `[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply)`, since the
elaborator takes the expected type, given by the target of the goal,
into account when processing the expression that is being applied. In
this case, however, `[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply)` would work just as well.

You can see the resulting proof term with the `#print` command:

```lean
theorem test (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q ∧ p := byp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p

You can write a tactic script incrementally. In VS Code, you can open
a window to display messages by pressing ``` `Ctrl``Shift``Enter` ```, and
that window will then show you the current goal whenever the cursor is
in a tactic block. If the proof is incomplete, the token `by` is
decorated with a red squiggly line, and the error message contains the
remaining goals.

Tactic commands can take compound expressions, not just single
identifiers. The following is a shorter version of the preceding
proof:

```lean
theorem test (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q ∧ p := byp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) hpp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) hq hpAll goals completed! 🐙
```

Multiple tactic applications can be written in a single line by concatenating with a semicolon.

```lean
theorem test (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q ∧ p := byp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) hpp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p; [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) hq hpAll goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

Tactics that may produce multiple subgoals often tag them. For
example, the tactic `[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)` tagged the first subgoal as
`leftleftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p`, and the second as `rightrightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p`. In the case of the `[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply)`
tactic, the tags are inferred from the parameters' names used in the
`[And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)` declaration. You can structure your tactics using the
notation `case`` <tag> => <tactics>`. The following is a structured
version of our first tactic proof in this chapter.

```lean
theorem test (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q ∧ p := byp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ prightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) left =>p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hpAll goals completed! 🐙
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) right =>p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ qrightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) left =>p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hqAll goals completed! 🐙
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) right =>p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hpAll goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

You can solve the subgoal `rightrightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p` before `leftleftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p` using the `[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case)`
notation:

```lean
theorem test (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q ∧ p := byp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ prightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) right =>p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ qrightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) left =>p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hqAll goals completed! 🐙
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) right =>p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hpAll goals completed! 🐙
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) left =>p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hpAll goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

Note that Lean hides the other goals inside the `[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case)` block. After `[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) left =>`,
the proof state is:

p:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q

We say that `[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case)` is “focusing” on the selected goal. Moreover, Lean flags an error
if the selected goal is not fully solved at the end of the `[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case)`
block.

For simple subgoals, it may not be worth selecting a subgoal using its
tag, but you may still want to structure the proof. Lean also provides
the “bullet” notation `. <tactics>` (or `· <tactics>`) for
structuring proofs:

```lean
theorem test (p q : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ q ∧ p := byp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ prightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
.leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hpAll goals completed! 🐙
.rightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p [apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)right.leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ qright.rightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p
.right.leftp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ q [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hqAll goals completed! 🐙
.right.rightp:Propq:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) hpAll goals completed! 🐙
```

### 5.2. Basic Tactics {#tpil-basic-tactics}

In addition to `[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply)` and `[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact)`, another useful tactic is
`[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro)`, which introduces a hypothesis. What follows is an example
of an identity from propositional logic that we proved in a previous
chapter, now proved using tactics.

```lean
example (p q r : Prop) : p ∧ (q ∨ r) ↔ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r) := byp:Propq:Propr:Prop⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)q [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) r[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [↔](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) r

The `[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro)` command can more generally be used to introduce a variable of any type:

```lean
example (α : Type) : α → α := byα:Type⊢ α → α
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) aα:Typea:α⊢ α
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) aAll goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
example (α : Type) : ∀ x : α, x = x := byα:Type⊢ ∀ (x : α), x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x
[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) xα:Typex:α⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) [Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) xAll goals completed! 🐙
```

You can use it to introduce several variables:

```lean

[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intro) a b c h₁ h₂a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) bh₂:a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) c⊢ c [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) [Eq.trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___trans) ([Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm) h₂) h₁All goals completed! 🐙
