```lean

```

In the first example, the left-hand side of the equality in the goal
is simplified using the usual identities involving 0 and 1, reducing
the goal to `x * y`` = ``x * y`. At that point, `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` applies
reflexivity to finish it off. In the second example, `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` reduces
the goal to `p (x * y)`, at which point the assumption `h`
finishes it off. Here are some more examples
with lists:

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) List
```

Moreover, you can use a “wildcard” asterisk to simplify all the hypotheses and the goal:

```lean
[attribute](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [local simp] Nat.mul_comm Nat.mul_assoc Nat.mul_left_comm
```

```lean
[attribute](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [local simp] Nat.add_assoc Nat.add_comm Nat.add_left_comm
```

For operations that are commutative and associative, like
multiplication on the natural numbers, the simplifier uses these two
facts to rewrite an expression, as well as *left commutativity*. In
the case of multiplication the latter is expressed as follows:
`x * (y * z) = y * (x * z)`. The `local` modifier tells the simplifier
to use these rules in the current file (or section or namespace, as
the case may be). It may seem that commutativity and
left-commutativity are problematic, in that repeated application of
either causes looping. But the simplifier detects identities that
permute their arguments, and uses a technique known as *ordered
rewriting*. This means that the system maintains an internal ordering
of terms, and only applies the identity if doing so decreases the
order. With the three identities mentioned above, this has the effect
that all the parentheses in an expression are associated to the right,
and the expressions are ordered in a canonical (though somewhat
arbitrary) way. Two expressions that are equivalent up to
associativity and commutativity are then rewritten to the same
canonical form.

```lean
[attribute](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [local simp] Nat.mul_comm Nat.mul_assoc Nat.mul_left_comm
[attribute](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [local simp] Nat.add_assoc Nat.add_comm Nat.add_left_comm
```

As with `rw`, you can send `simp` a list of facts to use,
including general lemmas, local hypotheses, definitions to unfold, and
compound expressions. The `simp` tactic also recognizes the `←t`
syntax that `rewrite` does. In any case, the additional rules are
added to the collection of identities that are used to simplify a
term.

```lean
def f (m n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
m + n + m
```

```lean
example {m n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} (h : n = 1) (h' : 0 = m) : (f m n) = n := bym:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1h':0 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) m⊢ f m n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [h, ←h', f]All goals completed! 🐙
```

A common idiom is to simplify a goal using local hypotheses:


To use all the hypotheses present in the local context when
simplifying, we can use the wildcard symbol, `*`:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

The simplifier will also do propositional rewriting. For example,
using the hypothesis `p`, it rewrites `p ∧ q` to `q` and `p ∨ q` to `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`,
which it then proves trivially. Iterating such
rewrites produces nontrivial propositional reasoning.

```lean
example (p q : Prop) (hp : p) : p ∧ q ↔ q := byp:Propq:Prophp:p⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q [↔](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) q
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [*]All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
example (p q : Prop) (hp : p) : p ∨ q := byp:Propq:Prophp:p⊢ p [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) q
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [*]All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
example (p q r : Prop) (hp : p) (hq : q) : p ∧ (q ∨ r) := byp:Propq:Propr:Prophp:phq:q⊢ p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)q [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) r[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [*]All goals completed! 🐙
```


One thing that makes the simplifier especially useful is that its
capabilities can grow as a library develops. For example, suppose we
define a list operation that symmetrizes its input by appending its
reversal:

```lean
def mk_symm (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) :=
xs ++ xs.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)
```

```lean

```

Then for any list `xs`, `(mk_symm xs).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)` is equal to `mk_symm xs`,
which can easily be proved by unfolding the definition:

```lean
def mk_symm (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) :=
xs ++ xs.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)
```

```lean
theorem reverse_mk_symm (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α)
: (mk_symm xs).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) = mk_symm xs := byα:Type u_1xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α⊢ (mk_symm xs).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) mk_symm xs
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [mk_symm]All goals completed! 🐙
```

But using `reverse_mk_symm` is generally the right thing to do, and
it would be nice if users did not have to invoke it explicitly. You can
achieve that by marking it as a simplification rule when the theorem
is defined:

```lean

xs ++ xs.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)
```

The attribute can also be applied any time after the theorem is declared:

```lean

xs ++ xs.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)
```

Once the attribute is applied, however, there is no way to permanently
remove it; it persists in any file that imports the one where the
attribute is assigned. As we will discuss further in
[Attributes](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Interacting-with-Lean/#attributes), one can limit the scope of an attribute to the
current file or section using the `local` modifier:

```lean
def mk_symm (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) :=
xs ++ xs.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)
```

```lean

: (mk_symm xs).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) = mk_symm xs := byα:Type u_1xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α⊢ (mk_symm xs).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) mk_symm xs
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [mk_symm]All goals completed! 🐙
```

Outside the section, the simplifier will no longer use
`reverse_mk_symm` by default.

Note that the various `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` options we have discussed—giving an
explicit list of rules, and using `at` to specify the location—can be combined,
but the order they are listed is rigid. You can see the correct order
in an editor by placing the cursor on the `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` identifier to see
the documentation string that is associated with it.

There are two additional modifiers that are useful. By default,
`[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` includes all theorems that have been marked with the
attribute `[simp]`. Writing `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [only](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` excludes these defaults,
allowing you to use a more explicitly crafted list of
rules. In the examples below, the minus sign and
`[only](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` are used to block the application of `reverse_mk_symm`.

```lean
def mk_symm (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) :=
xs ++ xs.[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)
```

```lean
@[simp] theorem reverse_mk_symm (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α)
: (mk_symm xs).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) = mk_symm xs := byα:Type u_1xs:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α⊢ (mk_symm xs).[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) mk_symm xs
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [mk_symm]All goals completed! 🐙
```

The `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` tactic has many configuration options. For example, we can enable contextual simplifications as follows:

```lean
example : [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x = 0 [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) y + x = y [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x ≠ 0 := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ if x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 then y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y else x ≠ 0
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) +[contextual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

With `+[contextual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk)`, the `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` tactic uses the fact that `x = 0` when simplifying `y + x = y`, and
`x ≠ 0` when simplifying the other branch. Here is another example:

```lean
example : ∀ (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (h : x = 0), y + x = y := byy:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ ∀ (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0 → y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) y
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) +[contextual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

Another useful configuration option is `+[arith](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk)` which enables arithmetical simplifications.

```lean
example : 0 < 1 + x ∧ x + y + 2 ≥ y + 1 := byx:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 0 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 2 ≥ y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) +[arith](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Simplifier/Configuring-Simplification/#Lean___Meta___Simp___Config___mk)All goals completed! 🐙
```

### 5.8. Split Tactic {#tpil-split-tactic}

The `[split](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#split)` tactic is useful for breaking nested `if`-`then`-`else` and `match` expressions in cases.
For a `match` expression with `n` cases, the `[split](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#split)` tactic generates at most `n` subgoals. Here is an example:

```lean
def f (x y z : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) x, y, z [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 5, _, _ => y
| _, 5, _ => y
| _, _, 5 => y
| _, _, _ => 1
```


The tactic `[split](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#split) <;> [first](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#first) | [contradiction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#contradiction) | [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)` first applies the `[split](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#split)` tactic,
and then for each generated goal it tries `[contradiction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#contradiction)`, and then `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl)` if `[contradiction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#contradiction)` fails.
Like `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)`, we can apply `[split](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#split)` to a particular hypothesis:

```lean
def g (xs ys : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) xs, ys [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [a, b], _ => a+b+1
| _, [b, _] => b+1
| _, _ => 1
```

### 5.9. Extensible Tactics {#tpil-extensible-tactics}

In the following example, we define the notation `triv` using the command `[syntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Command___syntax)`.
Then, we use the command `[macro_rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)` to specify what should
be done when `triv` is used. You can provide different expansions, and the tactic
interpreter will try all of them until one succeeds:

```lean
-- Define a new tactic notation
[syntax](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Defining-New-Syntax/#Lean___Parser___Command___syntax) "triv" : tactic
```

```lean
[macro_rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(tactic| triv) => `(tactic| [assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption))
```

```lean
example (h : p) : p := byp:Sort ?u.2h:p⊢ p
trivAll goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
-- You cannot prove the following theorem using `triv`
-- example (x : α) : x = x := by
-- triv
-- Let's extend `triv`. The tactic interpreter
-- tries all possible macro extensions for `triv` until one succeeds
[macro_rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules)
| `(tactic| triv) => `(tactic| [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rfl))
```

```lean
example (x : α) : x = x := byα:Sort u_1x:α⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x
trivAll goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
example (x : α) (h : p) : x = x ∧ p := byα:Sort u_1p:Propx:αh:p⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
[apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) [And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)leftα:Sort u_1p:Propx:αh:p⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) xrightα:Sort u_1p:Propx:αh:p⊢ p <;>leftα:Sort u_1p:Propx:αh:p⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) xrightα:Sort u_1p:Propx:αh:p⊢ p trivAll goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
-- We now add a (recursive) extension
[macro_rules](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Macros/#Lean___Parser___Command___macro_rules) | `(tactic| triv) => `(tactic| [apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) And.intro <;> triv)
```

```lean
example (x : α) (h : p) : x = x ∧ p := byα:Sort u_1p:Propx:αh:p⊢ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) x [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) p
trivAll goals completed! 🐙
```

### 5.10. Exercises {#tpil-Theorem-Proving-in-Lean-4--Tactics--Exercises}

1. Go back to the exercises in [Propositions and Proofs]](#tpil-propositions-and-proofs) and
   [Quantifiers and Equality]](#tpil-quantifiers-and-equality) and
   redo as many as you can now with tactic proofs, using also `rw`
   and `simp` as appropriate.
2. Use tactic combinators to obtain a one-line proof of the following:

```lean
example (p q r : Prop) (hp : p)
```

## Interacting with Lean {#tpil-interacting-with-lean}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Interacting-with-Lean/

You are now familiar with the fundamentals of dependent type theory,
both as a language for defining mathematical objects and a language
for constructing proofs. The one thing you are missing is a mechanism
for defining new data types. We will fill this gap in the next
chapter, which introduces the notion of an *inductive data type*. But
first, in this chapter, we take a break from the mechanics of type
theory to explore some pragmatic aspects of interacting with Lean.

Not all of the information found here will be useful to you right
away. We recommend skimming this section to get a sense of Lean's
features, and then returning to it as necessary.

### 6.1. Messages {#tpil-messages}

Lean produces three kinds of messages:

Errors
:   Errors are produced when an inconsistency in the code means that it can't
    be processed. Examples include syntax errors (e.g. a missing `)`) and type
    errors such as attempting to add a natural number to a function.

Warnings
:   Warnings describe potential problems with the code, such as the presence of `sorry`.
    Unlike with errors, the code is not meaningless; however, warnings deserve careful attention.

Information
:   Information doesn't indicate any problem with the code, and includes output from commands such as `#check` and `#eval`.

Lean can check that a command produces the expected messages. If the messages match,
then any errors are disregarded; this can be used to ensure that the right errors occur.
If they don't, an error is produced. You can use the `#guard_msgs` command to indicate
which messages are expected.

Here is an example:

```lean
/--
error: Type mismatch
"Not a number"
has type
String
but is expected to have type
Nat
-/
[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd) [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)
def x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := "Not a number"
```

```lean

```

Including a message category in parentheses after `[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)` causes it to check only
the specified category, letting others through. In this example, `[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval)` issues an error
due to the presence of `sorry`, but the warning that is always issued for `sorry` is displayed
as usual:

```lean
/--
error: Aborting evaluation since the expression depends on the
'sorry' axiom, which can lead to runtime instability and crashes.
To attempt to evaluate anyway despite the risks, use the '#eval!'
command.
-/
[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)(error) [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (sorry : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
declaration uses `sorry`
```

```lean

```

Without the configuration, both messages are captured:

```lean
/--
error: Aborting evaluation since the expression depends on the 'sorry'
axiom, which can lead to runtime instability and crashes.
To attempt to evaluate anyway despite the risks, use the '#eval!'
command.
---
warning: declaration uses `sorry`
-/
[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd) [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (sorry : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean

```

Some examples in this book use `[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)` to indicate expected errors.

### 6.2. Importing Files {#tpil-importing-files}

The goal of Lean's front end is to interpret user input, construct
formal expressions, and check that they are well-formed and type-correct.
Lean also supports the use of various editors, which provide
continuous checking and feedback. More information can be found on the
Lean [documentation pages](https://lean-lang.org/documentation/).

The definitions and theorems in Lean's standard library are spread
across multiple files. Users may also wish to make use of additional
libraries, or develop their own projects across multiple files. When
Lean starts, it automatically imports the contents of the library
`Init` folder, which includes a number of fundamental definitions
and constructions. As a result, most of the examples we present here
work “out of the box.”

If you want to use additional files, however, they need to be imported
manually, via an `import` statement at the beginning of a file. The
command

> `import`` Bar.Baz.Blah`

imports the file `Bar/Baz/Blah.olean`, where the descriptions are
interpreted relative to the Lean *search path*. Information as to how
the search path is determined can be found on the
[documentation pages](https://lean-lang.org/documentation/).
By default, it includes the standard library directory, and (in some contexts)
the root of the user's local project.

Importing is transitive. In other words, if you import `Foo` and `Foo` imports `Bar`,
then you also have access to the contents of `Bar`, and do not need to import it explicitly.

### 6.3. More on Sections {#tpil-more-on-sections}

Lean provides various sectioning mechanisms to help structure a
theory. You saw in [Variables and Sections]](#tpil-variables-and-sections) that the
`section` command makes it possible not only to group together
elements of a theory that go together, but also to declare variables
that are inserted as arguments to theorems and definitions, as
necessary. Remember that the point of the `variable` command is to
declare variables for use in theorems, as in the following example:

```lean
[section](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___section)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
def double := x + x
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) double y
```

```lean
double y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) double (2 * x)
```


The definition of `double` does not have to declare `x` as an
argument; Lean detects the dependence and inserts it
automatically. Similarly, Lean detects the occurrence of `x` in
`t1` and `t2`, and inserts it automatically there, too.
Note that `double` does *not* have `y` as argument. Variables are only
included in declarations where they are actually used.

### 6.4. More on Namespaces {#tpil-more-on-namespaces}

In Lean, identifiers are given by hierarchical *names* like
`Foo.Bar.baz`. We saw in [Namespaces]](#tpil-namespaces) that Lean provides
mechanisms for working with hierarchical names. The command
`namespace`` Foo` causes `Foo` to be prepended to the name of each
definition and theorem until `end`` Foo` is encountered. The command
`open`` Foo` then creates temporary *aliases* to definitions and
theorems that begin with prefix `Foo`.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Foo
```

```lean
def bar : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 1
```

```lean
end Foo
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Foo
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) bar
```

```lean
Foo.bar : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Foo.bar
```

```lean
Foo.bar : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

The following definition

```lean
def Foo.bar : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 1
```

```lean

```

is treated as a macro, and expands to

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Foo
```

```lean
def bar : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := 1
```

```lean
end Foo
```

```lean

```

Although the names of theorems and definitions have to be unique, the
aliases that identify them do not. When we open a namespace, an
identifier may be ambiguous. Lean tries to use type information to
disambiguate the meaning in context, but you can always disambiguate
by giving the full name. To that end, the string `_root_` is an
explicit description of the empty prefix.

```lean
def String.add (a b : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) :=
a ++ b
```

```lean
def Bool.add (a b : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
a != b
```

```lean
def add (α β : Type) : Type := [Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) α β
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Bool
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) String
```

```lean

-- #check add
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [String.add]](#tpil-String___add)
```

We can prevent the shorter alias from being created by using the `protected` keyword:



This is often used for names like `Nat.rec` and `Nat.recOn`, to prevent

The `[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open)` command admits variations. The command


```lean
3
```

creates aliases renaming `[Nat.mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___mul)` to `[times](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___mul)` and `[Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)` to `plus`.

It is sometimes useful to `export` aliases from one namespace to another, or to the top level. The command

```lean
[export](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___export) Nat ([succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) [sub](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___sub))
```

```lean

```

creates aliases for `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)`, and `[sub](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___sub)` in the current
namespace, so that whenever the namespace is open, these aliases are
available. If this command is used outside a namespace, the aliases
are exported to the top level.

### 6.5. Attributes {#tpil-attributes}

The main function of Lean is to translate user input to formal
expressions that are checked by the kernel for correctness and then
stored in the environment for later use. But some commands have other
effects on the environment, either assigning attributes to objects in
the environment, defining notation, or declaring instances of type
classes, as described in the chapter on [type classes](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Type-Classes/#type-classes). Most of
these commands have global effects, which is to say, they remain
in effect not only in the current file, but also in any file that
imports it. However, such commands often support the `local` modifier,
which indicates that they only have effect until
the current `section` or `[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace)` is closed, or until the end
of the current file.

In [Using the Simplifier]](#tpil-using-the-simplifier),
we saw that theorems can be annotated with the `[simp]` attribute,
which makes them available for use by the simplifier.
The following example defines the prefix relation on lists,
proves that this relation is reflexive, and assigns the `[simp]` attribute to that theorem.

```lean
def isPrefix (l₁ : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (l₂ : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : Prop :=
∃ t, l₁ ++ t = l₂
```

```lean
@[simp] theorem List.isPrefix_self (as : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : isPrefix as as :=
⟨[], byα:Type u_1as:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α⊢ as [++](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAppend___mk) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) as [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙⟩
```

```lean
example : isPrefix [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3] := by⊢ isPrefix [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)1[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

The simplifier then proves `isPrefix [1, 2, 3] [1, 2, 3]` by rewriting it to `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`.

One can also assign the attribute any time after the definition takes place:

```lean

∃ t, l₁ ++ t = l₂
```

```lean
theorem List.isPrefix_self (as : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) : isPrefix as as :=
⟨[], byα:Type u_1as:[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α⊢ as [++](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAppend___mk) [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) as [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙⟩
```

```lean
[attribute](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Attributes/#Lean___Parser___Command___attribute) [simp] List.isPrefix_self
```

```lean

```

In all these cases, the attribute remains in effect in any file that

In [Notation]](#tpil-notation) below, we will discuss Lean's
mechanisms for defining notation, and see that they also support the
`local` modifier. However, in [Setting Options]](#tpil-setting-options), we will
discuss Lean's mechanisms for setting options, which does *not* follow
this pattern: options can *only* be set locally, which is to say,
their scope is always restricted to the current section or current
file.

### 6.6. More on Implicit Arguments {#tpil-more-on-implicit-arguments}

In [Implicit Arguments]](#tpil-implicit-arguments),
we saw that if Lean displays the type
of a term `t` as `{x : α} → β x`, then the curly brackets
indicate that `x` has been marked as an *implicit argument* to
`t`. This means that whenever you write `t`, a placeholder, or
“hole,” is inserted, so that `t` is replaced by `@t _`. If you
don't want that to happen, you have to write `@t` instead.

Notice that implicit arguments are inserted eagerly. Suppose we define
a function `f : (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → {y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → (z : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
Then, when we write the expression `f 7` without further
arguments, it is parsed as `@f 7 _`.

Lean offers a weaker annotation which specifies that a placeholder should only be added
*before* a subsequent explicit argument. It can be written with double braces, so the type of `f` would be
`f : (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → {{y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}} → (z : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`.
With this annotation, the expression `f 7` would be parsed as is, whereas `f 7 3` would be
parsed as `@f 7 _ 3`, just as it would be with the strong annotation.
This annotation can also be written as `⦃y : Nat⦄`, where the Unicode brackets are entered
as `\{{` and `\}}`, respectively.

To illustrate the difference, consider the following example, which
shows that a reflexive euclidean relation is both symmetric and
transitive.

```lean
def reflexive {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop :=
∀ (a : α), r a a
```

```lean
def symmetric {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop :=
∀ {a b : α}, r a b → r b a
```

```lean
def transitive {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop :=
∀ {a b c : α}, r a b → r b c → r a c
```

```lean
def Euclidean {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop :=
∀ {a b c : α}, r a b → r a c → r b c
```

```lean
theorem th1 {α : Type u} {r : α → α → Prop}
(reflr : reflexive r) (euclr : Euclidean r)
: symmetric r :=
fun {a b : α} =>
fun (h : r a b) =>
show r b a from euclr h (reflr _)
```

```lean
theorem th2 {α : Type u} {r : α → α → Prop}
(symmr : symmetric r) (euclr : Euclidean r)
: transitive r :=
fun {a b c : α} =>
fun (rab : r a b) (rbc : r b c) =>
euclr (symmr rab) rbc
```

```lean
theorem th3 {α : Type u} {r : α → α → Prop}
(reflr : reflexive r) (euclr : Euclidean r)
: transitive r :=
th2 (th1 reflr @euclr) @euclr
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (r : α → α → Prop)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (euclr : Euclidean r)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) euclr
```

```lean
euclr : r ?m.3 ?m.4 → r ?m.3 ?m.5 → r ?m.4 ?m.5
```

```lean

```

The results are broken down into small steps: `th1` shows that a
relation that is reflexive and euclidean is symmetric, and `th2`
shows that a relation that is symmetric and euclidean is
transitive. Then `th3` combines the two results. But notice that we
have to manually disable the implicit arguments in `euclr`, because
otherwise too many implicit arguments are inserted. The problem goes
away if we use weak implicit arguments:

```lean
def reflexive {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop :=
∀ (a : α), r a a
```

```lean
def symmetric {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop :=
∀ {{a b : α}}, r a b → r b a
```

```lean
def transitive {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop :=
∀ {{a b c : α}}, r a b → r b c → r a c
```

```lean
def Euclidean {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Prop :=
∀ {{a b c : α}}, r a b → r a c → r b c
```

```lean
theorem th1 {α : Type u} {r : α → α → Prop}
(reflr : reflexive r) (euclr : Euclidean r)
: symmetric r :=
fun {a b : α} =>
fun (h : r a b) =>
show r b a from euclr h (reflr _)
```

```lean
theorem th2 {α : Type u} {r : α → α → Prop}
(symmr : symmetric r) (euclr : Euclidean r)
: transitive r :=
fun {a b c : α} =>
fun (rab : r a b) (rbc : r b c) =>
euclr (symmr rab) rbc
```

```lean
theorem th3 {α : Type u} {r : α → α → Prop}
(reflr : reflexive r) (euclr : Euclidean r)
: transitive r :=
th2 (th1 reflr euclr) euclr
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (r : α → α → Prop)
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (euclr : Euclidean r)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) euclr
```

```lean
euclr : Euclidean r
```

```lean

```

There is a third kind of implicit argument that is denoted with square
brackets, `[` and `]`. These are used for type classes, as
explained in the chapter on [type classes](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Type-Classes/#type-classes).

### 6.7. Notation {#tpil-notation}

Identifiers in Lean can include any alphanumeric characters, including
Greek characters (other than ∀ , Σ , and λ , which, as we have seen,
have a special meaning in the dependent type theory). They can also
include subscripts, which can be entered by typing `\_` followed by
the desired subscripted character.

Lean's parser is extensible, which is to say, we can define new notation.

Lean's syntax can be extended and customized by users at every level,
ranging from basic “mixfix” notations to custom elaborators. In fact,
all builtin syntax is parsed and processed using the same mechanisms
and APIs open to users. In this section, we will describe and explain
the various extension points.

While introducing new notations is a relatively rare feature in
programming languages and sometimes even frowned upon because of its
potential to obscure code, it is an invaluable tool in formalization
for expressing established conventions and notations of the respective
field succinctly in code. Going beyond basic notations, Lean's
ability to factor out common boilerplate code into (well-behaved)
macros and to embed entire custom domain specific languages (DSLs) to
textually encode subproblems efficiently and readably can be of great
benefit to both programmers and proof engineers alike.

#### 6.7.1. Notations and Precedence {#tpil-notations-and-precedence}

The most basic syntax extension commands allow introducing new (or
overloading existing) prefix, infix, and postfix operators.

```lean
infixl:65 " + " => [HAdd.hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) -- left-associative
```

```lean
infix:50 " = " => [Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) -- non-associative
```

```lean
infixr:80 " ^ " => [HPow.hPow](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HPow___mk) -- right-associative
```

```lean
prefix:100 "-" => [Neg.neg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk)
```

```lean
postfix:[max](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Precedence/#precMax) "⁻¹" => Inv.inv
```

```lean

```

After the initial command name describing the operator kind (its
“fixity”), we give the *parsing precedence* of the operator preceded
by a colon `:`, then a new or existing token surrounded by double
quotes (the whitespace is used for pretty printing), then the function
this operator should be translated to after the arrow `=>`.

The precedence is a natural number describing how “tightly” an
operator binds to its arguments, encoding the order of operations. We
can make this more precise by looking at the commands the above unfold to:

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation):65 lhs:65 " + " rhs:66 => [HAdd.hAdd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) lhs rhs
```

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation):50 lhs:51 " = " rhs:51 => [Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) lhs rhs
```

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation):80 lhs:81 " ^ " rhs:80 => [HPow.hPow](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HPow___mk) lhs rhs
```

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation):100 "-" arg:100 => [Neg.neg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Neg___mk) arg
```

```lean
 -- `max` is a shorthand for precedence 1024:
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation):1024 arg:1024 "⁻¹" => Inv.inv arg
```

```lean

```

It turns out that all commands from the first code block are in fact
command *macros* translating to the more general `[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation)` command.
We will learn about writing such macros below. Instead of a single
token, the `[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation)` command accepts a mixed sequence of tokens and
named term placeholders with precedences, which can be referenced on
the right-hand side of `=>` and will be replaced by the respective
term parsed at that position. A placeholder with precedence `p`
accepts only notations with precedence at least `p` in that place.
Thus the string `a + b + c` cannot be parsed as the equivalent of
`a + (b + c)` because the right-hand side operand of an `infixl` notation
has precedence one greater than the notation itself. In contrast,
`infixr` reuses the notation's precedence for the right-hand side
operand, so `a ^ b ^ c` *can* be parsed as `a ^ (b ^ c)`. Note that
if we used `[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation)` directly to introduce an infix notation like

```lean
def wobble : α → β → γ := sorry
```

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation):65 lhs:65 " ~ " rhs:65 => wobble lhs rhs
```

```lean

```

where the precedences do not sufficiently determine associativity,
Lean's parser will default to right associativity. More precisely,
Lean's parser follows a local *longest parse* rule in the presence of
ambiguous grammars: when parsing the right-hand side of `a ~` in
`a ~ b ~ c`, it will continue parsing as long as possible (as the current
precedence allows), not stopping after `b` but parsing `~ c` as well.
Thus the term is equivalent to `a ~ (b ~ c)`.

As mentioned above, the `[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation)` command allows us to define
arbitrary *mixfix* syntax freely mixing tokens and placeholders.

```lean
set_option quotPrecheck false
```

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation):[max](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Precedence/#precMax) "(" e ")" => e
```

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation):10 Γ " ⊢ " e " : " τ => Typing Γ e τ
```

```lean

```

Placeholders without precedence default to `0`, i.e. they accept notations of any precedence in their place.
If two notations overlap, we again apply the longest parse rule:

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation):65 a " + " b:66 " + " c:66 => a + b - c
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) 1 + 2 + 3
```

```lean
0
```

```lean

```

The new notation is preferred to the binary notation since the latter,
before chaining, would stop parsing after `1 + 2`. If there are
multiple notations accepting the same longest parse, the choice will
be delayed until elaboration, which will fail unless exactly one
overload is type-correct.

### 6.8. Coercions {#tpil-coercions}

In Lean, the type of natural numbers, `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, is different from the
type of integers, `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`. But there is a function `[Int.ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` that
embeds the natural numbers in the integers, meaning that we can view
any natural number as an integer, when needed. Lean has mechanisms to
detect and insert *coercions* of this sort. Coercions can be explicitly
requested using the overloaded `↑` operator.

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (m n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (i j : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat))
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) i + m
```

```lean
i [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ↑m : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) i + m + j
```

```lean
i [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ↑m [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) j : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) i + m + n
```

```lean
i [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ↑m [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) ↑n : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
```

```lean

```

### 6.9. Displaying Information {#tpil-displaying-information}

There are a number of ways in which you can query Lean for information
about its current state and the objects and theorems that are
available in the current context. You have already seen two of the
most common ones, `#check` and `#eval`. Remember that `#check`
is often used in conjunction with the `@` operator, which makes all
of the arguments to a theorem or definition explicit. In addition, you
can use the `#print` command to get information about any
identifier. If the identifier denotes a definition or theorem, Lean
prints the type of the symbol, and its definition. If it is a constant
or an axiom, Lean indicates that fact, and shows the type.

```lean
-- examples with equality
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)
```

```lean
[Eq.{u_1}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) {α : Sort u_1} : α → α → Prop
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl)[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) : {α : Sort u_1} → α → α → Prop
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) [Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm)
```

```lean
[Eq.symm.{u}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm) {α : Sort u} {a b : α} (h : a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b) : b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm)[Eq.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm) : ∀ {α : Sort u_1} {a b : α}, a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b → b [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a
```

### 6.10. Setting Options {#tpil-setting-options}

Lean maintains a number of internal variables that can be set by users
to control its behavior. The syntax for doing so is as follows:

`set_option`` <name> <value>`

One very useful family of options controls the way Lean's *pretty printer* displays terms. The following options take an input of true or false:

```
pp.explicit  : display implicit arguments
pp.universes : display hidden universe parameters
pp.notation  : display output using defined notations
```

As an example, the following settings yield much longer output:

```lean
set_option pp.explicit true
```

```lean
set_option pp.universes true
```

```lean
set_option pp.notation false
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) 2 + 2 = 4
```

```lean
  (@[HAdd.hAdd.{0, 0, 0}](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (@instHAdd.{0} [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) instAddNat)
```

The command `set_option pp.all true` carries out these settings all
at once, whereas `set_option pp.all false` reverts to the previous
values. Pretty printing additional information is often very useful
when you are debugging a proof, or trying to understand a cryptic
error message. Too much information can be overwhelming, though, and
Lean's defaults are generally sufficient for ordinary interactions.

### 6.11. Using the Library {#tpil-using-the-library}

To use Lean effectively you will inevitably need to make use of
definitions and theorems in the library. Recall that the `import`
command at the beginning of a file imports previously compiled results
from other files, and that importing is transitive; if you import
`Foo` and `Foo` imports `Bar`, then the definitions and theorems
from `Bar` are available to you as well. But the act of opening a
namespace, which provides shorter names, does not carry over. In each
file, you need to open the namespaces you wish to use.

In general, it is important for you to be familiar with the library
and its contents, so you know what theorems, definitions, notations,
and resources are available to you. Below we will see that Lean's
editor modes can also help you find things you need, but studying the
contents of the library directly is often unavoidable. Lean's standard
library can be found online, on GitHub:

- [https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/tree/master/src/Init](https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/tree/master/src/Init)
- [https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/tree/master/src/Std](https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/tree/master/src/Std)

You can see the contents of these directories and files using GitHub's
browser interface. If you have installed Lean on your own computer,
you can find the library in the `lean` folder, and explore it with
your file manager. Comment headers at the top of each file provide
additional information.

Lean's library developers follow general naming guidelines to make it
easier to guess the name of a theorem you need, or to find it using
tab completion in editors with a Lean mode that supports this, which
is discussed in the next section. Identifiers are generally
`camelCase`, and types are `CamelCase`. For theorem names,
we rely on descriptive names where the different components are separated
by `_`s. Often the name of theorem simply describes the conclusion:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Nat.succ_ne_zero
```

```lean
Nat.succ_ne_zero (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ≠ 0
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Nat.zero_add
```

```lean
Nat.zero_add (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : 0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Nat.mul_one
```

```lean
Nat.mul_one (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : n [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Nat.le_of_succ_le_succ
```

```lean
Nat.le_of_succ_le_succ {n m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} : n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) m.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → n [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) m
```

```lean

```

Remember that identifiers in Lean can be organized into hierarchical
namespaces. For example, the theorem named `le_of_succ_le_succ` in the
namespace `Nat` has full name `Nat.le_of_succ_le_succ`, but the shorter
name is made available by the command `open`` Nat` (for names not marked as
`protected`). We will see in the chapters on [inductive types](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Inductive-Types/#inductive-types)
and [structures and records](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Structures-and-Records/#structures-and-records)
that defining structures and inductive data types in Lean generates
associated operations, and these are stored in
a namespace with the same name as the type under definition. For
example, the product type comes with the following operations:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Prod.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)[Prod.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) : {α : Type u_1} → {β : Type u_2} → α → β → α [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) β
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Prod.fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)[Prod.fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) : {α : Type u_1} → {β : Type u_2} → α [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) β → α
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Prod.snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)[Prod.snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) : {α : Type u_1} → {β : Type u_2} → α [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) β → β
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Prod.rec
```

```lean
@Prod.rec : {α : Type u_2} →
  {β : Type u_3} → {motive : α [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) β → Sort u_1} → ((fst : α) → (snd : β) → motive [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)fst[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) snd[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)) → (t : α [×](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) β) → motive t
```

```lean

```

The first is used to construct a pair, whereas the next two,
`[Prod.fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)` and `[Prod.snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`, project the two elements. The last,
`Prod.rec`, provides another mechanism for defining functions on a
product in terms of a function on the two components. Names like
`Prod.rec` are *protected*, which means that one has to use the full
name even when the `Prod` namespace is open.

With the propositions as types correspondence, logical connectives are
also instances of inductive types, and so we tend to use dot notation
for them as well:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)[And.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) : ∀ {a b : Prop}, a → b → a [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) b
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @And.casesOn
```

```lean
@And.casesOn : {a b : Prop} →
  {motive : a [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) b → Sort u_1} → (t : a [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) b) → ((left : a) → (right : b) → motive ⋯) → motive t
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[And.left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)[And.left](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) : ∀ {a b : Prop}, a [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) b → a
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[And.right](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)[And.right](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) : ∀ {a b : Prop}, a [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) b → b
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)[Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) : ∀ {a b : Prop}, a → a [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) b
```

### 6.12. Auto Bound Implicit Arguments {#tpil-auto-bound-implicit-arguments}

In the previous section, we have shown how implicit arguments make functions more convenient to use.
However, functions such as `compose` are still quite verbose to define. Note that the universe
polymorphic `compose` is even more verbose than the one previously defined.

```lean
[universe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Universes/#Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u v w
```

```lean
def compose {α : Type u} {β : Type v} {γ : Type w}
(g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (x : α) : γ :=
g (f x)
```

```lean

```

You can avoid the `universe` command by providing the universe parameters when defining `compose`.

```lean
def compose.{u, v, w}
{α : Type u} {β : Type v} {γ : Type w}
(g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (x : α) : γ :=
g (f x)
```

```lean

```

Lean 4 supports a new feature called *auto bound implicit arguments*. It makes functions such as
`compose` much more convenient to write. When Lean processes the header of a declaration,
any unbound identifier is automatically added as an implicit argument. With this feature we can write `compose` as

```lean
def compose (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (x : α) : γ :=
g (f x)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @compose
```

```lean
@compose : {β : Sort u_1} → {γ : Sort u_2} → {α : Sort u_3} → (β → γ) → (α → β) → α → γ
```

```lean

```

Note that Lean inferred a more general type using `Sort` instead of `Type`.

Although we love this feature and use it extensively when implementing Lean,
we realize some users may feel uncomfortable with it. Thus, you can disable it using
the command `set_option [autoImplicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#autoImplicit) false`.

```lean
set_option [autoImplicit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Headers-and-Signatures/#autoImplicit) false
```

```lean
/--
error: Unknown identifier `β`
Note: It is not possible to treat `β` as an implicitly bound variable here because the `autoImplicit` option is set to `false`.
---
error: Unknown identifier `γ`
Note: It is not possible to treat `γ` as an implicitly bound variable here because the `autoImplicit` option is set to `false`.
---
error: Unknown identifier `α`
Note: It is not possible to treat `α` as an implicitly bound variable here because the `autoImplicit` option is set to `false`.
---
error: Unknown identifier `β`
Note: It is not possible to treat `β` as an implicitly bound variable here because the `autoImplicit` option is set to `false`.
---
error: Unknown identifier `α`
Note: It is not possible to treat `α` as an implicitly bound variable here because the `autoImplicit` option is set to `false`.
---
error: Unknown identifier `γ`
Note: It is not possible to treat `γ` as an implicitly bound variable here because the `autoImplicit` option is set to `false`.
-/
[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd) [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)
def compose (g : β → γ) (f : α → β) (x : α) : γ :=
g (f x)
```

```lean

```

### 6.13. Implicit Lambdas {#tpil-implicit-lambdas}

When the expected type of an expression is a function that is awaiting implicit
arguments, the elaborator automatically introduces the corresponding lambdas.
For example, `[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk)`'s type states that the first argument is an implicit type
`α`, but `[ReaderT.pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ReaderT___pure)`'s first argument is the reader monad's context type `ρ`.
It is automatically surrounded with a `fun`` {α} => ...`, which allows the elaborator to
correctly fill in the implicit arguments in the body.

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (ρ : Type) (m : Type → Type) [[Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) m]
```

```lean
instance : [Monad](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Monad___mk) ([ReaderT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ReaderT) ρ m) where
[pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Pure___mk) := [ReaderT.pure](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ReaderT___pure)
[bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/#Bind___mk) := [ReaderT.bind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Functors___-Monads-and--do--Notation/Varieties-of-Monads/#ReaderT___bind)
```

```lean

```

Users can disable the implicit lambda feature by using `@` or writing
a lambda expression with `{}` or `[]` binder annotations. Here are
few examples

```lean
set_option linter.unusedVariables false
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex2
```

```lean
def id1 : {α : Type} → α → α :=
fun x => x
```

```lean
def listId : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) ({α : Type} → α → α) :=
(fun x => x) :: []
```

```lean
-- In this example, implicit lambda introduction has been disabled because
-- we use `@` before {kw}`fun`
def id2 : {α : Type} → α → α :=
@fun α (x : α) => [id1]](#tpil-Ex2___id1) x
```

```lean
def id3 : {α : Type} → α → α :=
@fun α x => [id1]](#tpil-Ex2___id1) x
```

```lean
def id4 : {α : Type} → α → α :=
fun x => [id1]](#tpil-Ex2___id1) x
```

```lean
-- In this example, implicit lambda introduction has been disabled
-- because we used the binder annotation `{...}`
def id5 : {α : Type} → α → α :=
fun {α} x => [id1]](#tpil-Ex2___id1) x
```

```lean
end Ex2
```

### 6.14. Sugar for Simple Functions {#tpil-sugar-for-simple-functions}

Lean includes a notation for describing simple functions using anonymous
placeholders rather than `fun`. When `·` occurs as part of a term,
the nearest enclosing parentheses become a function with the `·` as its argument.
If the parentheses include multiple placeholders without other intervening parentheses,
then they are made into arguments from left to right. Here are a few examples:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex3
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) (· + 1)
```

```lean
fun x => x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) (2 - ·)
```

```lean
fun x => 2 [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].[foldl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___foldl) (· * ·) 1
```

```lean
120
```

```lean

```

```lean
def f (x y z : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
x + y + z
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) ([f]](#tpil-Ex3___f) · 1 ·)
```

```lean
fun x1 x2 => [f]](#tpil-Ex3___f) x1 1 x2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [(1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 6)].[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) (·.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
```

```lean
[1, 3, 5]
```

```lean
end Ex3
```

Nested parentheses introduce new functions. In the following example, two different lambda expressions are created:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) ([Prod.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) · (· + 1))
```


### 6.15. Named Arguments {#tpil-named-arguments}

Named arguments enable you to specify an argument for a parameter by
matching the argument with its name rather than with its position in
the parameter list. If you don't remember the order of the parameters
but know their names, you can send the arguments in any order. You may
also provide the value for an implicit parameter when Lean failed to
infer it. Named arguments also improve the readability of your code by
identifying what each argument represents.

```lean
def sum (xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
xs.[foldl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___foldl) (init := 0) (·+·)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [sum]](#tpil-sum) [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

```lean
10
```

