example {a b : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} {p : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop}
(h₁ : p a b b) (h₂ : b = a) :
p a a b :=
[Eq.subst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___subst) (motive := fun x => p a x b) h₂ h₁
```

x + y + w - z

You can use `..` to provide missing explicit arguments as `_`.
This feature combined with named arguments is useful for writing patterns. Here is an example:

```lean
inductive Term where
| var (name : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray))
| num (val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
| app (fn : Term) (arg : Term)
| lambda (name : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)) (type : Term) (body : Term)
```

```lean
def getBinderName : Term → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
| Term.lambda (name := n) .. => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) n
| _ => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

```lean
def getBinderType : Term → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) Term
| Term.lambda (type := t) .. => [some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) t
| _ => [none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)
```

```

Ellipses are also useful when explicit arguments can be automatically
inferred by Lean, and we want to avoid a sequence of `_`s.

```lean

[congrArg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#congrArg) f (Nat.add_assoc ..)
```

## Inductive Types {#tpil-inductive-types}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Inductive-Types/

We have seen that Lean's formal foundation includes basic types,
`Prop`, `Type 0`, `Type 1`, `Type 2`, ..., and allows for the formation of
dependent function types, `(x : α) → β`. In the examples, we have
also made use of additional types like `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`,
and type constructors, like `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`, and product, `×`. In fact, in
Lean's library, every concrete type other than the universes and every
type constructor other than dependent arrows is an instance of a general family of
type constructions known as *inductive types*. It is remarkable that
it is possible to construct a substantial edifice of mathematics based
on nothing more than the type universes, dependent arrow types, and inductive
types; everything else follows from those.

Intuitively, an inductive type is built up from a specified list of
constructors. In Lean, the syntax for specifying such a type is as
follows:

```
inductive Foo where
  | constructor₁ : ... → Foo
  | constructor₂ : ... → Foo
  ...
  | constructorₙ : ... → Foo
```

The intuition is that each constructor specifies a way of building new
objects of `Foo`, possibly from previously constructed values. The
type `Foo` consists of nothing more than the objects that are
constructed in this way.

We will see below that the arguments of the constructors can include
objects of type `Foo`, subject to a certain “positivity” constraint,
which guarantees that elements of `Foo` are built from the bottom
up. Roughly speaking, each `...` can be any arrow type constructed from
`Foo` and previously defined types, in which `Foo` appears, if at
all, only as the “target” of the dependent arrow type.

We will provide a number of examples of inductive types. We will also
consider slight generalizations of the scheme above, to mutually
defined inductive types, and so-called *inductive families*.

As with the logical connectives, every inductive type comes with
introduction rules, which show how to construct an element of the
type, and elimination rules, which show how to “use” an element of the
type in another construction. The analogy to the logical connectives
should not come as a surprise; as we will see below, they, too, are
examples of inductive type constructions. You have already seen the
introduction rules for an inductive type: they are just the
constructors that are specified in the definition of the type. The
elimination rules provide for a principle of recursion on the type,
which includes, as a special case, a principle of induction as well.

In the next chapter, we will describe Lean's function definition
package, which provides even more convenient ways to define functions
on inductive types and carry out inductive proofs. But because the
notion of an inductive type is so fundamental, we feel it is important
to start with a low-level, hands-on understanding. We will start with
some basic examples of inductive types, and work our way up to more
elaborate and complex examples.

### 7.1. Enumerated Types {#tpil-enumerated-types}

The simplest kind of inductive type is a type with a finite, enumerated list of elements.

```lean
inductive Weekday where
| sunday : Weekday
| monday : Weekday
| tuesday : Weekday
| wednesday : Weekday
| thursday : Weekday
| friday : Weekday
| saturday : Weekday
```

```lean

```

The `inductive` command creates a new type, `Weekday`. The
constructors all live in the `Weekday` namespace.

```lean
inductive Weekday where
| sunday : Weekday
| monday : Weekday
| tuesday : Weekday
| wednesday : Weekday
| thursday : Weekday
| friday : Weekday
| saturday : Weekday
```

You can omit `: Weekday` when declaring the `Weekday` inductive type.

```lean
inductive Weekday where
| sunday
| monday
| tuesday
| wednesday
| thursday
| friday
| saturday
```

```lean

```

Think of `sunday`, `monday`, ... , `saturday` as
being distinct elements of `Weekday`, with no other distinguishing
properties. The elimination principle, `Weekday.rec`, is defined
along with the type `Weekday` and its constructors. It is also known
as a *recursor*, and it is what makes the type “inductive”: it allows
us to define a function on `Weekday` by assigning values
corresponding to each constructor. The intuition is that an inductive
type is exhaustively generated by the constructors, and has no
elements beyond those they construct.

```lean
Weekday.rec.{u} {motive : Weekday → Sort u}
(sunday : motive Weekday.sunday)
(monday : motive Weekday.monday)
(tuesday : motive Weekday.tuesday)
(wednesday : motive Weekday.wednesday)
(thursday : motive Weekday.thursday)
(friday : motive Weekday.friday)
(saturday : motive [Weekday.saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next))
(t : Weekday) :
motive t
```

We will use the `match` expression to define a function from `Weekday`
to the natural numbers:

```lean
inductive Weekday where
| sunday : Weekday
| monday : Weekday
| tuesday : Weekday
| wednesday : Weekday
| thursday : Weekday
| friday : Weekday
| saturday : Weekday
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Weekday
```

```lean
def numberOfDay (d : Weekday) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) d [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| sunday => 1
| monday => 2
| tuesday => 3
| wednesday => 4
| thursday => 5
| friday => 6
| [saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next) => 7
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) numberOfDay Weekday.sunday

When using Lean's logic, the `match` expression is compiled using the *recursor* `Weekday.rec` generated when
you declare the inductive type. This ensures that the resulting term is well-defined in the type theory. For compiled code,
`match` is compiled as in other functional programming languages.

```lean
inductive Weekday where
| sunday : Weekday
| monday : Weekday
| tuesday : Weekday
| wednesday : Weekday
| thursday : Weekday
| friday : Weekday
| saturday : Weekday

| sunday => 1
| monday => 2

    (h_4 [Unit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)) (h_5 [Unit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)) (h_6 [Unit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)) (h_7 [Unit.unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit))
```

When declaring an inductive datatype, you can use `[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)` to instruct
Lean to generate a function that converts `Weekday` objects into text.
This function is used by the `#eval` command to display `Weekday` objects.
If no `[Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)` exists, `#eval` attempts to derive one on the spot.

```lean
inductive Weekday where
| sunday
| monday
| tuesday
| wednesday
| thursday
| friday
| saturday
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Weekday
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) tuesday
```

```lean
Weekday.tuesday
```

```lean

```

It is often useful to group definitions and theorems related to a
structure in a namespace with the same name. For example, we can put
the `numberOfDay` function in the `Weekday` namespace. We are
then allowed to use the shorter name when we open the namespace.

We can define functions from `Weekday` to `Weekday`:

```lean
inductive Weekday where
| sunday : Weekday
| monday : Weekday
| tuesday : Weekday
| wednesday : Weekday
| thursday : Weekday
| friday : Weekday
| saturday : Weekday
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Weekday
```

```lean
def next (d : Weekday) : Weekday :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) d [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| sunday => monday
| monday => tuesday
| tuesday => wednesday
| wednesday => thursday
| thursday => friday
| friday => [saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next)
| [saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next) => sunday
```

```lean
def previous (d : Weekday) : Weekday :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) d [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| sunday => [saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next)
| monday => sunday
| tuesday => monday
| wednesday => tuesday
| thursday => wednesday
| friday => thursday
| [saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next) => friday
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [next]](#tpil-Weekday___next) ([next]](#tpil-Weekday___next) tuesday)
```

How can we prove the general theorem that `[next]](#tpil-Weekday___next) ([previous]](#tpil-Weekday___next) d) = d`
for any Weekday `d`? You can use `match` to provide a proof of the claim for each
constructor:

```lean

| sunday : Weekday

| tuesday : Weekday

| friday : Weekday

[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Weekday
def next (d : Weekday) : Weekday :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) d [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| sunday => monday
| monday => tuesday
| tuesday => wednesday
| wednesday => thursday
| thursday => friday
| friday => [saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next)
| [saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next) => sunday
def previous (d : Weekday) : Weekday :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) d [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| sunday => [saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next)
| monday => sunday
| tuesday => monday
| wednesday => tuesday
| thursday => wednesday
| friday => thursday
| [saturday]](#tpil-Weekday-next-next) => friday
```

[Tactics for Inductive Types]](#tpil-tactics-for-inductive-types) below will introduce additional
tactics that are specifically designed to make use of inductive types.

Notice that, under the [propositions-as-types]](#tpil---tech-term-propositions-as-types) correspondence, we can
use `match` to prove theorems as well as define functions. In other
words, under the [propositions-as-types]](#tpil---tech-term-propositions-as-types) correspondence, the proof by
cases is a kind of definition by cases, where what is being “defined”
is a proof instead of a piece of data.

The `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` type in the Lean library is an instance of
enumerated type.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Bool where
| false : [Bool]](#tpil-Hidden___Bool)
| true : [Bool]](#tpil-Hidden___Bool)
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

(To run these examples, we put them in a namespace called `Hidden`,
so that a name like `Bool` does not conflict with the `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` in
the standard library. This is necessary because these types are part
of the Lean “prelude” that is automatically imported when the system
is started.)

As an exercise, you should think about what the introduction and
elimination rules for these types do. As a further exercise, we
suggest defining boolean operations `[and](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___and)`, `[or](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___or)`, `[not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)` on the
`[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` type, and verifying common identities. Note that you can define a
binary operation like `[and](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___and)` using `match`:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
def and (a b : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) a [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => b
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

Similarly, most identities can be proved by introducing suitable `match`, and then using `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)`.

### 7.2. Constructors with Arguments {#tpil-constructors-with-arguments}

Enumerated types are a very special case of inductive types, in which
the constructors take no arguments at all. In general, a
“construction” can depend on data, which is then represented in the
constructed argument. Consider the definitions of the product type and
sum type in the library:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Prod (α : Type u) (β : Type v)
| mk : α → β → Prod α β
```

```lean
inductive Sum (α : Type u) (β : Type v) where
| inl : α → Sum α β
| inr : β → Sum α β
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

Consider what is going on in these examples.
The product type has one constructor, `[Prod.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`,
which takes two arguments. To define a function on `Prod α β`, we
can assume the input is of the form `[Prod.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) a b`, and we have to
specify the output, in terms of `a` and `b`. We can use this to
define the two projections for `Prod`. Remember that the standard
library defines notation `α × β` for `Prod α β` and `(a, b)` for
`[Prod.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) a b`.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
inductive Prod (α : Type u) (β : Type v)
| mk : α → β → Prod α β
```

```lean
def fst {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (p : Prod α β) : α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) p [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| Prod.mk a b => a
```

```lean
def snd {α : Type u} {β : Type v} (p : Prod α β) : β :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) p [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| Prod.mk a b => b
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

The function `fst` takes a pair, `p`. The `match` interprets
`p` as a pair, `Prod.mk a b`. Recall also from [Dependent Type Theory]](#tpil-dependent-type-theory)
that to give these definitions the greatest generality possible, we allow
the types `α` and `β` to belong to any universe.

Here is another example where we use the recursor `Prod.casesOn` instead
of `match`.

```lean
def prod_example (p : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
Prod.casesOn (motive := fun _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) p
(fun b n => [cond](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#cond) b (2 * n) (2 * n + 1))
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [prod_example]](#tpil-prod_example) ([true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), 3)
```

```lean
6
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [prod_example]](#tpil-prod_example) ([false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), 3)
```

```lean
7
```

```lean

```

The argument `motive` is used to specify the type of the object you want to
construct, and it is a function because it may depend on the pair.
The `[cond](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#cond)` function is a boolean conditional: `[cond](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#cond) b t1 t2`
returns `t1` if `b` is true, and `t2` otherwise.
The function `prod_example` takes a pair consisting of a boolean,
`b`, and a number, `n`, and returns either `2 * n` or `2 * n + 1`
according to whether `b` is true or false.

In contrast, the sum type has *two* constructors, `[inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl)` and `[inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl)`
(for “insert left” and “insert right”), each of which takes *one*
(explicit) argument. To define a function on `[Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) α β`, we have to
handle two cases: either the input is of the form `[inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) a`, in which
case we have to specify an output value in terms of `a`, or the
input is of the form `[inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) b`, in which case we have to specify an
output value in terms of `b`.

```lean
def sum_example (s : [Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
Sum.casesOn (motive := fun _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) s
(fun n => 2 * n)
(fun n => 2 * n + 1)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [sum_example]](#tpil-sum_example) ([Sum.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) 3)
```

```lean
6
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [sum_example]](#tpil-sum_example) ([Sum.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) 3)
```

```lean
7
```

```lean

```

This example is similar to the previous one, but now an input to
`sum_example` is implicitly either of the form `[inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) n` or `[inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) n`.
In the first case, the function returns `2 * n`, and the second
case, it returns `2 * n + 1`.

Notice that the product type depends on parameters `α β : Type`
which are arguments to the constructors as well as `[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`. Lean
detects when these arguments can be inferred from later arguments to a
constructor or the return type, and makes them implicit in that case.

In [Defining the Natural Numbers]](#tpil-defining-the-natural-numbers)
we will see what happens when the
constructor of an inductive type takes arguments from the inductive
type itself. What characterizes the examples we consider in this
section is that each constructor relies only on previously specified types.

Notice that a type with multiple constructors is disjunctive: an
element of `[Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) α β` is either of the form `[inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) a` *or* of the
form `[inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl) b`. A constructor with multiple arguments introduces
conjunctive information: from an element `[Prod.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) a b` of
`[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) α β` we can extract `a` *and* `b`. An arbitrary inductive type can
include both features, by having any number of constructors, each of
which takes any number of arguments.

As with function definitions, Lean's inductive definition syntax will
let you put named arguments to the constructors before the colon:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Prod (α : Type u) (β : Type v) where
| mk (fst : α) (snd : β) : Prod α β
```

```lean
inductive Sum (α : Type u) (β : Type v) where
| inl (a : α) : Sum α β
| inr (b : β) : Sum α β
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

The results of these definitions are essentially the same as the ones given earlier in this section.

A type, like `Prod`, that has only one constructor is purely
conjunctive: the constructor simply packs the list of arguments into a
single piece of data, essentially a tuple where the type of subsequent
arguments can depend on the type of the initial argument. We can also
think of such a type as a “record” or a “structure”. In Lean, the
keyword `structure` can be used to define such an inductive type as
well as its projections, at the same time.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
structure Prod (α : Type u) (β : Type v) where
mk ::
fst : α
snd : β
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

This example simultaneously introduces the inductive type, `Prod`,
its constructor, `mk`, the usual eliminators (`rec` and
`recOn`), as well as the projections, `fst` and `snd`, as
defined above.

If you do not name the constructor, Lean uses `mk` as a default. For
example, the following defines a record to store a color as a triple
of RGB values:

```lean
structure Color where
red : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
green : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
blue : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

```lean
def yellow := Color.mk 255 255 0
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) Color.red [yellow]](#tpil-Color)
```

```lean
255
```

```lean

```

The definition of `yellow` forms the record with the three values
shown, and the projection `Color.red` returns the red component.

The `structure` command is especially useful for defining algebraic
structures, and Lean provides substantial infrastructure to support
working with them. Here, for example, is the definition of a
semigroup:

```lean
structure Semigroup where
carrier : Type u
mul : carrier → carrier → carrier
mul_assoc : ∀ a b c, mul (mul a b) c = mul a (mul b c)
```

```lean

```

We will see more examples in the chapter on [structures and records](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Structures-and-Records/#structures-and-records).

We have already discussed the dependent product type `Sigma`:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Sigma {α : Type u} (β : α → Type v) where
| mk : (a : α) → β a → [Sigma]](#tpil-Hidden___Sigma) β
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

Two more examples of inductive types in the library are the following:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Option (α : Type u) where
| none : [Option]](#tpil-Hidden___Option) α
| some : α → [Option]](#tpil-Hidden___Option) α
```

```lean
inductive Inhabited (α : Type u) where
| mk : α → [Inhabited]](#tpil-Hidden___Option) α
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

In the semantics of dependent type theory, there is no built-in notion
of a partial function. Every element of a function type `α → β` or a
dependent function type `(a : α) → β` is assumed to have a value
at every input. The `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` type provides a way of representing partial functions. An
element of `[Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) β` is either `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)` or of the form `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) b`,
for some value `b : β`. Thus we can think of an element `f` of the
type `α → [Option](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) β` as being a partial function from `α` to `β`:
for every `a : α`, `f a` either returns `[none](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none)`, indicating
`f a` is “undefined”, or `[some](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Optional-Values/#Option___none) b`.

An element of `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) α` is simply a witness to the fact that
there is an element of `α`. Later, we will see that `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)` is
an example of a *type class* in Lean: Lean can be instructed that
suitable base types are inhabited, and can automatically infer that
other constructed types are inhabited on that basis.

As exercises, we encourage you to develop a notion of composition for
partial functions from `α` to `β` and `β` to `γ`, and show
that it behaves as expected. We also encourage you to show that
`[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` and `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` are inhabited, that the product of two inhabited
types is inhabited, and that the type of functions to an inhabited
type is inhabited.

### 7.3. Inductively Defined Propositions {#tpil-inductively-defined-propositions}

Inductively defined types can live in any type universe, including the
bottom-most one, `Prop`. In fact, this is exactly how the logical
connectives are defined.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive False : Prop
```

```lean
inductive True : Prop where
| intro : [True]](#tpil-Hidden___False)
```

```lean
inductive And (a b : Prop) : Prop where
| intro : a → b → [And]](#tpil-Hidden___False) a b
```

```lean
inductive Or (a b : Prop) : Prop where
| inl : a → [Or]](#tpil-Hidden___False) a b
| inr : b → [Or]](#tpil-Hidden___False) a b
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

You should think about how these give rise to the introduction and
elimination rules that you have already seen. There are rules that
govern what the eliminator of an inductive type can eliminate *to*,
that is, what kinds of types can be the target of a recursor. Roughly
speaking, what characterizes inductive types in `Prop` is that one
can only eliminate to other types in `Prop`. This is consistent with
the understanding that if `p : Prop`, an element `hp : p` carries
no data. There is a small exception to this rule, however, which we
will discuss below, in [Inductive Families]](#tpil-inductive-families).

Even the existential quantifier is inductively defined:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Exists {α : Sort u} (p : α → Prop) : Prop where
| intro (w : α) (h : p w) : [Exists]](#tpil-Hidden___Exists) p
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

Keep in mind that the notation `∃ x : α, p` is syntactic sugar for `[Exists](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) (fun x : α => p)`.

The definitions of `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`, `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`, `[And](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)`, and `[Or](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)` are
perfectly analogous to the definitions of `[Empty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Empty-Type/#Empty)`, `[Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit)`,
`[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`, and `[Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl)`. The difference is that the first group yields
elements of `Prop`, and the second yields elements of `Type u` for
some `u`. In a similar way, `∃ x : α, p` is a `Prop`-valued
variant of `Σ x : α, β`.

This is a good place to mention another inductive type, denoted
`{x : α // p}`, which is sort of a hybrid between
`∃ x : α, p` and `Σ x : α, β`.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Subtype {α : Type u} (p : α → Prop) where
| mk : (x : α) → p x → Subtype p
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

In fact, in Lean, `Subtype` is defined using the structure command:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
structure Subtype {α : Sort u} (p : α → Prop) where
val : α
property : p val
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

The notation `{x : α // p x}` is syntactic sugar for `[Subtype](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Subtypes/#Subtype___mk) (fun x : α => p x)`.
It is modeled after subset notation in set theory: the idea is that `{x : α // p x}`
denotes the collection of elements of `α` that have property `p`.

### 7.4. Defining the Natural Numbers {#tpil-defining-the-natural-numbers}

The inductively defined types we have seen so far are “flat”:
constructors wrap data and insert it into a type, and the
corresponding recursor unpacks the data and acts on it. Things get
much more interesting when the constructors act on elements of the
very type being defined. A canonical example is the type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` of
natural numbers:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Nat where
| zero : Nat
| succ : Nat → Nat
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

There are two constructors. We start with `[zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`; it takes
no arguments, so we have it from the start. In contrast, the
constructor `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` can only be applied to a previously constructed
`[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`. Applying it to `[zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` yields `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`. Applying
it again yields `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and so on. Intuitively,
`[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is the “smallest” type with these constructors, meaning that
it is exhaustively (and freely) generated by starting with `[zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`
and applying `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` repeatedly.

As before, the recursor for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is designed to define a dependent
function `f` from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to any domain, that is, an element `f`
of `(n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → motive n` for some `motive : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Sort u`.
It has to handle two cases: the case where the input is `[zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and the case where
the input is of the form `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n` for some `n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`. In the first
case, we simply specify a target value with the appropriate type, as
before. In the second case, however, the recursor can assume that a
value of `f` at `n` has already been computed. As a result, the
next argument to the recursor specifies a value for `f ([succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n)` in
terms of `n` and `f n`. If we check the type of the recursor,
you find the following:

```lean
Nat.rec.{u} :
{motive : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Sort u} →
(zero : motive [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) →
(succ : (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → motive n → motive ([Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n)) →
(t : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → motive t
```

The implicit argument, `motive`, is the codomain of the function being defined.
In type theory it is common to say `motive` is the *motive* for the elimination/recursion,
since it describes the kind of object we wish to construct.
The next two arguments specify how to compute the zero and successor cases, as described above.
They are also known as the *minor premises*.
Finally, the `t : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is the input to the function. It is also known as the *major premise*.

The `Nat.recOn` is similar to `Nat.rec` but the major premise occurs before the minor premises.

```lean
Nat.recOn.{u} :
{motive : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Sort u} →
(t : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) →
(zero : motive [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) →
(succ : ((n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → motive n → motive ([Nat.succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n))) →
motive t
```

Consider, for example, the addition function `add m n` on the
natural numbers. Fixing `m`, we can define addition by recursion on
`n`. In the base case, we set `add m [zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `m`. In the
successor step, assuming the value `add m n` is already determined,
we define `add m ([succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n)` to be `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (add m n)`.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Nat where
| zero : Nat
| succ : Nat → Nat
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

```lean
def add (m n : Nat) : Nat :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| Nat.zero => m
| [Nat.succ]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) n => [Nat.succ]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) ([add]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) m n)
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Nat
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [add]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) ([succ]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) ([succ]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) zero)) ([succ]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) zero)
```

```lean
Hidden.Nat.succ (Hidden.Nat.succ (Hidden.Nat.succ (Hidden.Nat.zero)))
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

It is useful to put such definitions into a namespace, `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`. We can
then go on to define familiar notation in that namespace. The two
defining equations for addition now hold definitionally:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
inductive Nat where
| zero : Nat
| succ : Nat → Nat
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Nat
```

```lean
def add (m n : Nat) : Nat :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| Nat.zero => m
| [Nat.succ]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) n => [Nat.succ]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) ([add]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat___add) m n)
```

```lean
instance : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) Nat where
[add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) := [add]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat___add)
```

```lean
theorem add_zero (m : Nat) : m + zero = m := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
theorem add_succ (m n : Nat) : m + [succ]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) n = [succ]](#tpil-Hidden___Nat-next) (m + n) := rfl
```

```lean
end Nat
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

We will explain how the `instance` command works in
the [Type Classes](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Type-Classes/#type-classes) chapter. In the examples below, we will use
Lean's version of the natural numbers.

Proving a fact like `0 + n = n`, however, requires a proof by induction.
As observed above, the induction principle is just a special case of the recursion principle,
when the codomain `motive n` is an element of `Prop`. It represents the familiar
pattern of an inductive proof: to prove `∀ n, motive n`, first prove `motive 0`,
and then, for arbitrary `n`, assume `ih : motive n` and prove `motive (n + 1)`.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Nat
```

```lean
theorem zero_add (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : 0 + n = n :=
Nat.recOn (motive := fun x => 0 + x = x)
n
(show 0 + 0 = 0 from [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next))
(fun (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (ih : 0 + n = n) =>
show 0 + (n + 1) = n + 1 from
calc 0 + (n + 1)
_ = (0 + n) + 1 := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
_ = n + 1 := byn✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih:0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n⊢ 0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [rw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rw) [ihn✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih:0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n⊢ n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1]All goals completed! 🐙)

Notice that, once again, when `Nat.recOn` is used in the context of
a proof, it is really the induction principle in disguise. The
`rw` and `simp` tactics tend to be very effective in proofs
like these. In this case, each can be used to reduce the proof to:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Nat
```

As another example, let us prove the associativity of addition,
`∀ m n k, m + n + k = m + (n + k)`.
(The notation `+`, as we have defined it, associates to the left, so `m + n + k` is really `(m + n) + k`.)
The hardest part is figuring out which variable to do the induction on. Since addition is defined by recursion on the second argument,
`k` is a good guess, and once we make that choice the proof almost writes itself:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Nat
```

```lean
theorem add_assoc (m n k : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : m + n + k = m + (n + k) :=
Nat.recOn (motive := fun k => m + n + k = m + (n + k)) k
(show m + n + 0 = m + (n + 0) from [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next))
(fun k (ih : m + n + k = m + (n + k)) =>
show m + n + (k + 1) = m + (n + (k + 1)) from
calc m + n + (k + 1)
_ = (m + n + k) + 1 := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
_ = (m + (n + k)) + 1 := At this point, we see that we need another supporting fact, namely, that `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (n + m)`` = ``[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n + m`.
You can prove this by induction on `m`:

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Nat
```

### 7.5. Other Recursive Data Types {#tpil-other-recursive-data-types}

Let us consider some more examples of inductively defined types. For
any type, `α`, the type `[List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α` of lists of elements of `α` is
defined in the library.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive List (α : Type u) where
| nil : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α
| cons (h : α) (t : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α) : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α
```

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) List
```

```lean
def append (as bs : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α) : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) as [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [nil]](#tpil-Hidden___List) => bs
| [cons]](#tpil-Hidden___List) a as => [cons]](#tpil-Hidden___List) a ([append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) as bs)
```

```lean
theorem nil_append (as : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α) : [append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) [nil]](#tpil-Hidden___List) as = as :=
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
theorem cons_append (a : α) (as bs : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α) :
[append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) ([cons]](#tpil-Hidden___List) a as) bs = [cons]](#tpil-Hidden___List) a ([append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) as bs) :=
rfl
```

```lean
end List
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

A list of elements of type `α` is either the empty list, `nil`, or
an element `h : α` followed by a list `t : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α`.
The first element, `h`, is commonly known as the “head” of the list,
and the remainder, `t`, is known as the “tail.”

As an exercise, prove the following:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
inductive List (α : Type u) where
| nil : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α
| cons : α → [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α → [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) List
def append (as bs : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α) : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) as [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [nil]](#tpil-Hidden___List) => bs
| [cons]](#tpil-Hidden___List) a as => [cons]](#tpil-Hidden___List) a ([append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) as bs)
theorem nil_append (as : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α) : [append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) [nil]](#tpil-Hidden___List) as = as :=
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
theorem cons_append (a : α) (as bs : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α)
: [append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) ([cons]](#tpil-Hidden___List) a as) bs = [cons]](#tpil-Hidden___List) a ([append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) as bs) :=
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
theorem append_nil (as : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α) :
[append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) as [nil]](#tpil-Hidden___List) = as :=
sorry
```

```lean
theorem append_assoc (as bs cs : [List]](#tpil-Hidden___List) α) :
[append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) ([append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) as bs) cs = [append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) as ([append]](#tpil-Hidden___List) bs cs) :=
sorry

```lean
end List
end Hidden
```

Try also defining the function `length : {α : Type u} → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` that returns the length of a list,
and prove that it behaves as expected (for example, `length ([append](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Induction-and-Recursion/#append) as bs) = length as + length bs`).

For another example, we can define the type of binary trees:

```lean
inductive BinaryTree where
| leaf : [BinaryTree]](#tpil-BinaryTree)
| node : [BinaryTree]](#tpil-BinaryTree) → [BinaryTree]](#tpil-BinaryTree) → [BinaryTree]](#tpil-BinaryTree)
```

```lean

```

In fact, we can even define the type of countably branching trees:

```lean
inductive CBTree where
| leaf : [CBTree]](#tpil-CBTree)
| sup : ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [CBTree]](#tpil-CBTree)) → [CBTree]](#tpil-CBTree)
```

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) CBTree
```

```lean
def succ (t : [CBTree]](#tpil-CBTree)) : [CBTree]](#tpil-CBTree) :=
[sup]](#tpil-CBTree) (fun _ => t)
```

```lean
def toCBTree : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [CBTree]](#tpil-CBTree)
| 0 => [leaf]](#tpil-CBTree)
| n+1 => [succ]](#tpil-CBTree) ([toCBTree]](#tpil-CBTree) n)
```

```lean
def omega : [CBTree]](#tpil-CBTree) :=
[sup]](#tpil-CBTree) [toCBTree]](#tpil-CBTree)
```

```lean
end CBTree
```

### 7.6. Tactics for Inductive Types {#tpil-tactics-for-inductive-types}

Given the fundamental importance of inductive types in Lean, it should
not be surprising that there are a number of tactics designed to work
with them effectively. We describe some of them here.

The `cases` tactic works on elements of an inductively defined type,
and does what the name suggests: it decomposes the element according
to each of the possible constructors. In its most basic form, it is
applied to an element `x` in the local context. It then reduces the
goal to cases in which `x` is replaced by each of the constructions.

```lean

In the first branch, the proof state is:

zerop:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prophz:p 0hs:∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), p n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ p 0

In the second branch, it is:

succp:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prophz:p 0hs:∀ (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), p n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ p [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n✝ [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)

There are extra bells and whistles. For one thing, `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` allows
you to choose the names for each alternative using a
`with` clause. In the next example, for example, we choose the name
`m` for the argument to `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, so that the second case refers to
`[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) m`. More importantly, the cases tactic will detect any items
in the local context that depend on the target variable. It reverts
these elements, does the split, and reintroduces them. In the example
below, notice that the hypothesis `h : n ≠ 0` becomes `h : 0 ≠ 0`
in the first branch, and `h : m [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 ≠ 0` in the second.

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Nat
```

Notice that `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` can be used to produce data as well as prove propositions.

```lean
def f (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)

```

The syntax of the `with` is convenient for writing structured proofs.
Lean also provides a complementary `[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case)` tactic, which allows you to focus on goal
assign variable names.

```lean
inductive Foo where
| bar1 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Foo
| bar2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Foo
```

```lean

[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) bar1 a b =>a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) bAll goals completed! 🐙

The `[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case)` tactic is clever, in that it will match the constructor to the appropriate goal. For example, we can fill the goals above in the opposite order:

```lean

| bar1 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Foo
| bar2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Foo
```

You can also use `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` with an arbitrary expression. Assuming that
expression occurs in the goal, the cases tactic will generalize over
the expression, introduce the resulting universally quantified
variable, and case on that.

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Nat
```

zero or the successor of some number.” The result is functionally
equivalent to the following:

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Nat
```

Notice that the expression `m + 3 * k` is erased by `[generalize](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#generalize)`; all
that matters is whether it is of the form `0` or `n✝ [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1`. This
form of `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` will *not* revert any hypotheses that also mention
the expression in the equation (in this case, `m + 3 * k`). If such a
term appears in a hypothesis and you want to generalize over that as
well, you need to `revert` it explicitly.

If the expression you case on does not appear in the goal, the
`cases` tactic uses `have` to put the type of the expression into
the context. Here is an example:

```lean
example (p : Prop) (m n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
(h₁ : m < n → p) (h₂ : m ≥ n → p) : p := byp:Propm:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:m [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n → ph₂:m ≥ n → p⊢ p
[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases) Nat.lt_or_ge m ninlp:Propm:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:m [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n → ph₂:m ≥ n → ph✝:m [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n⊢ pinrp:Propm:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:m [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n → ph₂:m ≥ n → ph✝:m ≥ n⊢ p
[case](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#case) inl hlt =>p:Propm:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)n:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h₁:m [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n → ph₂:m ≥ n → phlt:m [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n⊢ p [exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) h₁ hltAll goals completed! 🐙

The theorem `Nat.lt_or_ge m n` says `m < n`` ∨ ``m ≥ n`, and it is
natural to think of the proof above as splitting on these two
cases. In the first branch, we have the hypothesis `hlt : m [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) n`, and
in the second we have the hypothesis `hge : m ≥ n`. The proof above
is functionally equivalent to the following:

After the first two lines, we have `h : m < n ∨ m ≥ n` as a
hypothesis, and we simply do cases on that.

Here is another example, where we use the decidability of equality on
the natural numbers to split on the cases `m = n` and `m ≠ n`.

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Nat.sub_self
```

```lean
Nat.sub_self (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : n [-](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HSub___mk) n [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 0
```

```lean

```

```lean

Remember that if you `open ``Classical`, you can use the law of the
excluded middle for any proposition at all. But using type class
inference (see [Type Classes](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Type-Classes/#type-classes)), Lean can actually
find the relevant decision procedure, which means that you can use the
case split in a computable function.

Just as the `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)` tactic can be used to carry out proof by cases,
the `[induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#induction)` tactic can be used to carry out proofs by
induction. The syntax is similar to that of `[cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#cases)`, except that the
argument can only be a term in the local context. Here is an example:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean

The `[induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#induction)` tactic also supports user-defined induction principles with
multiple targets (aka major premises). This example uses `[Nat.mod.inductionOn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___mod___inductionOn)`, which has the following signature:

```lean
[Nat.mod.inductionOn](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___mod___inductionOn)
{motive : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Sort u}
(x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
(ind : ∀ x y, 0 < y ∧ y ≤ x → motive (x - y) y → motive x y)
(base : ∀ x y, ¬(0 < y ∧ y ≤ x) → motive x y) :
motive x y
```

We close this section with one last tactic that is designed to
facilitate working with inductive types, namely, the `[injection](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#injection)`
tactic. By design, the elements of an inductive type are freely
generated, which is to say, the constructors are injective and have
disjoint ranges. The `[injection](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#injection)` tactic is designed to make use of
this fact:

```lean

context, and the second adds `h'' : m [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) n`.

The `[injection](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#injection)` tactic also detects contradictions that arise when different constructors

As the second example shows, the `[contradiction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#contradiction)` tactic also detects contradictions of this form.

### 7.7. Inductive Families {#tpil-inductive-families}

We are almost done describing the full range of inductive definitions
accepted by Lean. So far, you have seen that Lean allows you to
introduce inductive types with any number of recursive
constructors. In fact, a single inductive definition can introduce an
indexed *family* of inductive types, in a manner we now describe.

An inductive family is an indexed family of types defined by a
simultaneous induction of the following form:

```
inductive foo : ... → Sort u where
  | constructor₁ : ... → foo ...
  | constructor₂ : ... → foo ...
  ...
  | constructorₙ : ... → foo ...
```

In contrast to an ordinary inductive definition, which constructs an
element of some `Sort u`, the more general version constructs a
function `... → ``Sort u`, where “`...`” denotes a sequence of
argument types, also known as *indices*. Each constructor then
constructs an element of some member of the family. One example is the
definition of `Vect α n`, the type of vectors of elements of `α`
of length `n`:

```lean
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u where
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n + 1)
```

```lean

```

Notice that the `cons` constructor takes an element of
`Vect α n` and returns an element of `Vect α (n + 1)`, thereby using an
element of one member of the family to build an element of another.

A more exotic example is given by the definition of the equality type in Lean:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
inductive Eq {α : Sort u} (a : α) : α → Prop where
| refl : [Eq]](#tpil-Hidden___Eq) a a
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

For each fixed `α : Sort u` and `a : α`, this definition
constructs a family of types `[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a x`, indexed by `x : α`.
Notably, however, there is only one constructor, `refl`, which
is an element of `[Eq]](#tpil-Hidden___Eq) a a`.
Intuitively, the only way to construct a proof of `[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a x`
is to use reflexivity, in the case where `x` is `a`.
Note that `[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a a` is the only inhabited type in the family of types
`[Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a x`. The elimination principle generated by Lean is as follows:

```lean
set_option [pp.proofs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Reading-Proof-States/#pp___proofs) true
```

```lean
[universe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Universes/#Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u v
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) (@Eq.rec : {α : Sort u} → {a : α} →
{motive : (x : α) → a = x → Sort v} →
motive a [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) →
{b : α} → (h : a = b) → motive b h)
```

```lean
@Eq.rec : {α : Sort u} →
  {a : α} → {motive : (a_1 : α) → a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a_1 → Sort v} → motive a ([Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a) → {a_1 : α} → (t : a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a_1) → motive a_1 t
```

```lean

```

It is a remarkable fact that all the basic axioms for equality follow
from the constructor, `refl`, and the eliminator, `Eq.rec`. The
definition of equality is atypical, however; see the discussion in [Axiomatic Details]](#tpil-axiomatic-details).

The recursor `Eq.rec` is also used to define substitution:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
theorem subst {α : Type u} {a b : α} {p : α → Prop}
(h₁ : [Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a b) (h₂ : p a) : p b :=
Eq.rec (motive := fun x _ => p x) h₂ h₁
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

You can also define `subst` using `match`.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
theorem subst {α : Type u} {a b : α} {p : α → Prop}
(h₁ : [Eq](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a b) (h₂ : p a) : p b :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) h₁ [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) => h₂
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

Actually, Lean compiles the `match` expressions using a definition based on generated helpers
such as `Eq.casesOn` and `Eq.ndrec`, which are themselves defined using `Eq.rec`.

```lean
theorem subst {α : Type u} {a b : α} {p : α → Prop}
(h₁ : a = b) (h₂ : p a) : p b :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) h₁ [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) => h₂
```

```lean
set_option pp.all true
```

```lean
#print [subst]](#tpil-subst)
```
