The elaborator is designed to make definitions like this more
convenient. It accepts the following:

```lean
def div (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : 0 < y ∧ y ≤ x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
have : x - y < x := Nat.sub_lt (Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le h.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) h.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)) h.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)
div (x - y) y + 1
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
0
```

```lean

```

When Lean encounters a recursive definition, it first
tries structural recursion, and only when that fails, does it fall
back on well-founded recursion. Lean uses the tactic `decreasing_tactic`
to show that the recursive applications are smaller. The auxiliary
proposition `x - y < x` in the example above should be viewed as a hint
for this tactic.
The elaborator also proves a set of equational lemmas about the recursive definition, allowing it to be manipulated without resorting to low-level lemmas about accessible relations.

The defining equation for `div` does *not* hold definitionally, but
we can unfold `div` using the `unfold` tactic. We use [`conv`](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/The-Conversion-Tactic-Mode/#conv) to select which
`div` application we want to unfold.

```lean
def div (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : 0 < y ∧ y ≤ x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
have : x - y < x := Nat.sub_lt (Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le h.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) h.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)) h.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)
div (x - y) y + 1
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
0
```

The following example is similar: it converts any natural number to a
binary expression, represented as a list of 0's and 1's. We have to
provide evidence that the recursive call is
decreasing, which we do here with a `sorry`. The `sorry` does not
prevent the interpreter from evaluating the function successfully,
but `[#eval!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___evalBang)` must be used instead of `#eval` when a term contains `sorry`.

```lean
def natToBin : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 => [0]
| 1 => [1]
| n + 2 =>
have : (n + 2) / 2 < n + 2 := sorry
natToBin ((n + 2) / 2) ++ [n % 2]
```

```lean
[#eval!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___evalBang) natToBin 1234567
```

```lean

```

As a final example, we observe that Ackermann's function can be
defined directly, because it is justified by the well-foundedness of
the lexicographic order on the natural numbers. The `termination_by` clause
instructs Lean to use a lexicographic order. This clause is actually mapping
the function arguments to elements of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`. Then, Lean uses typeclass
resolution to synthesize an element of type `[WellFoundedRelation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#WellFoundedRelation___mk) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))`.

```lean
def ack : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, y => y+1
| x+1, 0 => ack x 1
| x+1, y+1 => ack x (ack (x+1) y)
termination_by x y => (x, y)
```

```lean

```

In many cases, Lean can automatically determine an appropriate lexicographical order.
Ackermann's function is one such case, so the `termination_by` clause is optional:

```lean
def ack : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, y => y+1
| x+1, 0 => ack x 1
| x+1, y+1 => ack x (ack (x+1) y)
```

```lean

```

Note that a lexicographic order is used in the example above because the instance
`[WellFoundedRelation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#WellFoundedRelation___mk) (α × β)` uses a lexicographic order. Lean also defines the instance

```lean
instance (priority := [low](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#prioLow)) [[SizeOf](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/#SizeOf___mk) α] : [WellFoundedRelation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#WellFoundedRelation___mk) α :=
sizeOfWFRel
```

```lean

```

In the following example, we prove termination by showing that `as.[size](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___size) - i` is decreasing
in the recursive application.


Once again, Lean can automatically recognize this pattern, so the `termination_by` clause is unnecessary:

By default, Lean uses the tactic `decreasing_tactic` to prove recursive applications are decreasing. The modifier `decreasing_by` allows us to provide our own tactic. Here is an example.

```lean
theorem div_lemma {x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} : 0 < y ∧ y ≤ x → x - y < x :=
fun ⟨ypos, ylex⟩ => Nat.sub_lt (Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le ypos ylex) ypos
```

```lean
def div (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : 0 < y ∧ y ≤ x [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
div (x - y) y + 1
[else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse)
0
decreasing_by [apply](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#apply) div_lemmay:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)h:0 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) y [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) y [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) x⊢ 0 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) y [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) y [≤](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LE___mk) x; [assumption](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#assumption)All goals completed! 🐙
```

Note that `decreasing_by` is not replacement for `termination_by`, they complement each other. `termination_by` is used to specify a well-founded relation, and `decreasing_by` for providing our own tactic for showing recursive applications are decreasing. In the following example, we use both of them.

```lean
def ack : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, y => y+1
| x+1, 0 => ack x 1
| x+1, y+1 => ack x (ack (x+1) y)
termination_by x y => (x, y)
decreasing_by
-- unfolds well-founded recursion auxiliary definitions:
```

We can use `decreasing_by [sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` to instruct Lean to “trust” us that the function terminates.

```lean
def natToBin : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0 => [0]
| 1 => [1]
| n + 2 => natToBin ((n + 2) / 2) ++ [n % 2]
decreasing_by [sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
[#eval!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___evalBang) natToBin 1234567
```

```lean

```

Recall that using `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` is equivalent to using a new axiom, and should be avoided. In the following example, we used the `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)` to prove `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`.
The command `[#print](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) unsound` shows that `unsound` depends on the unsound axiom `sorryAx` used to implement `[sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)`.

```lean
def unsound (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) :=
unsound (x + 1)
decreasing_by [sorry](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#sorry)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) unsound 0
```

```lean
unsound 0 : [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
```

```lean
-- `unsound 0` is a proof of `False`
[#print](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) [axioms](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___printAxioms) unsound
```

```lean
'unsound' depends on axioms: [sorryAx]
```

```lean

```

Summary:

- If there is no `termination_by`, a well-founded relation is derived (if possible) by selecting an argument and then using typeclass resolution to synthesize a well-founded relation for this argument's type.
- If `termination_by` is specified, it maps the arguments of the function to a type `α` and type class resolution is again used. Recall that, the default instance for `β × γ` is a lexicographic order based on the well-founded relations for `β` and `γ`.
- The default well-founded relation instance for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` is `(· < ·)`.
- By default, the tactic `decreasing_tactic` is used to show that recursive applications are smaller with respect to the selected well-founded relation. If `decreasing_tactic` fails, the error message includes the remaining goal `... |- G`. Note that, the `decreasing_tactic` uses `assumption`. So, you can include a `have`-expression to prove goal `G`. You can also provide your own tactic using `decreasing_by`.

### 8.6. Functional Induction {#tpil-functional-induction}

Lean generates bespoke induction principles for recursive functions. These induction principles follow the recursive structure of the function's definition, rather than the structure of the datatype. Proofs about functions typically follow the recursive structure of the function itself, so these induction principles allow statements about the function to be proved more conveniently.

For example, using the functional induction principle for `ack` to prove that the result is always greater than `0` requires one case for each arm of the pattern match in `ack`:

```lean
def ack : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, y => y+1
| x+1, 0 => ack x 1
| x+1, y+1 => ack x (ack (x+1) y)
```

```lean
theorem ack_gt_zero : ack n m > 0 := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)m:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ ack n m > 0
[fun_induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#fun_induction) ack with
| case1 y =>case1y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 > 0
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)All goals completed! 🐙
| case2 x ih =>case2x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih:ack x 1 > 0⊢ ack x 1 > 0
[exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#exact) ihAll goals completed! 🐙
| case3 x y ih1 ih2 =>case3x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih1:ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y > 0ih2:ack x (ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y) > 0⊢ ack x (ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y) > 0
```

In `case1case1y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 > 0`, the goal is:

case1y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ y [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1 > 0

The `y + 1` in the goal corresponds to the value returned in the first case of `ack`.

In `case2case2x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih:ack x 1 > 0⊢ ack x 1 > 0`, the goal is:

case2x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih:ack x 1 > 0⊢ ack x 1 > 0

The `ack x 1` in the goal corresponds to the value of `ack` applied to the pattern variables `x + 1` and `0` returned in the second case of `ack`.
This term is automatically simplified to the right-hand side.
Happily, the inductive hypothesis `ih : ack x 1 > 0` corresponds to the recursive call, which is exactly the answer returned in this case.

In `case3case3x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih1:ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y > 0ih2:ack x (ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y) > 0⊢ ack x (ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y) > 0`, the goal is:

case3x:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)y:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)ih1:ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y > 0ih2:ack x (ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y) > 0⊢ ack x (ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y) > 0

The `ack x (ack (x + 1) y)` in the goal corresponds to the value returned in the third case of `ack`, when `ack` applied to `x + 1` and `y + 1` has been reduced.
The inductive hypotheses `ih1 : ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y > 0` and `ih2 : ack x (ack [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)x [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) y) > 0` correspond to the recursive calls, with `ih1` matching the nested recursive call.
Once again, the induction hypothesis is suitable.

Using `[fun_induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#fun_induction) ack` results in goals and induction hypotheses that match the recursive structure of `ack`. As a result, the proof can be a single line:

```lean
def ack : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| 0, y => y+1
| x+1, 0 => ack x 1
| x+1, y+1 => ack x (ack (x+1) y)
```

There is also a `[fun_cases](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#fun_cases)` tactic which is analogous to the `cases` tactic.
It generates a case for each branch in a function's control flow.
Both it and `[fun_induction](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#fun_induction)` additionally provide assumptions that rule out the paths that were not taken.

This function `f` represents a five-way Boolean disjunction:

```lean
def f : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _, _, _ , _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _, [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _, _ , _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _, _, [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _ , _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _, _, _, [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _, _, _, _, x => x
```

```lean

```

To prove that it is disjunction, the last case requires knowledge that none of the arguments are `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
This knowledge is provided by the tactic:

```lean
def f : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _, _, _ , _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _, [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _, _ , _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _, _, [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _ , _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _, _, _, [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| _, _, _, _, x => x
```

```lean
| _, [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), _, _ , _ => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

### 8.7. Mutual Recursion {#tpil-mutual-recursion}

Lean also supports mutual recursive definitions. The syntax is similar to that for mutual inductive types. Here is an example:

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
def even : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| 0 => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| n+1 => [odd]](#tpil-even-next) n
def odd : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| 0 => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| n+1 => even n
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean
example : even (a + 1) = [odd]](#tpil-even-next) a := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ even [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)a [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [odd]](#tpil-even-next) a
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [even]All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
example : [odd]](#tpil-even-next) (a + 1) = even a := bya:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ [odd]](#tpil-even-next) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)a [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) even a
[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [[odd]](#tpil-even-next)]All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
theorem even_eq_not_odd : ∀ a, even a = [not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not) ([odd]](#tpil-even-next) a) := by⊢ ∀ (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)), even a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[odd]](#tpil-even-next) a

.succn✝:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)a✝:even n✝ [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[odd]](#tpil-even-next) n✝⊢ even [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n✝ [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [!](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___not)[odd]](#tpil-even-next) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk)n✝ [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [even, [odd]](#tpil-even-next), *]All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean

```

What makes this a mutual definition is that `even` is defined recursively in terms of `[odd]](#tpil-even-next)`, while `[odd]](#tpil-even-next)` is defined recursively in terms of `even`. Under the hood, this is compiled as a single recursive definition. The internally defined function takes, as argument, an element of a sum type, either an input to `even`, or an input to `[odd]](#tpil-even-next)`. It then returns an output appropriate to the input. To define that function, Lean uses a suitable well-founded measure. The internals are meant to be hidden from users; the canonical way to make use of such definitions is to use `[simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp)` (or `unfold`), as we did above.

Mutual recursive definitions also provide natural ways of working with mutual and nested inductive types. Recall the definition of `Even` and `Odd` as mutual inductive predicates as presented before.

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive Even : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| even_zero : [Even](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Introduction/#Even___zero-next) 0
| even_succ : ∀ n, Odd n → [Even](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Introduction/#Even___zero-next) (n + 1)
inductive Odd : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| odd_succ : ∀ n, [Even](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Introduction/#Even___zero-next) n → Odd (n + 1)
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean

```

The constructors, `even_zero`, `even_succ`, and `odd_succ` provide positive means for showing that a number is even or odd. We need to use the fact that the inductive type is generated by these constructors to know that zero is not odd, and that the latter two implications reverse. As usual, the constructors are kept in a namespace that is named after the type being defined, and the command `[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Even Odd` allows us to access them more conveniently.

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
inductive Even : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| even_zero : [Even](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Introduction/#Even___zero-next) 0
| even_succ : ∀ n, Odd n → [Even](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Introduction/#Even___zero-next) (n + 1)
inductive Odd : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop where
| odd_succ : ∀ n, [Even](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Introduction/#Even___zero-next) n → Odd (n + 1)
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Even Odd
```

```lean
theorem not_odd_zero : ¬ Odd 0 :=
fun h => [nomatch](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___nomatch) h
```

```lean
theorem even_of_odd_succ : ∀ n, Odd (n + 1) → [Even](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Introduction/#Even___zero-next) n
| _, odd_succ n h => h
```

```lean
theorem odd_of_even_succ : ∀ n, [Even](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Introduction/#Even___zero-next) (n + 1) → Odd n
| _, even_succ n h => h
```

```lean

```

For another example, suppose we use a nested inductive type to define a set of terms inductively, so that a term is either a constant (with a name given by a string), or the result of applying a constant to a list of constants.

```lean
inductive Term where
| const : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → Term
| app : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) Term → Term
```

```lean

```

We can then use a mutual recursive definition to count the number of constants occurring in a term, as well as the number occurring in a list of terms.

```lean
inductive Term where
| const : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → Term
| app : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) Term → Term
```

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Term
```

```lean
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
def numConsts : Term → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [const]](#tpil-Term-next) _ => 1
| [app]](#tpil-Term) _ cs => [numConstsLst]](#tpil-Term___numConsts) cs
def numConstsLst : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) Term → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [] => 0
| c :: cs => [numConsts]](#tpil-Term___numConsts) c + [numConstsLst]](#tpil-Term___numConsts) cs
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```


As a final example, we define a function `[replaceConst]](#tpil-Term___replaceConst) a b e` that replaces a constant `a` with `b` in a term `e`, and then prove the number of constants is the same. Note that, our proof uses mutual recursion (aka induction).

```lean
inductive Term where
| const : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → Term
| app : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) Term → Term
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Term
[mutual](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
def numConsts : Term → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [const]](#tpil-Term-next) _ => 1
| [app]](#tpil-Term) _ cs => [numConstsLst]](#tpil-Term___numConsts) cs
def numConstsLst : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) Term → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| [] => 0
| c :: cs => [numConsts]](#tpil-Term___numConsts) c + [numConstsLst]](#tpil-Term___numConsts) cs
[end](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#Lean___Parser___Command___mutual)
```

```lean
| [app]](#tpil-Term) f cs => [app]](#tpil-Term) f ([replaceConstLst]](#tpil-Term___replaceConst) a b cs)

| [] => []
```

### 8.8. Dependent Pattern Matching {#tpil-dependent-pattern-matching}

All the examples of pattern matching we considered in the section on
[pattern matching]](#tpil-pattern-matching) can easily be written using `casesOn`
and `recOn`. However, this is often not the case with indexed
inductive families such as `Vect α n`, since case splits impose
constraints on the values of the indices. Without the equation
compiler, we would need a lot of boilerplate code to define very
simple functions such as `map`, `zip`, and `unzip` using
recursors. To understand the difficulty, consider what it would take
to define a function `tail` which takes a vector
`v : Vect α (n + 1)` and deletes the first element.

```lean
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n + 1)
```

```lean

```

A first thought might be to use the `Vect.casesOn` function:

```lean
Vect.casesOn.{u, v}
{α : Type v} {motive : (a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → Vect α a → Sort u}
{a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}
(t : Vect α a)
(nil : motive 0 nil)
(cons : (a : α) → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → (a_1 : Vect α n) →
motive (n + 1) (cons a a_1)) :
motive a t
```

But what value should we return in the `nil` case? Something funny
is going on: if `v` has type `Vect α (n + 1)`, it *can't* be
`nil`, but it is not clear how to tell that to `Vect.casesOn`.

One solution is to define an auxiliary function:

```lean
set_option linter.unusedVariables false
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n+1)
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Vect
```

```lean
def tailAux (v : Vect α m) : m = n + 1 → Vect α n :=
Vect.casesOn (motive := fun x _ => x = n + 1 → Vect α n) v
(fun h : 0 = n + 1 => Nat.noConfusion h)
(fun (a : α) (m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (as : Vect α m) =>
fun (h : m + 1 = n + 1) =>
Nat.noConfusion h (fun h1 : m = n => h1 ▸ as))
```

```lean
def tail (v : Vect α (n+1)) : Vect α n :=
[tailAux]](#tpil-Vect___tailAux) v rfl
```

```lean
end Vect
```

In the `nil` case, `m` is instantiated to `0`, and
`Nat.noConfusion` makes use of the fact that `0 = n + 1` cannot
occur. Otherwise, `v` is of the form `cons ``a`` ``as`, and we can simply
return `as`, after casting it from a vector of length `m` to a
vector of length `n`.

The difficulty in defining `tail` is to maintain the relationships between the indices.
The hypothesis `m = n + 1` in `tailAux` is used to communicate the relationship
between `n` and the index associated with the minor premise.
Moreover, the `0 = n + 1` case is unreachable, and the canonical way to discard such
a case is to use `Nat.noConfusion`.

The `tail` function is, however, easy to define using recursive
equations, and the equation compiler generates all the boilerplate
code automatically for us. Here are a number of similar examples:

```lean
set_option linter.unusedVariables false
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n+1)
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Vect
```

```lean
def head : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α (n+1) → α
| n, cons a as => a
```

```lean
def tail : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α (n+1) → Vect α n
| n, cons a as => as
```

```lean
theorem eta : ∀ {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} (v : Vect α (n+1)), cons (head v) (tail v) = v
| n, cons a as => [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
def map (f : α → β → γ) : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect γ n
| 0, nil, nil => nil
| n+1, cons a as, cons b bs => cons (f a b) (map f as bs)
```

```lean
def zip : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect (α × β) n
| 0, nil, nil => nil
| n+1, cons a as, cons b bs => cons (a, b) (zip as bs)
```

```lean
end Vect
```

Note that we can omit recursive equations for “unreachable” cases such
as `head`` ``nil`. The automatically generated definitions for indexed
families are far from straightforward. For example:

```lean
set_option linter.unusedVariables false
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n+1)
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Vect
```

```lean
def zipWith (f : α → β → γ) : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect γ n
| 0, nil, nil => nil
| n+1, cons a as, cons b bs => cons (f a b) ([zipWith]](#tpil-Vect___zipWith) f as bs)
```

```lean
#print [zipWith]](#tpil-Vect___zipWith)
```

```lean
def Vect.zipWith.{u_1, u_2, u_3} : {α : Type u_1} →
  {β : Type u_2} → {γ : Type u_3} → (α → β → γ) → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect γ n :=
fun {α} {β} {γ} f x x_1 x_2 => Vect.brecOn (motive := fun x x_3 => Vect β x → Vect γ x) x_1 (zipWith._f f) x_2
```

```lean
#print zipWith.match_1
```

```lean
@[instance_reducible] def Vect.zipWith.match_1.{u_1, u_2, u_3} : {α : Type u_1} →
  {β : Type u_2} →
    (motive : (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) → Vect α x → Vect β x → Sort u_3) →
      (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) →
        (x_1 : Vect α x) →
          (x_2 : Vect β x) →
            ([Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) → motive 0 nil nil) →
              ((n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) →
                  (a : α) → (as : Vect α n) → (b : β) → (bs : Vect β n) → motive n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (cons a as) (cons b bs)) →
                motive x x_1 x_2 :=
fun {α} {β} motive x x_1 x_2 h_1 h_2 =>
  Nat.casesOn (motive := fun x => (x_3 : Vect α x) → (x_4 : Vect β x) → motive x x_3 x_4) x
    (fun x x_3 =>
      casesOn (motive := fun a x_4 => [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a → x [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) x_4 → motive [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) x x_3) x
        (fun h h_3 =>
          ⋯ ▸
            casesOn (motive := fun a x => [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a → x_3 [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) x → motive [Nat.zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) nil x_3) x_3
              (fun h h_4 => ⋯ ▸ h_1 [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit___unit)) (fun a {n} a_1 h => [False.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False___elim) ⋯) ⋯ ⋯)
        (fun a {n} a_1 h => [False.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False___elim) ⋯) ⋯ ⋯)
    (fun n x x_3 =>
      casesOn (motive := fun a x_4 => n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a → x [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) x_4 → motive n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) x x_3) x (fun h => [False.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False___elim) ⋯)
        (fun a {n_1} a_1 h =>
          Nat.Internal.elimOffset n n_1 1 h fun x_4 =>
            Eq.ndrec (motive := fun {n_2} => (a_2 : Vect α n_2) → x [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) cons a a_2 → motive n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) x x_3)
              (fun a_2 h =>
                ⋯ ▸
                  casesOn (motive := fun a_3 x => n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a_3 → x_3 [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) x → motive n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (cons a a_2) x_3) x_3
                    (fun h => [False.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False___elim) ⋯)
                    (fun a_3 {n_2} a_4 h =>
                      Nat.Internal.elimOffset n n_2 1 h fun x =>
                        Eq.ndrec (motive := fun {n_3} =>
                          (a_5 : Vect β n_3) → x_3 [≍](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#HEq___refl) cons a_3 a_5 → motive n.[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (cons a a_2) x_3)
                          (fun a_5 h => ⋯ ▸ h_2 n a a_2 a_3 a_5) x a_4)
                    ⋯ ⋯)
              x_4 a_1)
        ⋯ ⋯)
    x_1 x_2
```

```lean
end Vect
```

The `zipWith` function is even more tedious to define by hand than the
`tail` function. We encourage you to try it, using `Vect.recOn`,
`Vect.casesOn` and `Vect.noConfusion`.

### 8.9. Inaccessible Patterns {#tpil-inaccessible-patterns}

Sometimes an argument in a dependent matching pattern is not essential
to the definition, but nonetheless has to be included to specialize
the type of the expression appropriately. Lean allows users to mark
such subterms as *inaccessible* for pattern matching. These
annotations are essential, for example, when a term occurring in the
left-hand side is neither a variable nor a constructor application,
because these are not suitable targets for pattern matching. We can
view such inaccessible patterns as “don't care” components of the
patterns. You can declare a subterm inaccessible by writing
`.(t)`. If the inaccessible pattern can be inferred, you can also write
`_`.

The following example, we declare an inductive type that defines the
property of “being in the image of `f`”. You can view an element of
the type `[ImageOf]](#tpil-ImageOf) f b` as evidence that `b` is in the image of
`f`, whereby the constructor `imf` is used to build such
evidence. We can then define any function `f` with an “inverse”
which takes anything in the image of `f` to an element that is
mapped to it. The typing rules forces us to write `f a` for the
first argument, but this term is neither a variable nor a constructor
application, and plays no role in the pattern-matching definition. To
define the function `inverse` below, we *have to* mark `f a`
inaccessible.

```lean
inductive ImageOf {α β : Type u} (f : α → β) : β → Type u where
| imf : (a : α) → [ImageOf]](#tpil-ImageOf) f (f a)
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) ImageOf
```

```lean
def inverse {f : α → β} : (b : β) → [ImageOf]](#tpil-ImageOf) f b → α
| .(f a), [imf]](#tpil-ImageOf) a => a
```

```lean
def inverse' {f : α → β} : (b : β) → [ImageOf]](#tpil-ImageOf) f b → α
| _, [imf]](#tpil-ImageOf) a => a
```

```lean

```

In the example above, the inaccessible annotation makes it clear that
`f` is *not* a pattern matching variable.

Inaccessible patterns can be used to clarify and control definitions that
make use of dependent pattern matching. Consider the following
definition of the function `Vect.add`, which adds two vectors of
elements of a type, assuming that type has an associated addition
function:

```lean
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n+1)
```

```lean
def Vect.add [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α n → Vect α n
| 0, nil, nil => nil
| n+1, cons a as, cons b bs => cons (a + b) (add as bs)
```

```lean

```

The argument `{n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}` appear after the colon, because it cannot
be held fixed throughout the definition. When implementing this
definition, the equation compiler starts with a case distinction as to
whether the first argument is `0` or of the form `n+1`. This is
followed by nested case splits on the next two arguments, and in each
case the equation compiler rules out the cases are not compatible with
the first pattern.

But, in fact, a case split is not required on the first argument; the
`casesOn` eliminator for `Vect` automatically abstracts this
argument and replaces it by `0` and `n + 1` when we do a case
split on the second argument. Using inaccessible patterns, we can prompt
the equation compiler to avoid the case split on `n`.

```lean
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n+1)
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Vect
```

```lean
def add [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α n → Vect α n
| .(_), nil, nil => nil
| .(_), cons a as, cons b bs => cons (a + b) (add as bs)
```

```lean
end Vect
```

Marking the position as an inaccessible pattern tells the
equation compiler first, that the form of the argument should be
inferred from the constraints posed by the other arguments, and,
second, that the first argument should *not* participate in pattern
matching.

The inaccessible pattern `.(_)` can be written as `_` for convenience.

```lean
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n+1)
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Vect
```

```lean
def add [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] : {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α n → Vect α n
| _, nil, nil => nil
| _, cons a as, cons b bs => cons (a + b) (add as bs)
```

```lean
end Vect
```

As we mentioned above, the argument `{n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)}` is part of the
pattern matching, because it cannot be held fixed throughout the
definition. Rather than requiring that these discriminants be provided explicitly, Lean implicitly includes
these extra discriminants automatically for us.

```lean
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n+1)
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Vect
```

```lean
def add [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} : Vect α n → Vect α n → Vect α n
| nil, nil => nil
| cons a as, cons b bs => cons (a + b) (add as bs)
```

```lean
end Vect
```

When combined with the *auto bound implicits* feature, you can simplify
the declare further and write:

```lean
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n+1)
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Vect
```

```lean
def add [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] : Vect α n → Vect α n → Vect α n
| nil, nil => nil
| cons a as, cons b bs => cons (a + b) (add as bs)
```

```lean
end Vect
```

Using these new features, you can write the other vector functions defined
in the previous sections more compactly as follows:

```lean
set_option linter.unusedVariables false
inductive Vect (α : Type u) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Type u
| nil : Vect α 0
| cons : α → {n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} → Vect α n → Vect α (n+1)
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Vect
```

```lean
def head : Vect α (n+1) → α
| cons a as => a
```

```lean
def tail : Vect α (n+1) → Vect α n
| cons a as => as
```

```lean
theorem eta : (v : Vect α (n+1)) → cons (head v) (tail v) = v
| cons a as => [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
def map (f : α → β → γ) : Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect γ n
| nil, nil => nil
| cons a as, cons b bs => cons (f a b) (map f as bs)
```

```lean
def zip : Vect α n → Vect β n → Vect (α × β) n
| nil, nil => nil
| cons a as, cons b bs => cons (a, b) (zip as bs)
```

```lean
end Vect
```

### 8.10. Match Expressions {#tpil-match-expressions}

Lean also provides a compiler for `match`-`with` expressions found in
many functional languages:

```lean
set_option linter.unusedVariables false
```

```lean
def isNotZero (m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) m [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| n + 1 => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean

```

This does not look very different from an ordinary pattern matching
definition, but the point is that a `match` can be used anywhere in
an expression, and with arbitrary arguments.

```lean
set_option linter.unusedVariables false
```

```lean
def isNotZero (m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) m [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0 => [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
| n + 1 => [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
def filter (p : α → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α
| [] => []
| a :: as =>
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) p a [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => a :: [filter]](#tpil-isNotZero-next) p as
| [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => [filter]](#tpil-isNotZero-next) p as
```

```lean
example : [filter]](#tpil-isNotZero-next) isNotZero [1, 0, 0, 3, 0] = [1, 3] := rfl
```

```lean

```

Here is another example:

```lean
def foo (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (b c : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)) :=
5 + [match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) n - 5, b && c [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| 0, [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => 0
| m + 1, [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => m + 7
| 0, [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => 5
| m + 1, [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) => m + 3
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) foo 7 [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
9
```

```lean

```

```lean
example : foo 7 [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) = 9 := rfl
```

```lean

```

Lean uses the `match` construct internally to implement pattern-matching in all parts of the system.
Thus, all four of these definitions have the same net effect:

```lean
def bar₁ : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
| (m, n) => m + n
```

```lean
def bar₂ (p : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) p [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| (m, n) => m + n
```

```lean
def bar₃ : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
fun (m, n) => m + n
```

```lean
def bar₄ (p : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
let (m, n) := p; m + n
```

```lean

```

These variations are equally useful for destructing propositions:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (p q : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → Prop)
```

```lean
example : (∃ x, p x) → (∃ y, q y) → ∃ x y, p x ∧ q y
| ⟨x, px⟩, ⟨y, qy⟩ => ⟨x, y, px, qy⟩
```

```lean
example (h₀ : ∃ x, p x) (h₁ : ∃ y, q y)
: ∃ x y, p x ∧ q y :=
[match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) h₀, h₁ [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| ⟨x, px⟩, ⟨y, qy⟩ => ⟨x, y, px, qy⟩
```

```lean
example : (∃ x, p x) → (∃ y, q y) → ∃ x y, p x ∧ q y :=
fun ⟨x, px⟩ ⟨y, qy⟩ => ⟨x, y, px, qy⟩
```

```lean
example (h₀ : ∃ x, p x) (h₁ : ∃ y, q y)
: ∃ x y, p x ∧ q y :=
let ⟨x, px⟩ := h₀
let ⟨y, qy⟩ := h₁
⟨x, y, px, qy⟩
```

```lean

```

### 8.11. Exercises {#tpil-Theorem-Proving-in-Lean-4--Induction-and-Recursion--Exercises}

1. Open a namespace `Hidden` to avoid naming conflicts, and use the
   equation compiler to define addition, multiplication, and
   exponentiation on the natural numbers. Then use the equation
   compiler to derive some of their basic properties.
2. Similarly, use the equation compiler to define some basic
   operations on lists (like the `[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse)` function) and prove
   theorems about lists by induction (such as the fact that
   `[reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) ([reverse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___reverse) xs) = xs` for any list `xs`).
3. Define your own function to carry out course-of-value recursion on
   the natural numbers. Similarly, see if you can figure out how to
   define `[WellFounded.fix](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Definitions/Recursive-Definitions/#WellFounded___fix)` on your own.
4. Following the examples in the section on [dependent pattern matching]](#tpil-dependent-pattern-matching),
   define a function that will append two vectors.
   This is tricky; you will have to define an auxiliary function.
5. Consider the following type of arithmetic expressions. The idea is
   that `var`` ``n` is a variable, `vₙ`, and `const`` ``n` is the
   constant whose value is `n`.

   ```lean
   inductive Expr where
   | const : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | var : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | plus : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | times : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   [deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
   ```

   ```lean
   [open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Expr
   ```

   ```lean
   def sampleExpr : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) :=
   [plus]](#tpil-Expr) ([times]](#tpil-Expr) ([var]](#tpil-Expr) 0) ([const]](#tpil-Expr) 7)) ([times]](#tpil-Expr) ([const]](#tpil-Expr) 2) ([var]](#tpil-Expr) 1))
   ```

   ```lean

   ```

   Here `sampleExpr` represents `(v₀ * 7) + (2 * v₁)`.

   Write a function that evaluates such an expression, evaluating each `[var]](#tpil-Expr) n` to `v n`.

   ```lean
   inductive Expr where
   | const : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | var : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | plus : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | times : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   [deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
   [open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Expr
   def sampleExpr : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) :=
   [plus]](#tpil-Expr) ([times]](#tpil-Expr) ([var]](#tpil-Expr) 0) ([const]](#tpil-Expr) 7)) ([times]](#tpil-Expr) ([const]](#tpil-Expr) 2) ([var]](#tpil-Expr) 1))
   ```

   ```lean
   def eval (v : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
   | [const]](#tpil-Expr) n => sorry
   | [var]](#tpil-Expr) n => v n
   | [plus]](#tpil-Expr) e₁ e₂ => sorry
   | [times]](#tpil-Expr) e₁ e₂ => sorry
   ```

   ```lean
   def sampleVal : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
   | 0 => 5
   | 1 => 6
   | _ => 0
   ```

   ```lean
   -- Try it out. You should get 47 here.
   -- #eval eval sampleVal sampleExpr
   ```

   Implement “constant fusion,” a procedure that simplifies subterms like
   `5 + 7` to `12`. Using the auxiliary function `simpConst`,
   define a function “fuse”: to simplify a plus or a times, first
   simplify the arguments recursively, and then apply `simpConst` to
   try to simplify the result.

   ```lean
   inductive Expr where
   | const : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | var : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | plus : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | times : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   [deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
   [open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Expr
   def eval (v : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
   | [const]](#tpil-Expr) n => sorry
   | [var]](#tpil-Expr) n => v n
   | [plus]](#tpil-Expr) e₁ e₂ => sorry
   | [times]](#tpil-Expr) e₁ e₂ => sorry
   ```

   ```lean
   def simpConst : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr)
   | [plus]](#tpil-Expr) ([const]](#tpil-Expr) n₁) ([const]](#tpil-Expr) n₂) => [const]](#tpil-Expr) (n₁ + n₂)
   | [times]](#tpil-Expr) ([const]](#tpil-Expr) n₁) ([const]](#tpil-Expr) n₂) => [const]](#tpil-Expr) (n₁ * n₂)
   | e => e
   ```

   ```lean
   def fuse : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) → [Expr]](#tpil-Expr) := sorry
   ```

   ```lean
   theorem simpConst_eq (v : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
   : ∀ e : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr), [eval]](#tpil-eval) v ([simpConst]](#tpil-simpConst) e) = [eval]](#tpil-eval) v e :=
   sorry
   ```

   ```lean
   theorem fuse_eq (v : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
   : ∀ e : [Expr]](#tpil-Expr), [eval]](#tpil-eval) v ([fuse]](#tpil-simpConst) e) = [eval]](#tpil-eval) v e :=
   sorry
   ```

   ```lean

   ```

   The last two theorems show that the definitions preserve the value.
