## Structures and Records {#tpil-structures-and-records}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Structures-and-Records/

We have seen that Lean's foundational system includes inductive
types. We have, moreover, noted that it is a remarkable fact that it
is possible to construct a substantial edifice of mathematics based on
nothing more than the type universes, dependent arrow types, and inductive types;
everything else follows from those. The Lean standard library contains
many instances of inductive types (e.g., `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, `[Prod](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`, `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)`),
and even the logical connectives are defined using inductive types.

Recall that a non-recursive inductive type that contains only one
constructor is called a *structure* or *record*. The product type is a
structure, as is the dependent product (Sigma) type.
In general, whenever we define a structure `S`, we usually
define *projection* functions that allow us to “destruct” each
instance of `S` and retrieve the values that are stored in its
fields. The functions `[Prod.fst](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)` and `[Prod.snd](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)`, which return the
first and second elements of a pair, are examples of such projections.

When writing programs or formalizing mathematics, it is not uncommon
to define structures containing many fields. The `structure`
command, available in Lean, provides infrastructure to support this
process. When we define a structure using this command, Lean
automatically generates all the projection functions. The
`structure` command also allows us to define new structures based on
previously defined ones. Moreover, Lean provides convenient notation
for defining instances of a given structure.

### 9.1. Declaring Structures {#tpil-declaring-structures}

The structure command is essentially a “front end” for defining
inductive data types. Every `structure` declaration introduces a
namespace with the same name. The general form is as follows:

```
    structure <name> <parameters> <parent-structures> where
      <constructor> :: <fields>
```

Most parts are optional. Here is an example:

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
mk ::
x : α
y : α
```

```lean

```

Values of type `Point` are created using `[Point.mk]](#tpil-Point) a b`, and the
fields of a point `p` are accessed using `Point.x p` and
`Point.y p` (but `p.x` and `p.y` also work, see below).
The structure command also generates useful recursors and
theorems. Here are some of the constructions generated for the
declaration above.

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
mk ::
x : α
y : α
```

```lean
-- a Type
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Point
```

```lean
Point.{u} (α : Type u) : Type u
```

```lean

```

```lean
-- the eliminator
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Point.rec
```

```lean
@Point.rec : {α : Type u_2} →
  {motive : Point α → Sort u_1} → ((x y : α) → motive [{]](#tpil-Point) x [:=]](#tpil-Point) x[,]](#tpil-Point) y [:=]](#tpil-Point) y [}]](#tpil-Point)) → (t : Point α) → motive t
```

```lean

```

```lean
-- the constructor
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[Point.mk]](#tpil-Point)
```

```lean
[@]](#tpil-Point)[Point.mk]](#tpil-Point) : {α : Type u_1} → α → α → Point α
```

```lean

```

```lean
-- a projection
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Point.x
```

```lean
@Point.x : {α : Type u_1} → Point α → α
```

```lean

```

```lean
-- a projection
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Point.y
```

```lean
@Point.y : {α : Type u_1} → Point α → α
```

```lean

```

If the constructor name is not provided, then a constructor is named
`mk` by default.

Here are some simple theorems and expressions that use the generated
constructions. As usual, you can avoid the prefix `Point` by using
the command `[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Point`.

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
x : α
y : α
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) Point.x ([Point.mk]](#tpil-Point) 10 20)
```

```lean
10
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) Point.y ([Point.mk]](#tpil-Point) 10 20)
```

```lean
20
```

```lean

```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Point
```

```lean
example (a b : α) : x ([mk]](#tpil-Point) a b) = a :=
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
example (a b : α) : y ([mk]](#tpil-Point) a b) = b :=
rfl
```

```lean

```

Given `p : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, the dot notation `p.x` is shorthand for
`Point.x p`. This provides a convenient way of accessing the fields
of a structure.

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
x : α
y : α
```

```lean
def p := [Point.mk]](#tpil-Point) 10 20
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) p.x
```

```lean
p.x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) p.x
```

```lean
10
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) p.y
```

```lean
20
```

```lean

```

The dot notation is convenient not just for accessing the projections
of a record, but also for applying functions defined in a namespace
with the same name. Recall from the [Conjunction section]](#tpil-conjunction) if `p`
has type `Point`, the expression `p.foo` is interpreted as
`Point.foo p`, assuming that the first non-implicit argument to
`foo` has type `Point`. The expression `p.[add]](#tpil-Point-next) q` is therefore
shorthand for `Point.add p q` in the example below.

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
x : α
y : α
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

```lean
def Point.add (p q : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
[mk]](#tpil-Point) (p.x + q.x) (p.y + q.y)
```

```lean
def p : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [Point.mk]](#tpil-Point) 1 2
```

```lean
def q : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [Point.mk]](#tpil-Point) 3 4
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) p.[add]](#tpil-Point-next) q
```

```lean
{ x := 4, y := 6 }
```

```lean

```

In the next chapter, you will learn how to define a function like
`[add]](#tpil-Point-next)` so that it works generically for elements of `Point α`
rather than just `Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, assuming `α` has an associated
addition operation.

More generally, given an expression `p.foo x y z` where `p : Point`,
Lean will insert `p` at the first argument to `Point.foo` of type
`Point`. For example, with the definition of scalar multiplication
below, `p.[smul]](#tpil-Point___smul) 3` is interpreted as `[Point.smul]](#tpil-Point___smul) 3 p`.

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
x : α
y : α
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

```lean
def Point.smul (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) (p : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
[Point.mk]](#tpil-Point) (n * p.x) (n * p.y)
```

```lean
def p : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [Point.mk]](#tpil-Point) 1 2
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) p.[smul]](#tpil-Point___smul) 3
```

```lean
{ x := 3, y := 6 }
```

```lean

```

```lean
example {p : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)} : p.[smul]](#tpil-Point___smul) 3 = [Point.smul]](#tpil-Point___smul) 3 p := rfl
```

```lean

```

It is common to use a similar trick with the `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)` function,
which takes a list as its second non-implicit argument:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map)[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) : {α : Type u_1} → {β : Type u_2} → (α → β) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) β
```

```lean

```

```lean
def xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [1, 2, 3]
```

```lean
def f : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := fun x => x * x
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [xs]](#tpil-xs).[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f
```

```lean
[1, 4, 9]
```

```lean

```

```lean
example {xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α} {f : α → β} :
xs.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f = [List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f xs :=
rfl
```

```lean

```

Here `[xs]](#tpil-xs).[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f` is interpreted as `[List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) f xs`.

### 9.2. Objects {#tpil-objects}

We have been using constructors to create elements of a structure
type. For structures containing many fields, this is often
inconvenient, because we have to remember the order in which the
fields were defined. Lean therefore provides the following alternative
notations for defining elements of a structure type.

```
    { (<field-name> := <expr>)* : structure-type }
    or
    { (<field-name> := <expr>)* }
```

The suffix `: structure-type` can be omitted whenever the name of
the structure can be inferred from the expected type. For example, we
use this notation to define “points.” The order that the fields are
specified does not matter, so all the expressions below define the
same point.

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
x : α
y : α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) { x := 10, y := 20 : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) }
```

```lean
[{]](#tpil-Point) x [:=]](#tpil-Point) 10[,]](#tpil-Point) y [:=]](#tpil-Point) 20 [}]](#tpil-Point) : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) { y := 20, x := 10 : Point _ }
```

```lean
[{]](#tpil-Point) x [:=]](#tpil-Point) 10[,]](#tpil-Point) y [:=]](#tpil-Point) 20 [}]](#tpil-Point) : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) ({ x := 10, y := 20 } : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
[{]](#tpil-Point) x [:=]](#tpil-Point) 10[,]](#tpil-Point) y [:=]](#tpil-Point) 20 [}]](#tpil-Point) : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
example : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
{ y := 20, x := 10 }
```

```lean

```

Fields can be marked as implicit using curly braces.
Implicit fields become implicit parameters to the constructor.

If the value of a field is not specified, Lean tries to infer it. If
the unspecified fields cannot be inferred, Lean flags an error
indicating the corresponding placeholder could not be synthesized.

```lean
structure MyStruct where
{α : Type u}
{β : Type v}
a : α
b : β
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) { [a]](#tpil-MyStruct) := 10, [b]](#tpil-MyStruct) := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) : [MyStruct]](#tpil-MyStruct) }
```

```lean
{ [α]](#tpil-MyStruct) := [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero), [β]](#tpil-MyStruct) := [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false), [a]](#tpil-MyStruct) := 10, [b]](#tpil-MyStruct) := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) } : [MyStruct]](#tpil-MyStruct)
```

```lean

```

*Record update* is another common operation which amounts to creating
a new record object by modifying the value of one or more fields in an
old one. Lean allows you to specify that unassigned fields in the
specification of a record should be taken from a previously defined
structure object `s` by adding the annotation `s ``with` before the field
assignments. If more than one record object is provided, then they are
visited in order until Lean finds one that contains the unspecified
field. Lean raises an error if any of the field names remain
unspecified after all the objects are visited.

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
x : α
y : α
[deriving](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Deriving-Instances/#Lean___Parser___Command___optDeriving-next) [Repr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Repr___mk)
```

```lean
def p : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
{ x := 1, y := 2 }
```


### 9.3. Inheritance {#tpil-inheritance}

We can *extend* existing structures by adding new fields. This feature
allows us to simulate a form of *inheritance*.

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
x : α
y : α
```

```lean
inductive Color where
| red | green | blue
```

```lean
structure ColorPoint (α : Type u) extends Point α where
c : Color
```

```lean

```

In the next example, we define a structure using multiple inheritance,
and then define an object using objects of the parent structures.

```lean
structure Point (α : Type u) where
x : α
y : α
z : α
```

```lean
structure RGBValue where
red : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
green : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
blue : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
structure RedGreenPoint (α : Type u) extends Point α, [RGBValue]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next) where
no_blue : blue = 0
```

```lean
def p : Point [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
{ x := 10, y := 10, [z]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next) := 20 }
```

```lean
def rgp : [RedGreenPoint]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
{ p with [red]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next) := 200, [green]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next) := 40, [blue]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next) := 0, [no_blue]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next) := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next) }
```

```lean
example : [rgp]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next).x = 10 := [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
example : [rgp]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next).[red]](#tpil-Point-next-next-next-next-next) = 200 := rfl
```


## Type Classes {#tpil-type-classes}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Type-Classes/

Type classes were introduced as a principled way of enabling
ad-hoc polymorphism in functional programming languages. We first observe that it
would be easy to implement an ad-hoc polymorphic function (such as addition) if the
function simply took the type-specific implementation of addition as an argument
and then called that implementation on the remaining arguments. For example,
suppose we declare a structure in Lean to hold implementations of addition.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
```

```lean
structure Add (α : Type) where
add : α → α → α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Add.add
```

```lean
@Add.add : {α : Type} → Add α → α → α → α
```

```lean
end Ex
```

In the above Lean code, the field `add` has type
`Add.add : {α : Type} → Add α → α → α → α`
where the curly braces around the type `α` mean that it is an implicit argument.
We could implement `double` by:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
structure Add (α : Type) where
add : α → α → α
```

```lean
def double (s : Add α) (x : α) : α :=
s.add x x
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) double { add := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) } 10
```

```lean
20
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) double { add := [Nat.mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___mul) } 10
```

```lean
100
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) double { add := [Int.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___add) } 10
```

```lean
20
```

```lean
end Ex
```

Note that you can double a natural number `n` by `double { add := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add) } n`.
Of course, it would be highly cumbersome for users to manually pass the
implementations around in this way.
Indeed, it would defeat most of the potential benefits of ad-hoc
polymorphism.

The main idea behind type classes is to make arguments such as `Add α` implicit,
and to use a database of user-defined instances to synthesize the desired instances
automatically through a process known as typeclass resolution. In Lean, by changing
`structure` to `class` in the example above, the type of `Add.add` becomes:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
```

```lean
class Add (α : Type) where
add : α → α → α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Add.add
```

```lean
@Add.add : {α : Type} → [self : Add α] → α → α → α
```

```lean
end Ex
```

where the square brackets indicate that the argument of type `Add α` is *instance implicit*,
i.e. that it should be synthesized using typeclass resolution. This version of
`add` is the Lean analogue of the Haskell term `add :: Add a => a -> a -> a`.
Similarly, we can register instances by:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
class Add (α : Type) where
add : α → α → α
```

```lean
instance : Add [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
add := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)
```

```lean
instance : Add [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) where
add := [Int.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___add)
```

```lean
instance : Add [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel) where
add := [Float.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___add)
```

```lean
end Ex
```

Then for `n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` and `m : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, the term `Add.add n m` triggers typeclass resolution with
the goal of `Add [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, and typeclass resolution will synthesize the instance for `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` above.
We can now reimplement `double` using an instance implicit by:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
class Add (α : Type) where
add : α → α → α
instance : Add [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
add := [Nat.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___add)
instance : Add [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) where
add := [Int.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___add)
instance : Add [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel) where
add := [Float.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___add)
```

```lean
def double [Add α] (x : α) : α :=
Add.add x x
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @double
```

```lean
@double : {α : Type} → [Add α] → α → α
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) double 10
```

```lean
20
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) double (10 : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat))
```

```lean
20
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) double (7 : [Float](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Floating-Point-Numbers/#Float___ofModel))
```

```lean
14.000000
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) double (239.0 + 2)
```

```lean
482.000000
```

```lean

```

```lean
end Ex
```

In general, instances may depend on other instances in complicated ways. For example,
you can declare an instance stating that if `α` has addition, then `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α`
has addition:

```lean
instance [[Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) α] : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) ([Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) α) where
[add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) x y := [Array.zipWith](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___zipWith) (· + ·) x y
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [Add.add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) #[1, 2] #[3, 4]
```

```lean
#[4, 6]
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) #[1, 2] + #[3, 4]
```

```lean
#[4, 6]
```

```lean

```

Note that `(· + ·)` is notation for `fun x y => x + y` in Lean.

The example above demonstrates how type classes are used to overload notation.
Now, we explore another application. We often need an arbitrary element of a given type.
Recall that types may not have any elements in Lean.
It often happens that we would like a definition to return an arbitrary element in a “corner case.”
For example, we may like the expression `head xs` to be of type `α` when `xs` is of type `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`.
Similarly, many theorems hold under the additional assumption that a type is not empty.
For example, if `α` is a type, `∃ x : α, x = x` is true only if `α` is not empty.
The standard library defines a type class `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)` to enable type class inference to infer a
“default” element of an inhabited type.
Let us start with the first step of the program above, declaring an appropriate class:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
```

```lean
class Inhabited (α : Type u) where
default : α
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Inhabited.default
```

```lean
[@]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited)[Inhabited.default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) : {α : Type u_1} → [self : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) α] → α
```

```lean
end Ex
```

Note `Inhabited.default` doesn't have any explicit arguments.

An element of the class `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) α` is simply an expression of the form `[Inhabited.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) x`, for some element `x : α`.
The projection `[Inhabited.default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)` will allow us to “extract” such an element of `α` from an element of `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) α`.
Now we populate the class with some instances:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
class Inhabited (a : Type _) where
default : a
```

```lean
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := 0
```

```lean
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := ()
```

```lean
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) Prop where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([Inhabited.default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
0
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([Inhabited.default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
```

```lean
true
```

```lean
end Ex
```

You can use the command `export` to create the alias `[default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)` for `[Inhabited.default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)`.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
class Inhabited (a : Type _) where
default : a
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := 0
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) [Unit](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/The-Unit-Type/#Unit) where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := ()
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) Prop where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)
```

```lean
[export](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___export) Inhabited ([default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited))
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
0
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
```

```lean
true
```

```lean
end Ex
```

### 10.1. Chaining Instances {#tpil-chaining-instances}

If that were the extent of type class inference, it would not be all that impressive;
it would be simply a mechanism of storing a list of instances for the elaborator to find in a lookup table.
What makes type class inference powerful is that one can *chain* instances. That is,
an instance declaration can in turn depend on an implicit instance of a type class.
This causes class inference to chain through instances recursively, backtracking when necessary, in a Prolog-like search.

For example, the following definition shows that if two types `α` and `β` are inhabited, then so is their product:

```lean
instance [[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) α] [[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) β] : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) (α × β) where
[default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) := ([default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk), [default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk))
```

```lean

```

With this added to the earlier instance declarations, type class instance can infer, for example, a default element of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
class Inhabited (α : Type u) where
default : α
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
instance : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := 0
opaque default [[Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) α] : α :=
[Inhabited.default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited)
```

```lean
instance [[Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) α] [[Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) β] : [Inhabited]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) (α × β) where
[default]](#tpil-Ex___Inhabited) := (default, default)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (default : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false))
```

```lean
(0, true)
```

```lean
end Ex
```

Similarly, we can inhabit type function with suitable constant functions:

```lean
instance [[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) β] : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) (α → β) where
[default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) := fun _ => [default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)
```

```lean

```

As an exercise, try defining default instances for other types, such as `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)` and `[Sum](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Sum-Types/#Sum___inl)` types.

The Lean standard library contains the definition `[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)`. It has type `{α : Sort u} → [i : α] → α`,
and is useful for triggering the type class resolution procedure when the expected type is an instance.

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) ([inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
def foo : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) :=
[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)
```

```lean
theorem ex : foo.[default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) = ([default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk), [default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)) :=
rfl
```

```lean

```

You can use the command `#print` to inspect how simple `inferInstance` is.

```lean
#print inferInstance
```

```lean
@[reducible] def inferInstance.{u} : {α : Sort u} → [i : α] → α :=
fun {α} [i : α] => i
```


### 10.2. ToString {#tpil-ToString}

The polymorphic method `toString` has type `{α : Type u} → [ToString α] → α → [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)`. You implement the instance
for your own types and use chaining to convert complex values into strings. Lean comes with `ToString` instances
for most builtin types.

```lean
structure Person where
name : [String](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Strings/#String___ofByteArray)
age : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
instance : ToString [Person]](#tpil-Person) where
toString p := p.[name]](#tpil-Person) ++ "@" ++ toString p.[age]](#tpil-Person)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) toString { [name]](#tpil-Person) := "Leo", [age]](#tpil-Person) := 542 : [Person]](#tpil-Person) }
```

```lean
"Leo@542"
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) toString ({ [name]](#tpil-Person) := "Daniel", [age]](#tpil-Person) := 18 : [Person]](#tpil-Person) }, "hello")
```

```lean
"(Daniel@18, hello)"
```

```lean

```

### 10.3. Numerals {#tpil-numerals}

Numerals are polymorphic in Lean. You can use a numeral (e.g., `2`) to denote an element of any type that implements
the type class `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)`.

```lean
structure Rational where
num : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
den : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
inv : den ≠ 0
```

```lean
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) Rational n where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := { num := n, den := 1, inv := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 1 ≠ 0 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙 }
```

```lean
instance : ToString Rational where
toString r := s!"{r.num}/{r.den}"
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) (2 : Rational)
```

```lean
2/1
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) (2 : Rational)
```

```lean
2 : Rational
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) (2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

Lean elaborates the terms `(2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))` and `(2 : Rational)` as
`@[OfNat.ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) 2 (@instOfNatNat 2)` and
`@[OfNat.ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) Rational 2 (@instOfNatRational 2)` respectively.
We say the numerals `2` occurring in the elaborated terms are *raw* natural numbers.
You can input the raw natural number `2` using the macro `nat_lit 2`.

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) nat_lit 2
```

```lean
2 : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

Raw natural numbers are *not* polymorphic.

The `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` instance is parametric on the numeral. So, you can define instances for particular numerals.
The second argument is often a variable as in the example above, or a *raw* natural number.

```lean
class Monoid (α : Type u) where
unit : α
op : α → α → α
```

```lean
instance [s : [Monoid]](#tpil-Monoid) α] : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) α (nat_lit 1) where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := s.[unit]](#tpil-Monoid)
```

```lean
def getUnit [[Monoid]](#tpil-Monoid) α] : α :=
1
```

```lean

```

### 10.4. Output Parameters {#tpil-output-parameters}

By default, Lean only tries to synthesize an instance `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) T` when the term `T` is known and does not
contain missing parts. The following command produces the error
`typeclass instance problem is stuck, it is often due to metavariables` because the type has a missing part (i.e., the `_`).

```lean
/--
error: typeclass instance problem is stuck, it is often due to metavariables
Inhabited (Nat × ?m.2)
-/
[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd) (error) [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) ([inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) × _))
```

```lean

```

You can view the parameter of the type class `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)` as an *input* value for the type class synthesizer.
When a type class has multiple parameters, you can mark some of them as *output parameters*.
Lean will start type class synthesizer even when these parameters have missing parts.
In the following example, we use output parameters to define a *heterogeneous* polymorphic
multiplication.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
```

```lean
class HMul (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type w)) where
hMul : α → β → γ
```

```lean
[export](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___export) HMul (hMul)
```

```lean
instance : HMul [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
hMul := [Nat.mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___mul)
```

```lean
instance : HMul [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) ([Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
hMul a bs := bs.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___map) (fun b => hMul a b)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) hMul 4 3
```

```lean
12
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) hMul 4 #[2, 3, 4]
```

```lean
#[8, 12, 16]
```

```lean
end Ex
```

The parameters `α` and `β` are considered input parameters and `γ` an output one.
Given an application `hMul a b`, after the types of `a` and `b` are known, the type class
synthesizer is invoked, and the resulting type is obtained from the output parameter `γ`.
In the example above, we defined two instances. The first one is the homogeneous
multiplication for natural numbers. The second is the scalar multiplication for arrays.
Note that you chain instances and generalize the second instance.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
```

```lean
class HMul (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type w)) where
hMul : α → β → γ
```

```lean
[export](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___export) HMul (hMul)
```

```lean
instance : HMul [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) where
hMul := [Nat.mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___mul)
```

```lean
instance : HMul [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) where
hMul := [Int.mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___mul)
```

```lean
instance [HMul α β γ] : HMul α ([Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β) ([Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) γ) where
hMul a bs := bs.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___map) (fun b => hMul a b)
```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) hMul 4 3
```

```lean
12
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) hMul 4 #[2, 3, 4]
```

```lean
#[8, 12, 16]
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) hMul (-2) #[3, -1, 4]
```

```lean
#[-6, 2, -8]
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) hMul 2 #[#[2, 3], #[0, 4]]
```

```lean
#[#[4, 6], #[0, 8]]
```

```lean
end Ex
```

You can use our new scalar array multiplication instance on arrays of type `[Array](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Arrays/#Array___mk) β`
with a scalar of type `α` whenever you have an instance `HMul α β γ`.
In the last `#eval`, note that the instance was used twice on an array of arrays.

Output parameters are ignored during instance synthesis. Even when instance synthesis occurs in a
context in which the values of output parameters are already determined, their values are ignored.
Once an instance is found using its input parameters, Lean ensures that the already-known values of
the output parameters match those which were found.

Lean also features *semi-output parameters*, which have some features of input parameters
and some features of output parameters. Like input parameters, semi-output parameters are considered
when selecting instances. Like output parameters, they can be used to instantiate unknown values.
However, they do not do so uniquely. Instance synthesis with semi-output parameters can be more difficult
to predict, because the order in which instances are considered can determine which is selected, but it is
also more flexible.

### 10.5. Default Instances {#tpil-default-instances}

In the class `HMul`, the parameters `α` and `β` are treated as input values.
Thus, type class synthesis only starts after these two types are known. This may often
be too restrictive.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
```

```lean
class HMul (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type w)) where
hMul : α → β → γ
```

```lean
[export](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___export) HMul (hMul)
```

```lean
instance : HMul [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) where
hMul := [Int.mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___mul)
```

```lean
def xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) := [1, 2, 3]
```

```lean
/--
error: typeclass instance problem is stuck
HMul Int ?m.2 (?m.11 y)
Note: Lean will not try to resolve this typeclass instance problem because the second type argument to `HMul` is a metavariable. This argument must be fully determined before Lean will try to resolve the typeclass.
Hint: Adding type annotations and supplying implicit arguments to functions can give Lean more information for typeclass resolution. For example, if you have a variable `x` that you intend to be a `Nat`, but Lean reports it as having an unresolved type like `?m`, replacing `x` with `(x : Nat)` can get typeclass resolution un-stuck.
-/
[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd) (error) [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) fun y => xs.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) (fun x => hMul x y)
```

```lean
end Ex
```

The instance `HMul` is not synthesized by Lean because the type of `y` has not been provided.
However, it is natural to assume that the type of `y` and `x` should be the same in
this kind of situation. We can achieve exactly that using *default instances*.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
```

```lean
class HMul (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type w)) where
hMul : α → β → γ
```

```lean
[export](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___export) HMul (hMul)
```

```lean
@[[default_instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#Lean___Parser___Attr___default_instance)]
instance : HMul [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) where
hMul := [Int.mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___mul)
```

```lean
def xs : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) := [1, 2, 3]
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) fun y => xs.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) (fun x => hMul x y)
```

```lean
fun y => [List.map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) (fun x => hMul x y) xs : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat) → [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
```

```lean
end Ex
```

By tagging the instance above with the attribute `[default_instance]`, we are instructing Lean
to use this instance on pending type class synthesis problems.
The actual Lean implementation defines homogeneous and heterogeneous classes for arithmetical operators.
Moreover, `a + b`, `a * b`, `a - b`, `a / b`, and `a % b` are notations for the heterogeneous versions.
The instance `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n` is the default instance (with priority 100) for the `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk)` class. This is why the numeral
`2` has type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` when the expected type is not known. You can define default instances with higher
priority to override the builtin ones.

```lean
structure Rational where
num : [Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)
den : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
inv : den ≠ 0
```

```lean
@[[default_instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#Lean___Parser___Attr___default_instance) 200]
instance : [OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) Rational n where
[ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) := { num := n, den := 1, inv := byn:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)⊢ 1 ≠ 0 [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙 }
```

```lean
instance : ToString Rational where
toString r := s!"{r.num}/{r.den}"
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) 2
```

```lean
2 : Rational
```

```lean

```

Priorities are also useful to control the interaction between different default instances.
For example, suppose `xs` has type `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`. When elaborating `xs.[map](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___map) (fun x => 2 * x)`, we want the homogeneous instance for multiplication
to have higher priority than the default instance for `[OfNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) α 2`. This is particularly important when we have implemented only the instance
`[HMul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) α α α`, and did not implement `[HMul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) α α`.
Now, we reveal how the notation `a * b` is defined in Lean.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Ex
```

```lean
class OfNat (α : Type u) (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) where
ofNat : α
```

```lean
@[[default_instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#Lean___Parser___Attr___default_instance)]
instance (n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [OfNat]](#tpil-Ex___OfNat) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) n where
[ofNat]](#tpil-Ex___OfNat) := n
```

```lean
class HMul (α : Type u) (β : Type v) (γ : [outParam](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#outParam) (Type w)) where
hMul : α → β → γ
```

```lean
class Mul (α : Type u) where
mul : α → α → α
```

```lean
@[[default_instance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#Lean___Parser___Attr___default_instance) 10]
instance [[Mul]](#tpil-Ex___OfNat) α] : HMul α α α where
hMul a b := [Mul.mul]](#tpil-Ex___OfNat) a b
```

```lean
infixl:70 " * " => HMul.hMul
```

```lean
end Ex
```

The `Mul` class is convenient for types that only implement the homogeneous multiplication.

### 10.6. Local Instances {#tpil-local-instances}

Type classes are implemented using attributes in Lean. Thus, you can
use the `local` modifier to indicate that they only have effect until
the current `section` or `namespace` is closed, or until the end
of the current file.

```lean
structure Point where
x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
[section](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___section)
```

```lean
local instance : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) Point where
[add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) a b := { x := a.x + b.x, y := a.y + b.y }
```

```lean
def double (p : Point) :=
p + p
```

```lean
end -- instance `Add Point` is not active anymore
```

```lean
/--
error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
HAdd Point Point ?m.5
Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
-/
[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd) [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)
def triple (p : Point) :=
p + p + p
```

```lean

```

### 10.8. Decidable Propositions {#tpil-decidable-propositions}

Let us consider another example of a type class defined in the
standard library, namely the type class of `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)`
propositions. Roughly speaking, an element of `Prop` is said to be
decidable if we can decide whether it is true or false. The
distinction is only useful in constructive mathematics; classically,
every proposition is decidable. But if we use the classical principle,
say, to define a function by cases, that function will not be
computable. Algorithmically speaking, the `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` type class can
be used to infer a procedure that effectively determines whether or
not the proposition is true. As a result, the type class supports such
computational definitions when they are possible while at the same
time allowing a smooth transition to the use of classical definitions
and classical reasoning.

In the standard library, `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` is defined formally as follows:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
class inductive Decidable (p : Prop) where
| isFalse (h : ¬p) : Decidable p
| isTrue (h : p) : Decidable p
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

Logically speaking, having an element `t : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) p` is stronger
than having an element `t' : p ∨ ¬p`; it enables us to define values
of an arbitrary type depending on the truth value of `p`. For
example, for the expression `[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) p [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) a else b` to make sense, we
need to know that `p` is decidable. That expression is syntactic
sugar for `ite p a b`, where `ite` is defined as follows:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
def ite {α : Sort u}
(c : Prop) [h : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) c]
(t e : α) : α :=
h.casesOn (motive := fun _ => α) (fun _ => e) (fun _ => t)
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

The standard library also contains a variant of `ite` called
`dite`, the dependent if-then-else expression. It is defined as
follows:

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
def dite {α : Sort u}
(c : Prop) [h : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) c]
(t : c → α) (e : [Not](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not) c → α) : α :=
Decidable.casesOn (motive := fun _ => α) h e t
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

That is, in `dite c t e`, we can assume `hc : c` in the “then”
branch, and `hnc : ¬c` in the “else” branch. To make `dite` more
convenient to use, Lean allows us to write `[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) h : c [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) t [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termDepIfThenElse) e`
instead of `dite c (fun h : c => t h) (fun h : ¬c => e h)`.

Without classical logic, we cannot prove that every proposition is
decidable. But we can prove that *certain* propositions are
decidable. For example, we can prove the decidability of basic
operations like equality and comparisons on the natural numbers and
the integers. Moreover, decidability is preserved under propositional
connectives:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @instDecidableAnd
```

```lean
@instDecidableAnd : {p q : Prop} → [dp : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) p] → [dq : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) q] → [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)p [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) q[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @instDecidableOr
```

```lean
@instDecidableOr : {p q : Prop} → [dp : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) p] → [dq : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) q] → [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)p [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) q[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @instDecidableNot
```

```lean
@instDecidableNot : {p : Prop} → [dp : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) p] → [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)p
```

```lean

```

Thus we can carry out definitions by cases on decidable predicates on
the natural numbers:

```lean
def step (a b x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
[if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) x < a ∨ x > b [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 0 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 1
```

```lean
set_option pp.explicit true
```

```lean
#print step
```

```lean
def step : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
fun a b x =>
  @ite [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) ([Or](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) (@[LT.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) instLTNat x a) (@GT.gt [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) instLTNat x b))
    (@instDecidableOr (@[LT.lt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) instLTNat x a) (@GT.gt [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) instLTNat x b) ([Nat.decLt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___decLt) x a) ([Nat.decLt](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___decLt) b x))
    (@[OfNat.ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (nat_lit 0) (instOfNatNat (nat_lit 0))) (@[OfNat.ofNat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Numeric-Literals/#OfNat___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (nat_lit 1) (instOfNatNat (nat_lit 1)))
```

```lean

```

Turning on implicit arguments shows that the elaborator has inferred
the decidability of the proposition `x < a ∨ x > b`, simply by
applying appropriate instances.

With the classical axioms, we can prove that every proposition is
decidable. You can import the classical axioms and make the generic
instance of decidability available by opening the `Classical` namespace.

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Classical
```

```lean

```

Thereafter `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) p` has an instance for every `p`.
Thus all theorems in the library
that rely on decidability assumptions are freely available when you
want to reason classically. In [Axioms and Computation](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Axioms-and-Computation/#axioms-and-computation),
we will see that using the law of the
excluded middle to define functions can prevent them from being used
computationally. Thus, the standard library assigns a low priority to
the `propDecidable` instance.

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Hidden
```

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Classical
```

```lean
noncomputable scoped
instance (priority := [low](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#prioLow)) propDecidable (a : Prop) : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) a :=
choice <| [match](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match) em a [with](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Pattern-Matching/#Lean___Parser___Term___match)
| [Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) h => ⟨[isTrue](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) h⟩
| [Or.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) h => ⟨[isFalse](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) h⟩
```

```lean
end Hidden
```

This guarantees that Lean will favor other instances and fall back on
`propDecidable` only after other attempts to infer decidability have
failed.

The `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` type class also provides a bit of small-scale
automation for proving theorems. The standard library introduces the
tactic `decide` that uses the `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` instance to solve simple goals,
as well as a function `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___decide)` that uses a `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` instance to compute the
corresponding `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.

```lean
example : 10 < 5 ∨ 1 > 0 := by⊢ 10 [<](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#LT___mk) 5 [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) 1 > 0
[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
example : ¬([True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) ∧ [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)) := by⊢ [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)[(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro)
[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
example : 10 * 20 = 200 := by⊢ 10 [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) 20 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 200
[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
theorem ex : [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) ∧ 2 = 1 + 1 := by⊢ [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [∧](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#And___intro) 2 [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) 1 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) 1
[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#decide)All goals completed! 🐙
```

```lean
#print ex
```

