```lean
of_decide_eq_true (id ([Eq.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)))
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @of_decide_eq_true
```

```lean
@of_decide_eq_true : ∀ {p : Prop} [inst : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) p], [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___decide) p [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) → p
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @decide
```

```lean
[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___decide) : (p : Prop) → [h : [Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) p] → [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean

```

They work as follows. The expression `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___decide) p` tries to infer a
decision procedure for `p`, and, if it is successful, evaluates to
either `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` or `[false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`. In particular, if `p` is a true closed
expression, `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___decide) p` will reduce definitionally to the Boolean `[true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`.
On the assumption that `[decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___decide) p = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` holds, `of_decide_eq_true`
produces a proof of `p`. The tactic `decide` puts it all together to
prove a target `p`. By the previous observations,
`decide` will succeed any time the inferred decision procedure
for `p` has enough information to evaluate, definitionally, to the `[isTrue](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` case.

### 10.9. Managing Type Class Inference {#tpil-managing-type-class-inference}

If you are ever in a situation where you need to supply an expression
that Lean can infer by type class inference, you can ask Lean to carry
out the inference using `[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)`:

```lean
def foo : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := [inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)
```

```lean
def bar : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) ([Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) → [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := [inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @inferInstance
```

```lean
[@](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : {α : Sort u_1} → [i : α] → α
```

```lean

```

In fact, you can use Lean's `(t : T)` notation to specify the class whose instance you are looking for,
in a concise manner:

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) ([inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))
```

```lean
[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance) : [Add](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Add___mk) [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

Sometimes Lean can't find an instance because the class is buried
under a definition. For example, Lean cannot
find an instance of `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) (Set α)`. We can declare one
explicitly:

```lean
def Set (α : Type u) := α → Prop
```

```lean
/--
error: failed to synthesize instance of type class
Inhabited (Set α)
Hint: Type class instance resolution failures can be inspected with the `set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true` command.
-/
[#guard_msgs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd) [in](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___guardMsgsCmd)
example : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) (Set α) :=
[inferInstance](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#inferInstance)
```

```lean
instance : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) (Set α) :=
inferInstanceAs ([Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) (α → Prop))
```

```lean

```

At times, you may find that the type class inference fails to find an
expected instance, or, worse, falls into an infinite loop and times
out. To help debug in these situations, Lean enables you to request a
trace of the search:

```lean
set_option trace.Meta.synthInstance true
```

```lean

```

If you are using VS Code, you can read the results by hovering over
the relevant theorem or definition, or opening the messages window
with ``` `Ctrl``Shift``Enter` ```.

You can also limit the search using the following options:

```lean
set_option [synthInstance.maxHeartbeats](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Synthesis/#synthInstance___maxHeartbeats) 10000
```

```lean
set_option synthInstance.maxSize 400
```

```lean

```

Option `synthInstance.maxHeartbeats` specifies the maximum amount of
heartbeats per typeclass resolution problem. A heartbeat is the number of
(small) memory allocations (in thousands), 0 means there is no limit.
Option `synthInstance.maxSize` is the maximum number of instances used
to construct a solution in the type class instance synthesis procedure.

Remember also that in both the VS Code and Emacs editor modes, tab
completion works in `set_option`, to help you find suitable options.

As noted above, the type class instances in a given context represent
a Prolog-like program, which gives rise to a backtracking search. Both
the efficiency of the program and the solutions that are found can
depend on the order in which the system tries the instance. Instances
which are declared last are tried first. Moreover, if instances are
declared in other modules, the order in which they are tried depends
on the order in which namespaces are opened. Instances declared in
namespaces which are opened later are tried earlier.

You can change the order that type class instances are tried by
assigning them a *priority*. When an instance is declared, it is
assigned a default priority value. You can assign other priorities
when defining an instance. The following example illustrates how this
is done:

```lean
class Foo where
a : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
b : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean
instance (priority := [default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#prioDefault) + 1) i1 : Foo where
a := 1
[b]](#tpil-Foo-next) := 1
```

```lean
instance i2 : Foo where
a := 2
[b]](#tpil-Foo-next) := 2
```

```lean
example : Foo.a = 1 :=
[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)
```

```lean
instance (priority := [default](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#prioDefault) + 2) i3 : Foo where
a := 3
[b]](#tpil-Foo-next) := 3
```

```lean
example : Foo.a = 3 :=
rfl
```

```lean

```

### 10.10. Coercions using Type Classes {#tpil-coercions-using-type-classes}

The most basic type of coercion maps elements of one type to another. For example, a coercion from `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` to `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)` allows us to view any element `n : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` as an element of `[Int](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Integers/#Int___ofNat)`. But some coercions depend on parameters; for example, for any type `α`, we can view any element `as : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α` as an element of `Set α`, namely, the set of elements occurring in the list. The corresponding coercion is defined on the “family” of types `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α`, parameterized by `α`.

Lean allows us to declare three kinds of coercions:

- from a family of types to another family of types
- from a family of types to the class of sorts
- from a family of types to the class of function types

The first kind of coercion allows us to view any element of a member of the source family as an element of a corresponding member of the target family. The second kind of coercion allows us to view any element of a member of the source family as a type. The third kind of coercion allows us to view any element of the source family as a function. Let us consider each of these in turn.

In Lean, coercions are implemented on top of the type class resolution framework. We define a coercion from `α` to `β` by declaring an instance of `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) α β`. For example, we can define a coercion from `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)` to `Prop` as follows:

```lean
instance : [Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) Prop where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) b := b = [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)
```

```lean

```

This enables us to use boolean terms in `if`-`then`-`else` expressions:

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [true](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 5 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 3
```

```lean
5
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) [if](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) [false](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) [then](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 5 [else](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Terms/Conditionals/#termIfThenElse) 3
```

```lean
3
```

```lean

```

We can define a coercion from `[List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α` to `Set α` as follows:

```lean
def Set (α : Type u) := α → Prop
def Set.empty {α : Type u} : Set α := fun _ => [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
def Set.mem (a : α) (s : Set α) : Prop := s a
def Set.singleton (a : α) : Set α := fun x => x = a
def Set.union (a b : Set α) : Set α := fun x => a x ∨ b x
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation) "{ " a " }" => Set.singleton a
infix:55 " ∪ " => Set.union
```

```lean
def List.toSet : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Set α
| [] => [Set.empty](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Axioms-and-Computation/#Set___empty)
| a::as => {a} ∪ as.[toSet]](#tpil-List___toSet)
```

```lean
instance : [Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (Set α) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) a := a.[toSet]](#tpil-List___toSet)
```

```lean
def s : Set [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := {1}
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) s ∪ [2, 3]
```

```lean
s ∪ [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).[toSet]](#tpil-List___toSet) : Set [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

We can use the notation `↑` to force a coercion to be introduced in a particular place. It is also helpful to make our intent clear, and work around limitations of the coercion resolution system.

```lean
def Set (α : Type u) := α → Prop
def Set.empty {α : Type u} : Set α := fun _ => [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
def Set.mem (a : α) (s : Set α) : Prop := s a
def Set.singleton (a : α) : Set α := fun x => x = a
def Set.union (a b : Set α) : Set α := fun x => a x ∨ b x
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation) "{ " a " }" => Set.singleton a
infix:55 " ∪ " => Set.union
def List.toSet : [List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α → Set α
| [] => [Set.empty](https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Axioms-and-Computation/#Set___empty)
| a::as => {a} ∪ as.[toSet]](#tpil-List___toSet)
instance : [Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) ([List](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) α) (Set α) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) a := a.[toSet]](#tpil-List___toSet)
```

```lean
def s : Set [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) := {1}
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) let x := ↑[2, 3]; s ∪ x
```

```lean
let x := [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil).[toSet]](#tpil-List___toSet);
s ∪ x : Set [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

```lean

```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) let x := [2, 3]; s ∪ x
```

```lean
let x := [[](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil)2[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil) 3[]](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Linked-Lists/#List___nil);
s ∪ x.[toSet]](#tpil-List___toSet) : Set [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)
```

Lean also supports dependent coercions using the type class `[CoeDep](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#CoeDep___mk)`. For example, we cannot coerce arbitrary propositions to `[Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false)`, only the ones that implement the `[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse)` typeclass.

```lean
instance (p : Prop) [[Decidable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___isFalse) p] : [CoeDep](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#CoeDep___mk) Prop p Bool where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#CoeDep___mk) := [decide](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Decidable___decide) p
```

```lean

```

Lean will also chain (non-dependent) coercions as necessary. Actually, the type class `[CoeT](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-Between-Types/#CoeT___mk)` is the transitive closure of `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk)`.

Let us now consider the second kind of coercion. By the *class of sorts*, we mean the collection of universes `Type u`. A coercion of the second kind is of the form:

```
    c : (x1 : A1) → ... → (xn : An) → F x1 ... xn → Type u
```

where `F` is a family of types as above. This allows us to write `s : t` whenever `t` is of type `F a₁ ... aₙ`. In other words, the coercion allows us to view the elements of `F a₁ ... aₙ` as types. This is very useful when defining algebraic structures in which one component, the carrier of the structure, is a `Type`. For example, we can define a semigroup as follows:

```lean
structure Semigroup where
carrier : Type u
mul : carrier → carrier → carrier
mul_assoc (a b c : carrier) : mul (mul a b) c = mul a (mul b c)
```

```lean
instance (S : Semigroup) : [Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) S.carrier where
[mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) a b := S.mul a b
```

```lean

```

In other words, a semigroup consists of a type, `carrier`, and a multiplication, `mul`, with the property that the multiplication is associative. The `instance` command allows us to write `a * b` instead of `Semigroup.mul S a b` whenever we have `a b : S.carrier`; notice that Lean can infer the argument `S` from the types of `a` and `b`. The function `Semigroup.carrier` maps the class `Semigroup` to the sort `Type u`:

```lean
structure Semigroup where
carrier : Type u
mul : carrier → carrier → carrier
mul_assoc (a b c : carrier) : mul (mul a b) c = mul a (mul b c)
instance (S : Semigroup) : [Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) S.carrier where
[mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) a b := S.mul a b
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) Semigroup.carrier
```

```lean
Semigroup.carrier.{u} (self : Semigroup) : Type u
```

```lean

```

If we declare this function to be a coercion, then whenever we have a semigroup `S : Semigroup`, we can write `a : S` instead of `a : S.carrier`:

```lean
structure Semigroup where
carrier : Type u
mul : carrier → carrier → carrier
mul_assoc (a b c : carrier) : mul (mul a b) c = mul a (mul b c)
instance (S : Semigroup) : [Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) S.carrier where
[mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) a b := S.mul a b
```

```lean
instance : [CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) Semigroup (Type u) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) s := s.carrier
```

```lean
example (S : Semigroup) (a b c : S) : (a * b) * c = a * (b * c) :=
Semigroup.mul_assoc _ a b c
```

```lean

```

It is the coercion that makes it possible to write `(a b c : S)`. Note that, we define an instance of `[CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) Semigroup (Type u)` instead of `[Coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/#Coe___mk) Semigroup (Type u)`.

By the *class of function types*, we mean the collection of Pi types `(z : B) → C`. The third kind of coercion has the form:

```
    c : (x₁ : A₁) → ... → (xₙ : Aₙ) → (y : F x₁ ... xₙ) → (z : B) → C
```

where `F` is again a family of types and `B` and `C` can depend on `x₁, ..., xₙ, y`. This makes it possible to write `t s` whenever `t` is an element of `F a₁ ... aₙ`. In other words, the coercion enables us to view elements of `F a₁ ... aₙ` as functions. Continuing the example above, we can define the notion of a morphism between semigroups `S1` and `S2`. That is, a function from the carrier of `S1` to the carrier of `S2` (note the implicit coercion) that respects the multiplication. The projection `Morphism.mor` takes a morphism to the underlying function:

```lean
structure Semigroup where
carrier : Type u
mul : carrier → carrier → carrier
mul_assoc (a b c : carrier) : mul (mul a b) c = mul a (mul b c)
instance (S : Semigroup) : [Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) S.carrier where
[mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) a b := S.mul a b
instance : [CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) Semigroup (Type u) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) s := s.carrier
```

```lean
structure Morphism (S1 S2 : Semigroup) where
mor : S1 → S2
resp_mul : ∀ a b : S1, mor (a * b) = (mor a) * (mor b)
```

```lean
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) @Morphism.mor
```

```lean
[@]](#tpil-Morphism)[Morphism.mor]](#tpil-Morphism) : {S1 : Semigroup} → {S2 : Semigroup} → [Morphism]](#tpil-Morphism) S1 S2 → S1.carrier → S2.carrier
```

```lean

```

As a result, it is a prime candidate for the third type of coercion.

```lean
structure Semigroup where
carrier : Type u
mul : carrier → carrier → carrier
mul_assoc (a b c : carrier) : mul (mul a b) c = mul a (mul b c)
instance (S : Semigroup) : [Mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) S.carrier where
[mul](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Mul___mk) a b := S.mul a b
instance : [CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) Semigroup (Type u) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk) s := s.carrier
structure Morphism (S1 S2 : Semigroup) where
mor : S1 → S2
resp_mul : ∀ a b : S1, mor (a * b) = (mor a) * (mor b)
```

```lean
instance (S1 S2 : Semigroup) :
[CoeFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk) ([Morphism]](#tpil-Morphism) S1 S2) (fun _ => S1 → S2) where
[coe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk) m := m.[mor]](#tpil-Morphism)
```

```lean
theorem resp_mul {S1 S2 : Semigroup} (f : [Morphism]](#tpil-Morphism) S1 S2) (a b : S1)
: f (a * b) = f a * f b :=
f.[resp_mul]](#tpil-Morphism) a b
```

With the coercion in place, we can write `f (a * a * a)` instead of `f.[mor]](#tpil-Morphism) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk)a [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) a [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) a[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk)`. When the `[Morphism]](#tpil-Morphism)`, `f`, is used where a function is expected, Lean inserts the coercion. Similar to `[CoeSort](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Sorts/#CoeSort___mk)`, we have yet another class `[CoeFun](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Coercions/Coercing-to-Function-Types/#CoeFun___mk)` for this class of coercions. The parameter `γ` is used to specify the function type we are coercing to. This type may depend on the type we are coercing from.

## The Conversion Tactic Mode {#tpil-the-conversion-tactic-mode}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/The-Conversion-Tactic-Mode/

Inside a tactic block, one can use the keyword `conv` to enter
*conversion mode*. This mode allows to travel inside assumptions and
goals, even inside function abstractions and dependent arrows, to apply rewriting or
simplifying steps.

### 11.1. Basic navigation and rewriting {#tpil-basic-navigation-and-rewriting}

As a first example, let us prove example
`(a b c : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : a * (b * c) = a * (c * b)`
(examples in this file are somewhat artificial since
other tactics could finish them immediately). The naive
first attempt is to enter tactic mode and try `[rw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rw) [Nat.mul_comm]`. But this
transforms the goal into `b [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) c [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) a [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) a [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) [(](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk)c [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) b[)](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk)`, after commuting the
very first multiplication appearing in the term. There are several
ways to fix this issue, and one way is to use a more precise tool:
the conversion mode. The following code block shows the current target
after each line.

```lean

```

The above snippet shows three navigation commands:

- `[lhs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___lhs)` navigates to the left-hand side of a relation (equality, in this case).
  There is also a `rhs` to navigate to the right-hand side.
- `[congr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___congr)` creates as many targets as there are (nondependent and explicit) arguments to the current head function
  (here the head function is multiplication).
- `[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convRfl)` closes target using reflexivity.

Once arrived at the relevant target, we can use `[rw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#rw)` as in normal
tactic mode.

The second main reason to use conversion mode is to rewrite under
binders. Suppose we want to prove example
`(fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => 0 + x) = (fun x => x)`.
The naive first attempt is to enter tactic mode and try
`[rw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convRw__) [Nat.zero_add]`. But this fails with a frustrating

```
error: tactic 'rewrite' failed, did not find instance of the pattern
       in the target expression
  0 + ?n
⊢ (fun x => 0 + x) = fun x => x
```

The solution is:

```lean
example : (fun x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) => 0 + x) = (fun x => x) := by⊢ (fun x => 0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) fun x => x
conv =>| (fun x => 0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x) [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) fun x => x
[lhs](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___lhs)| fun x => 0 [+](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HAdd___mk) x
```


or just


`conv` can also rewrite a hypothesis `h` from the local context, using `conv at`` h`.

### 11.2. Pattern matching {#tpil-pattern-matching-conv}

Navigation using the above commands can be tedious. One can shortcut it using pattern matching as follows:

```lean

conv in b * c =>a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)| b [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) c
[rw](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convRw__) [Nat.mul_comm]a:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)b:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)c:[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)| c [*](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#HMul___mk) b
```

- `enter`` [1, x, 2, y]` iterate `[arg](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___arg)` and `[intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Targeted-Rewriting-with--conv/#Lean___Parser___Tactic___Conv___convIntro___)` with the given arguments.
- `done` fail if there are unsolved goals.
- `trace_state` display the current tactic state.
- `whnf` put term in weak head normal form.
- `tactic`` => <tactic sequence>` go back to regular tactic mode. This
  is useful for discharging goals not supported by `conv` mode, and
  applying custom congruence and extensionality lemmas.

## Axioms and Computation {#tpil-axioms-and-computation}

> 📄 Source: https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Axioms-and-Computation/

We have seen that the version of the Calculus of Constructions that
has been implemented in Lean includes dependent function types,
inductive types, and a hierarchy of universes that starts with an
[impredicative]](#tpil---tech-term-impredicative), [proof-irrelevant]](#tpil---tech-term-proof-irrelevance) `Prop` at the bottom. In this
chapter, we consider ways of extending the CIC with additional axioms
and rules. Extending a foundational system in such a way is often
convenient; it can make it possible to prove more theorems, as well as
make it easier to prove theorems that could have been proved
otherwise. But there can be negative consequences of adding additional
axioms, consequences which may go beyond concerns about their
correctness. In particular, the use of axioms bears on the
computational content of definitions and theorems, in ways we will
explore here.

Lean is designed to support both computational and classical
reasoning. Users that are so inclined can stick to a “computationally
pure” fragment, which guarantees that closed expressions in the system
evaluate to canonical normal forms. In particular, any closed
computationally pure expression of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)`, for example, will
reduce to a numeral.

Lean's standard library defines an additional axiom, propositional
extensionality, and a quotient construction which in turn implies the
principle of function extensionality. These extensions are used, for
example, to develop theories of sets and finite sets. We will see
below that using these theorems can block evaluation in Lean's kernel,
so that closed terms of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` no longer evaluate to numerals. But
Lean erases types and propositional information when compiling
definitions to executable code, and since
these axioms only add new propositions, they are compatible with that
computational interpretation. Even computationally inclined users may
wish to use the classical law of the excluded middle to reason about
computation. This also blocks evaluation in the kernel, but it is
compatible with compiled code.

The standard library also defines a choice principle that is entirely
antithetical to a computational interpretation, since it magically
produces “data” from a proposition asserting its existence. Its use is
essential to some classical constructions, and users can import it
when needed. But expressions that use this construction to produce
data do not have computational content, and in Lean we are required to
mark such definitions as `noncomputable` to flag that fact.

Using a clever trick (known as Diaconescu's theorem), one can use
propositional extensionality, function extensionality, and choice to
derive the law of the excluded middle. As noted above, however, use of
the law of the excluded middle is still compatible with
compilation, as are other classical principles, as
long as they are not used to manufacture data.

To summarize, then, on top of the underlying framework of universes,
dependent function types, and inductive types, the standard library
adds three additional components:

- the axiom of propositional extensionality
- a quotient construction, which implies function extensionality
- a choice principle, which produces data from an existential proposition.

The first two of these block normalization within Lean, but are
compatible with code generation, whereas the third is not amenable
to computational interpretation. We will spell out the details more
precisely below.

### 12.1. Historical and Philosophical Context {#tpil-historical-and-philosophical-context}

For most of its history, mathematics was essentially computational:
geometry dealt with constructions of geometric objects, algebra was
concerned with algorithmic solutions to systems of equations, and
analysis provided means to compute the future behavior of systems
evolving over time. From the proof of a theorem to the effect that
“for every `x`, there is a `y` such that ...”, it was generally
straightforward to extract an algorithm to compute such a `y` given
`x`.

In the nineteenth century, however, increases in the complexity of
mathematical arguments pushed mathematicians to develop new styles of
reasoning that suppress algorithmic information and invoke
descriptions of mathematical objects that abstract away the details of
how those objects are represented. The goal was to obtain a powerful
“conceptual” understanding without getting bogged down in
computational details, but this had the effect of admitting
mathematical theorems that are simply *false* on a direct
computational reading.

There is still fairly uniform agreement today that computation is
important to mathematics. But there are different views as to how best
to address computational concerns. From a *constructive* point of
view, it is a mistake to separate mathematics from its computational
roots; every meaningful mathematical theorem should have a direct
computational interpretation. From a *classical* point of view, it is
more fruitful to maintain a separation of concerns: we can use one
language and body of methods to write computer programs, while
maintaining the freedom to use nonconstructive theories and methods
to reason about them. Lean is designed to support both of these
approaches. Core parts of the library are developed constructively,
but the system also provides support for carrying out classical
mathematical reasoning.

Computationally, the purest part of dependent type theory avoids the
use of `Prop` entirely. Inductive types and dependent function types
can be viewed as data types, and terms of these types can be
“evaluated” by applying reduction rules until no more rules can be
applied. In principle, any closed term (that is, term with no free
variables) of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` should evaluate to a numeral, `[succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) (… ([succ](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) [zero](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero))…)`.

Introducing a proof-irrelevant `Prop` and marking theorems
irreducible represents a first step towards separation of
concerns. The intention is that elements of a type `p : Prop` should
play no role in computation, and so the particular construction of a
term `prf : p` is “irrelevant” in that sense. One can still define
computational objects that incorporate elements of type `Prop`; the
point is that these elements can help us reason about the effects of
the computation, but can be ignored when we extract “code” from the
term. Elements of type `Prop` are not entirely innocuous,
however. They include equations `s = t : α` for any type `α`, and
such equations can be used as casts, to type check terms. Below, we
will see examples of how such casts can block computation in the
system. However, computation is still possible under an evaluation
scheme that erases propositional content, ignores intermediate typing
constraints, and reduces terms until they reach a normal form. This is
precisely what Lean's virtual machine does.

Having adopted a proof-irrelevant `Prop`, one might consider it
legitimate to use, for example, the law of the excluded middle,
`p ∨ ¬p`, where `p` is any proposition. Of course, this, too, can block
computation according to the rules of CIC, but it does not prevent the generation
of executable code, as described above. It is only the choice
principles discussed in [the section on choice]](#tpil-choice) that completely erase the
distinction between the proof-irrelevant and data-relevant parts of
the theory.

### 12.2. Propositional Extensionality {#tpil-propositional-extensionality}

Propositional extensionality is the following axiom:

```lean
[axiom](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Axioms/#Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) propext {a b : Prop} : (a ↔ b) → a = b
```

It asserts that when two propositions imply one another, they are
actually equal. This is consistent with set-theoretic interpretations
in which any element `a : Prop` is either empty or the singleton set
`\{\ast\}`, for some distinguished element `\ast`. The axiom has the
effect that equivalent propositions can be substituted for one another
in any context:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) (a b c d e : Prop)
```

```lean
theorem thm₁ (h : a ↔ b) : (c ∧ a ∧ d → e) ↔ (c ∧ b ∧ d → e) :=
[propext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/#propext) h ▸ Iff.refl _
```

```lean
theorem thm₂ (p : Prop → Prop) (h : a ↔ b) (h₁ : p a) : p b :=
[propext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/#propext) h ▸ h₁
```

```lean

```

### 12.3. Function Extensionality {#tpil-function-extensionality}

Similar to propositional extensionality, function extensionality
asserts that any two functions of type `(x : α) → β x` that agree on
all their inputs are equal:

```lean
[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#funext).{u, v}
{α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v}
{f g : (x : α) → β x}
(h : ∀ (x : α), f x = g x) :
f = g
```

From a classical, set-theoretic perspective, this is exactly what it
means for two functions to be equal. This is known as an “extensional”
view of functions. From a constructive perspective, however, it is
sometimes more natural to think of functions as algorithms, or
computer programs, that are presented in some explicit way. It is
certainly the case that two computer programs can compute the same
answer for every input despite the fact that they are syntactically
quite different. In much the same way, you might want to maintain a
view of functions that does not force you to identify two functions
that have the same input / output behavior. This is known as an
“intensional” view of functions.

In fact, function extensionality follows from the existence of
quotients, which we describe in the next section. In the Lean standard
library, therefore, `[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#funext)` is thus
[proved from the quotient construction](https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/master/src/Init/Core.lean).

Suppose that for `α : Type u` we define the `Set ``α``:= α → Prop` to
denote the type of subsets of `α`, essentially identifying subsets
with predicates. By combining `[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#funext)` and `[propext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/#propext)`, we obtain an
extensional theory of such sets:

```lean
def Set (α : Type u) := α → Prop
```

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Set
```

```lean
def mem (x : α) (a : Set α) := a x
```

```lean
infix:50 (priority := [high](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#prioHigh)) "∈" => [mem]](#tpil-Set-next)
```

```lean
theorem setext {a b : Set α} (h : ∀ x, x ∈ a ↔ x ∈ b) : a = b :=
[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#funext) (fun x => [propext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/#propext) (h x))
```

```lean
end Set
```

```lean

```

We can then proceed to define the empty set and set intersection, for
example, and prove set identities:

```lean
def Set (α : Type u) := α → Prop
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Set
def mem (x : α) (a : Set α) := a x
infix:50 (priority := [high](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#prioHigh)) "∈" => [mem]](#tpil-Set-next)
theorem setext {a b : Set α} (h : ∀ x, x ∈ a ↔ x ∈ b) : a = b :=
[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#funext) (fun x => [propext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/#propext) (h x))
```

```lean
def empty : Set α := fun _ => [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)
```

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation) (priority := [high](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Instance-Declarations/#prioHigh)) "∅" => [empty]](#tpil-Set___empty)
```

```lean
def inter (a b : Set α) : Set α :=
fun x => x ∈ a ∧ x ∈ b
```

```lean
infix:70 " ∩ " => [inter]](#tpil-Set___empty)
```

```lean
theorem inter_self (a : Set α) : a ∩ a = a :=
[setext]](#tpil-Set-next) fun x => [Iff.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)
(fun ⟨h, _⟩ => h)
(fun h => ⟨h, h⟩)
```

```lean
theorem inter_empty (a : Set α) : a ∩ ∅ = ∅ :=
[setext]](#tpil-Set-next) fun _ => [Iff.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)
(fun ⟨_, h⟩ => h)
(fun h => [False.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False___elim) h)
```

```lean
theorem empty_inter (a : Set α) : ∅ ∩ a = ∅ :=
[setext]](#tpil-Set-next) fun _ => [Iff.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)
(fun ⟨h, _⟩ => h)
(fun h => [False.elim](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False___elim) h)
```

```lean
theorem inter.comm (a b : Set α) : a ∩ b = b ∩ a :=
[setext]](#tpil-Set-next) fun _ => [Iff.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro)
(fun ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ => ⟨h₂, h₁⟩)
(fun ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ => ⟨h₂, h₁⟩)
```

```lean
end Set
```

The following is an example of how function extensionality blocks
computation inside the Lean kernel:

```lean
def f (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := x
```

```lean
def g (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) := 0 + x
```

```lean
theorem f_eq_g : f = g :=
[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#funext) fun x => (Nat.zero_add x).[symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___symm)
```

```lean
def val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
Eq.recOn (motive := fun _ _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) [f_eq_g]](#tpil-f-next-next-next-next-next-next-next-next-next-next) 0
```

```lean
-- does not reduce to 0
[#reduce](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___reduceCmd) val
```

```lean
[f_eq_g]](#tpil-f-next-next-next-next-next-next-next-next-next-next) ▸ 0
```

```lean

```

```lean
-- evaluates to 0
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) val
```

```lean
0
```

```lean

```

First, we show that the two functions `f` and `g` are equal using
function extensionality, and then we cast `0` of type `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` by
replacing `f` by `g` in the type. Of course, the cast is
vacuous, because `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` does not depend on `f`. But that is enough
to do the damage: under the computational rules of the system, we now
have a closed term of `[Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)` that does not reduce to a numeral. In this
case, we may be tempted to reduce the expression to `0`. But in
nontrivial examples, eliminating cast changes the type of the term,
which might make an ambient expression type incorrect. The virtual
machine, however, has no trouble evaluating the expression to
`0`. Here is a similarly contrived example that shows how
`[propext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/#propext)` can get in the way:

```lean
theorem tteq : ([True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) ∧ [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)) = [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) :=
[propext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/#propext) ([Iff.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) (fun ⟨h, _⟩ => h) (fun h => ⟨h, h⟩))
```

```lean
def val : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero) :=
Eq.recOn (motive := fun _ _ => [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) [tteq]](#tpil-tteq) 0
```

```lean
-- does not reduce to 0
[#reduce](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___reduceCmd) val
```

```lean
[tteq]](#tpil-tteq) ▸ 0
```

```lean

```

```lean
-- evaluates to 0
[#eval](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___eval) val
```

```lean
0
```

```lean

```

Current research programs, including work on *observational type
theory* and *cubical type theory*, aim to extend type theory in ways
that permit reductions for casts involving function extensionality,
quotients, and more. But the solutions are not so clear-cut, and the
rules of Lean's underlying calculus do not sanction such reductions.

In a sense, however, a cast does not change the meaning of an
expression. Rather, it is a mechanism to reason about the expression's
type. Given an appropriate semantics, it then makes sense to reduce
terms in ways that preserve their meaning, ignoring the intermediate
bookkeeping needed to make the reductions type-correct. In that case,
adding new axioms in `Prop` does not matter; by [proof irrelevance]](#tpil---tech-term-proof-irrelevance),
an expression in `Prop` carries no information, and can be safely
ignored by the reduction procedures.

### 12.4. Quotients {#tpil-quotients}

Let `α` be any type, and let `r` be an equivalence relation on
`α`. It is mathematically common to form the “quotient” `α / r`,
that is, the type of elements of `α` “modulo” `r`. Set
theoretically, one can view `α / r` as the set of equivalence
classes of `α` modulo `r`. If `f : α → β` is any function that
respects the equivalence relation in the sense that for every
`x y : α`, `r x y` implies `f x = f y`, then `f` “lifts” to a function
`f' : α / r → β` defined on each equivalence class `⟦x⟧` by
`f' ⟦x⟧ = f x`. Lean's standard library extends the Calculus of
Constructions with additional constants that perform exactly these
constructions, and installs this last equation as a definitional
reduction rule.

In its most basic form, the quotient construction does not even
require `r` to be an equivalence relation. The following constants
are built into Lean:

```lean
[universe](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Universes/#Lean___Parser___Command___universe-next) u v
```

```lean
[axiom](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Axioms/#Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Quot : {α : Sort u} → (α → α → Prop) → Sort u
```

```lean
[axiom](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Axioms/#Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Quot.mk : {α : Sort u} → (r : α → α → Prop) → α → [Quot]](#tpil-Hidden___Quot) r
```

```lean
[axiom](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Axioms/#Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Quot.ind :
∀ {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {β : [Quot]](#tpil-Hidden___Quot) r → Prop},
(∀ a, β ([Quot.mk]](#tpil-Hidden___Quot) r a)) → (q : [Quot]](#tpil-Hidden___Quot) r) → β q
```

```lean
[axiom](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Axioms/#Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Quot.lift :
{α : Sort u} → {r : α → α → Prop} → {β : Sort u} → (f : α → β)
→ (∀ a b, r a b → f a = f b) → [Quot]](#tpil-Hidden___Quot) r → β
```

The first one forms a type `[Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) r` given a type `α` by any binary
relation `r` on `α`. The second maps `α` to `Quot α`, so that
if `r : α → α → Prop` and `a : α`, then `[Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) r a` is an
element of `[Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) r`. The third principle, `[Quot.ind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___ind)`, says that
every element of `[Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) r a` is of this form. As for
`[Quot.lift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___lift)`, given a function `f : α → β`, if `h` is a proof
that `f` respects the relation `r`, then `[Quot.lift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___lift) f h` is the
corresponding function on `[Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) r`. The idea is that for each
element `a` in `α`, the function `[Quot.lift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___lift) f h` maps
`[Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) r a` (the `r`-class containing `a`) to `f a`, wherein `h`
shows that this function is well defined. In fact, the computation
principle is declared as a reduction rule, as the proof below makes
clear.

```lean
def mod7Rel (x y : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : Prop :=
x % 7 = y % 7
```

```lean
-- the quotient type
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) ([Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) [mod7Rel]](#tpil-mod7Rel) : Type)
```

```lean
[Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) [mod7Rel]](#tpil-mod7Rel) : Type
```

```lean

```

```lean
-- the class of numbers equivalent to 4
[#check](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Interacting-with-Lean/#Lean___Parser___Command___check) ([Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) [mod7Rel]](#tpil-mod7Rel) 4 : [Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) [mod7Rel]](#tpil-mod7Rel))
```

```lean
[Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) [mod7Rel]](#tpil-mod7Rel) 4 : [Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) [mod7Rel]](#tpil-mod7Rel)
```

```lean

```

```lean
def f (x : [Nat](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Natural-Numbers/#Nat___zero)) : [Bool](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Booleans/#Bool___false) :=
x % 7 = 0
```

```lean

```

The four constants, `[Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot)`, `[Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk)`, `[Quot.ind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___ind)`, and
`[Quot.lift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___lift)` in and of themselves are not very strong. You can check
that the `[Quot.ind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___ind)` is satisfied if we take `[Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) r` to be simply
`α`, and take `[Quot.lift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___lift)` to be the identity function (ignoring
`h`). For that reason, these four constants are not viewed as
additional axioms.

They are, like inductively defined types and the associated
constructors and recursors, viewed as part of the logical framework.

What makes the `[Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot)` construction into a bona fide quotient is the
following additional axiom:

```lean
[axiom](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Axioms/#Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) Quot.sound :
∀ {α : Type u} {r : α → α → Prop} {a b : α},
r a b → [Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) r a = [Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) r b
```

```lean

```

This is the axiom that asserts that any two elements of `α` that are
related by `r` become identified in the quotient. If a theorem or
definition makes use of `Quot.sound`, it will show up in the
`#print axioms` command.

Of course, the quotient construction is most commonly used in
situations when `r` is an equivalence relation. Given `r` as
above, if we define `r'` according to the rule `r' a b` iff
`[Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) r a = [Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) r b`, then it's clear that `r'` is an
equivalence relation. Indeed, `r'` is the *kernel* of the function
`fun a => [Quot.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) r a`. The axiom `[Quot.sound](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___sound)` says that `r a b`
implies `r' a b`. Using `[Quot.lift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___lift)` and `[Quot.ind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___ind)`, we can show
that `r'` is the smallest equivalence relation containing `r`, in
the sense that if `r''` is any equivalence relation containing
`r`, then `r' a b` implies `r'' a b`. In particular, if `r`
was an equivalence relation to start with, then for all `a` and
`b` we have `r a b` iff `r' a b`.

To support this common use case, the standard library defines the
notion of a *setoid*, which is simply a type with an associated
equivalence relation:

```lean
class Setoid (α : Sort u) where
r : α → α → Prop
iseqv : [Equivalence](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Equivalence___mk) r
```

```lean
instance {α : Sort u} [[Setoid]](#tpil-Hidden___Setoid) α] : [HasEquiv](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#HasEquiv___mk) α :=
⟨[Setoid.r]](#tpil-Hidden___Setoid)⟩
```

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) Setoid
```

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) {α : Sort u} [[Setoid]](#tpil-Hidden___Setoid) α]
```

```lean
theorem refl (a : α) : a ≈ a :=
[iseqv]](#tpil-Hidden___Setoid).[refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Equivalence___mk) a
```

```lean
theorem symm {a b : α} (hab : a ≈ b) : b ≈ a :=
[iseqv]](#tpil-Hidden___Setoid).[symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Equivalence___mk) hab
```

```lean
theorem trans {a b c : α} (hab : a ≈ b) (hbc : b ≈ c) : a ≈ c :=
[iseqv]](#tpil-Hidden___Setoid).[trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Equivalence___mk) hab hbc
```

```lean
end Setoid
```

Given a type `α`, a relation `r`
on `α`, and a proof `iseqv`
that `r` is an equivalence relation, we can define an
instance of the `Setoid` class.

```lean
def Quotient {α : Sort u} (s : [Setoid](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Setoid___mk) α) :=
@[Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) α Setoid.r
```

The constants `[Quotient.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___mk)`, `[Quotient.ind](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___ind)`, `[Quotient.lift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___lift)`,
and `[Quotient.sound](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___sound)` are nothing more than the specializations of
the corresponding elements of `[Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot)`. The fact that type class
inference can find the setoid associated to a type `α` brings a
number of benefits. First, we can use the notation `a ≈ b` (entered
with `\approx`) for `[Setoid.r](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Setoid___mk) a b`, where the instance of
`[Setoid](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Setoid___mk)` is implicit in the notation `[Setoid.r](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Setoid___mk)`. We can use the
generic theorems `[Setoid.refl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Setoid___refl)`, `[Setoid.symm](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Setoid___symm)`, `[Setoid.trans](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Setoid___trans)` to
reason about the relation. Specifically with quotients we can use the
theorem `[Quotient.exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___exact)`:

```lean
[Quotient.exact](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___exact) {α : Sort u} {s : [Setoid](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Setoid___mk) α} {a b : α} :
[Quotient.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___mk) s a = [Quotient.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___mk) s b →
a ≈ b
```

Together with `[Quotient.sound](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___sound)`, this implies that the elements of
the quotient correspond exactly to the equivalence classes of elements
in `α`.

Recall that in the standard library, `α × β` represents the
Cartesian product of the types `α` and `β`. To illustrate the use
of quotients, let us define the type of *unordered* pairs of elements
of a type `α` as a quotient of the type `α × α`. First, we define
the relevant equivalence relation:

```lean
private def eqv (p₁ p₂ : α × α) : Prop :=
(p₁.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = p₂.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) ∧ p₁.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = p₂.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)) ∨ (p₁.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = p₂.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) ∧ p₁.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = p₂.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
```

```lean
infix:50 " ~ " => eqv
```

```lean

```

The next step is to prove that `eqv` is in fact an equivalence
relation, which is to say, it is reflexive, symmetric and
transitive. We can prove these three facts in a convenient and
readable way by using dependent pattern matching to perform
case-analysis and break the hypotheses into pieces that are then
reassembled to produce the conclusion.

```lean
private def eqv (p₁ p₂ : α × α) : Prop :=
(p₁.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = p₂.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) ∧ p₁.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = p₂.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk)) ∨ (p₁.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = p₂.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) ∧ p₁.[2](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk) = p₂.[1](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Tuples/#Prod___mk))
infix:50 " ~ " => [eqv]](#tpil-_private___0___eqv)
```

```lean
private theorem eqv.refl (p : α × α) : p ~ p :=
[Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) ⟨[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next), [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)⟩
```

```lean
def UProd (α : Type u) : Type u :=
[Quotient](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient) ([uprodSetoid]](#tpil-uprodSetoid) α)
```

```lean
[namespace](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___namespace) UProd
```

```lean
def mk {α : Type} (a₁ a₂ : α) : [UProd]](#tpil-uprodSetoid) α :=
[Quotient.mk'](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___mk___) (a₁, a₂)
```

```lean
[notation](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Notations-and-Macros/Notations/#Lean___Parser___Command___notation) "{ " a₁ ", " a₂ " }" => [mk]](#tpil-uprodSetoid) a₁ a₂
```

```lean
end UProd
```

```lean

```

Notice that we locally define the notation `{a₁, a₂}` for unordered
pairs as `[Quotient.mk'](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___mk___) (a₁, a₂)`. This is useful for illustrative
purposes, but it is not a good idea in general, since the notation
will shadow other uses of curly brackets, such as for records and
sets.

We can easily prove that `{a₁, a₂} = {a₂, a₁}` using `[Quot.sound](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___sound)`,
since we have `(a₁, a₂) ~ (a₂, a₁)`.

```lean
theorem mk_eq_mk (a₁ a₂ : α) : {a₁, a₂} = {a₂, a₁} :=
[Quot.sound](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___sound) ([Or.inr](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) ⟨[rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next), [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)⟩)
```

```lean
end UProd
```

To complete the example, given `a : α` and `u : [UProd]](#tpil-uprodSetoid) α`, we
define the proposition `a`` ∈ ``u` which should hold if `a` is one of
the elements of the unordered pair `u`. First, we define a similar
proposition `mem_fn``a``u` on (ordered) pairs; then we show that
`mem_fn` respects the equivalence relation `[eqv]](#tpil-_private___0___eqv)` with the lemma
`mem_respects`. This is an idiom that is used extensively in the
Lean standard library.

For convenience, the standard library also defines `[Quotient.lift₂](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quotient___lift___)`
for lifting binary functions, and `Quotient.ind₂` for induction on
two variables.

We close this section with some hints as to why the quotient
construction implies function extensionality. It is not hard to show
that extensional equality on the `(x : α) → β x` is an equivalence
relation, and so we can consider the type `extfun α β` of functions
“up to equivalence.” Of course, application respects that equivalence
in the sense that if `f₁` is equivalent to `f₂`, then `f₁ a` is
equal to `f₂ a`. Thus application gives rise to a function
`extfun_app : extfun α β → (x : α) → β x`. But for every `f`,
`extfun_app ([.mk](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___mk) _ f)` is definitionally equal to `fun x => f x`, which is
in turn definitionally equal to `f`. So, when `f₁` and `f₂` are
extensionally equal, we have the following chain of equalities:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) {α : Sort u} {β : α → Sort v}
def extfun (α : Sort u) (β : α → Sort v) := [Quot](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot) (fun (f g : (x : α) → β x) => ∀ x, f x = g x)
def extfun_app {α β} (f : extfun α β) (x : α) : β x :=
[Quot.lift](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/#Quot___lift) (· x) (byα✝:Sort uβ✝:α✝ → Sort vα:Sort ?u.9β:α → Sort ?u.8f:extfun α βx:α⊢ ∀ (a b : (x : α) → β x), (∀ (x : α), a x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b x) → a x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b x [intros](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#intros)α✝:Sort uβ✝:α✝ → Sort vα:Sort ?u.9β:α → Sort ?u.8f:extfun α βx:αa✝¹:(x : α) → β xb✝:(x : α) → β xa✝:∀ (x : α), a✝¹ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b✝ x⊢ a✝¹ x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) b✝ x; [simp](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/Tactic-Reference/#simp) [*]All goals completed! 🐙) f
```

### 12.5. Choice {#tpil-choice}

To state the final axiom defined in the standard library, we need the
`Nonempty` type, which is defined as follows:

```lean
class inductive Nonempty (α : Sort u) : Prop where
| intro (val : α) : [Nonempty]](#tpil-Hidden___Nonempty) α
```

Because `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α` has type `Prop` and its constructor contains data, it can only eliminate to `Prop`.
In fact, `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α` is equivalent to `∃ x : α, [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`:

```lean
example (α : Type u) : [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α ↔ ∃ x : α, [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) :=
[Iff.intro](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Iff___intro) (fun ⟨a⟩ => ⟨a, trivial⟩) (fun ⟨a, h⟩ => ⟨a⟩)
```

```lean

```

Our axiom of choice is now expressed simply as follows:

```lean
[axiom](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Axioms/#Lean___Parser___Command___axiom-next) choice {α : Sort u} : [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α → α
```

Given only the assertion `h` that `α` is nonempty, `choice h`
magically produces an element of `α`. Of course, this blocks any
meaningful computation: by the interpretation of `Prop`, `h`
contains no information at all as to how to find such an element.

This is found in the `Classical` namespace, so the full name of the
theorem is `Classical.choice`. The choice principle is equivalent to
the principle of **indefinite description**, which can be expressed with
subtypes as follows:

```lean
noncomputable def indefiniteDescription {α : Sort u}
(p : α → Prop) (h : ∃ x, p x) : {x // p x} :=
[choice]](#tpil-Hidden___choice) <| let ⟨x, px⟩ := h; ⟨⟨x, px⟩⟩
```

Because it depends on `choice`, Lean cannot generate executable code for
`indefiniteDescription`, and so requires us to mark the definition
as `noncomputable`. Also in the `Classical` namespace, the
function `choose` and the property `choose_spec` decompose the two
parts of the output of `indefiniteDescription`:

```lean
[variable](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___variable) {α : Sort u} {p : α → Prop}
```

```lean
noncomputable def choose (h : ∃ x, p x) : α :=
(indefiniteDescription p h).[val](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Types/Subtypes/#Subtype___mk)
```

```lean
theorem choose_spec (h : ∃ x, p x) : p ([choose]](#tpil-Hidden___choose) h) :=
(indefiniteDescription p h).property
```

The `choice` principle also erases the distinction between the
property of being `[Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro)` and the more constructive property of
being `[Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk)`:

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Classical
```

```lean
noncomputable def inhabited_of_nonempty (h : [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α) : [Inhabited](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Inhabited___mk) α :=
choice (let ⟨a⟩ := h; ⟨⟨a⟩⟩)
```

```lean

```

In the next section, we will see that `[propext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/#propext)`, `[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#funext)`, and
`choice`, taken together, imply the law of the excluded middle and
the decidability of all propositions. Using those, one can strengthen
the principle of indefinite description as follows:

```lean
strongIndefiniteDescription {α : Sort u} (p : α → Prop)
(h : [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α) :
{x // (∃ (y : α), p y) → p x}
```

Assuming the ambient type `α` is nonempty,
`strongIndefiniteDescription`` ``p` produces an element of `α`
satisfying `p` if there is one. The data component of this
definition is conventionally known as **Hilbert's epsilon function**:

```lean
epsilon {α : Sort u} [h : [Nonempty](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Type-Classes/Basic-Classes/#Nonempty___intro) α] (p : α → Prop) : α
```

```lean
epsilon_spec {α : Sort u} {p : α → Prop}
(hex : ∃ (y : α), p y) :
p (@epsilon _ hex.nonempty p)
```

### 12.6. The Law of the Excluded Middle {#tpil-the-law-of-the-excluded-middle}

The law of the excluded middle is the following:

```lean
Classical.em : ∀ (p : Prop), p ∨ ¬p
```

[Diaconescu's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diaconescu%27s_theorem) states
that the axiom of choice is sufficient to derive the law of excluded
middle. More precisely, it shows that the law of the excluded middle
follows from `Classical.choice`, `[propext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/#propext)`, and `[funext](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/The-Type-System/Functions/#funext)`. We
sketch the proof that is found in the standard library.

First, we import the necessary axioms, and define two predicates `U` and `V`:

```lean
[open](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Namespaces-and-Sections/#Lean___Parser___Command___open) Classical
theorem em (p : Prop) : p ∨ ¬p := byp:Prop⊢ p [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)p
[let](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#let) U (x : Prop) : Prop := x = [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) ∨ pp:PropU:Prop → Prop := fun x => x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) p⊢ p [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)p

[have](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#have) exU : ∃ x, U x := ⟨[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro), [Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)⟩p:PropU:Prop → Prop := fun x => x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) pV:Prop → Prop := fun x => x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) pexU:[∃](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) x[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) U x⊢ p [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)p
[have](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Tactic-Proofs/The-Tactic-Language/#have) exV : ∃ x, V x := ⟨[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False), [Or.inl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [rfl](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#rfl-next)⟩p:PropU:Prop → Prop := fun x => x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro) [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) pV:Prop → Prop := fun x => x [=](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Propositional-Equality/#Eq___refl) [False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False) [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) pexU:[∃](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) x[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) U xexV:[∃](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) x[,](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Quantifiers/#Exists___intro) V x⊢ p [∨](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Or___inl) [¬](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Logical-Connectives/#Not)p
```

If `p` is true, then every element of `Prop` is in both `U` and `V`.
If `p` is false, then `U` is the singleton `[True](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#True___intro)`, and `V` is the singleton `[False](https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.33.0/Basic-Propositions/Truth/#False)`.

Next, we use `choose` to choose an element from each of `U` and `V`:

definition of `u` and `v`, this implies that they are equal as well.
